en: Preface to the *Biographies of the Jewel-like Monks of the Southern Song, Yuan, and Ming Dynasties*:

Where there is a transmission of the Teaching, there must necessarily be a transmitter of that Teaching. Where there is a transmitter of the Teaching, there must especially be a transmission of the texts.
For the Teaching is that by which the Way is practiced; the person is that by which the Teaching is promoted; and the text is that by which the former sages [transmitted it].
[Blank]. [Blank]... is that by which one reflects. Therefore, the Great Way is vast and boundless; [blank].
Only one or two people in a thousand may attain it, serving as its eyes and ears. It is like a poor person [blank]... a guest wearing a pearl.
They too will ultimately remain in a state of delusion. If one truly attains [the Way], they shall then undertake the Great Matter; yet this illusory body is easily exhausted.
Practical realization has long since faded from view. Like the udumbara flower, which appears but once in a thousand years, how could it possibly reappear hereafter?

For this reason, Confucian scholars have composed biographies, records, treatises, and encomia to bequeath them to posterity. When the writings are transmitted, the person is transmitted; when the person is transmitted, their teaching begins to be transmitted.

Although it is said that the Great Compassionate One’s entry into Zhendan (China) constituted a "separate transmission outside the teachings," [it was nevertheless through these means that his legacy endured].
Although it is said that "no reliance is placed on words and letters," the successive patriarchs have transmitted this legacy, and the various schools have arisen.
The karmic conditions for entering the Way, the proclamations made upon ascending the dais, and the evidence of attaining *nirvāṇa* remain as if witnessed with one’s own eyes even to this day.
This single volume, *Juefan Sengbao*, together with the *Dachuan Huiyuan*, serves as a mirror for the Buddhist forest. From this point forward...
For several hundred years since its decline, his voice and traces have gradually become distant.

The Great Master Rongzhuan of Huanjin was the grandson of Venerable Miyun of Tiantong and the successor of Chan Master Hongjue. His resolve was firm and resolute, and his functional mastery was vast and pervasive.

He erected the banner of luminous fearlessness; his purple bamboo sandals were always filled with followers, and the staff of auspicious clouds was raised once more. At that time, I was avoiding [the world]...

I traveled to Luancheng and went specifically to visit the Elder in the mountains. Morning and evening, I sought his instruction and benefit; he was fully endowed with the compassionate heart of a patriarch.

Although my own vision and wisdom as a subordinate official still leave much unresolved within the ocean of the Dharma, the deceased Master’s [Zhenxie Qingliao’s] approach regarding the mountain valleys constitutes a truly supreme manifestation.

Consequently, I was able to peruse the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Southern Song, Yuan, and Ming Dynasties* that you have compiled; its purport is profound and its meaning lucid, and the phrasing—

This comprehensive treatise covers [the subject]. Formerly, Fan Weizong remarked that Sima Qian’s prose was straightforward while his facts were verified, whereas Fan Ye’s prose was abundant while his facts were detailed;
taken together, they seem to complement one another. After Master Hong came Master Rong, who was likely just as Mengjian followed Zichang.
The practice of using rattan staffs and white whisks in the degenerate age has reached its extreme. The inscriptions on their stupas and accounts of their lives are filled with excessive praise;
yet, those compiled in the *Continued Biographies* number no more than eighty-one, and even the *Supplementary Biographies* do not exceed ninety-seven.

This was truly done with great caution, so that the various quarters might have something to rely upon that is not superficial. Thus, they are like pearls suspended in Indra’s net, each radiating light that reflects the others.
Ying [the Master] sliced open the lion’s udder; every drop was authentic. He succeeded the past and opened the way for the future, causing the ancestral flame to shine once more.

How could he be merely longed for his historical talent like those of Sima Qian or Ban Gu? I heard that in the autumn of the Dingwei year, the Elder [Shou] set ablaze a single torch of purple sheaths.
Only the chamber remains; the manuscript has also flown away into the bamboo grove where a rabbit was caught.

Truly, it is as if the diligent efforts of this propagator of the Teaching are being protected by the eight classes of dragon-deities and heavenly beings. Thus, the transmission of both the person and the book shall surely be inexhaustible.
I have reverently washed my hands to compose this preface.
On the full moon day of the first month of autumn in the Ding-si year of the Kangxi era, the Buddha’s disciple Lin Youwang of Min-Fu paid his respects and inscribed this at Chan Yue Peak in Ruiyun.
Preface to the *Song-Yuan-Ming Sengbao Zhuan* (Biographies of the Sangha Treasures of the Southern Song, Yuan, and Ming Dynasties).
People transmit through writing, and writing is esteemed according to its era. That era is a time that must not be neglected; that writing is a book that cannot be dispensed with by the age.
This is the case with Chan Master Guangrun Huanjin, who continued the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* from the Southern Song through the Yuan and Ming dynasties.
While I was serving in Guocheng, I once privately took up and examined his work; at times, the writing...

Regarding this Dharma: as the Song dynasty moved south, the *śaṅkha* (banner-poles) of the monasteries likewise pointed south. Initially, during the Zhenghe era, the ruler of the state venerated the Daoist path while suppressing Buddhism;

he styled himself Emperor Daojun and compelled the monastic community to grow their hair and don crowns, renaming them "Virtuous Scholars" (*de-shi*) and relegating them to a position subordinate to the Daoists.
When Emperor Daojun fell into obscurity, Buddhism once again suffered under the Northern [Jurchen] regime.

When the Jin general Wuzhuo was defeated and eliminated, there was no monastery in the northern forests that was not defiled and disgraced. Fortunately, the masters of the Chan school had already planned for a southern retreat;

had they not heard [of this], this transmission would have begun in the Dingwei year of the Jianyan era, passed through the end of the Song dynasty, and only with the Mandate of Heaven established by the Yuan would it have been revived again.
Furthermore, through the end of the Yuan and the reign of the Ming’s Gaozu, it was brought to completion.
The Patriarchs caused the Dharma realm to flourish and prosper, and their influence continued without ceasing until the Dinghai year of the Shunzhi era—five hundred and twenty-one years later.
Is this not a time that one must not treat with negligence? As for the method of recording these patriarchs, it began with Fodeng Xun;
indeed, Xun entered nirvana at the beginning of the Southern Song dynasty, continuing through Huqiu, Dahui, Mianan, Wuzhun, and Zhongfeng.
Haizhou Miyun, Wuxueqiao Xin, and those such as Hongzhi, Zhenxie, Zide, Xuanhui, Quanxiu, Yuanwu,
Tiantong Ruojing, Xuedou Wuyin, Shouchang Xiansheng, and Boshan Liaoyuan constitute the single lineage of Linji.
Regarding the single school of the Cavernous Upper (Dongshang), both the Qianfeng and Yunmen lineages are interwoven within it.
Is this not a time when one cannot do without such a person? Given that the person is like this and the times are like that, the transmission of his will must be attributed to his merit.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* with its "Acquisition of the Qilin" and the *Iron Casket Heart History* share the same principle across ancient and modern times:

both were composed out of necessity, moved by the times and incensed by current affairs. They are of great concern to the decline or flourishing of the Way and Dharma, and to the severance or continuity of the spiritual lineage;
they are indelible scriptures. How could the literary expressions of different eras be spoken of as being on the same level? I have specifically written this preface to bear witness to this.

To manifest his aspirations and record his merits: In ancient Min, there was Huo Tong’s Cui Bingjing. In the Song, Southern and Northern Dynasties, the *Biographies of the Jewel-like Monks* (Sengbaozhuan) records that the Way came from the East;
it does not rely on written words. The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye transmits mind by means of mind, like one lamp passing its light to another.
As one lamp continues the flame of another, worldly people could not help but give rise to doubts.

Master Chongling Song, unable to bear it, compiled the *Zutang Tu* (Chart of the Patriarchal Hall) and the *Zhengfa Zongzong Ji* (Record of the Orthodox Lineage of the Transmission of the Dharma) and presented them to the ruler of the state;

these were subsequently promulgated with official seals throughout the realm. From this point on, books compiling the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Transmission of the Lamp) appeared one after another; their texts were not uniform and were often prolix.
It is like the division of the Vinaya-piṭaka in India into five sections; though divided, they originally stem from a single source.
Master Dàchuān has gathered all the essential principles, and the *Lamp* (Dēng) has brought their origins together. With the emergence of the *Huìyuán*, the history of the *Lamp* is established.

Once the history of the *Lamp* is settled, every word and phrase therein will serve to relieve ailments and rescue those drowning; how could there be any further doubts or obstructions that would not melt away like ice?
How profound this is! Furthermore, the Chan Master Hong of Juefan once composed the *Sengbao zhuan* (Biographies of the Jewel of the Sangha).
He held that recording matters in empty words is not as effective as witnessing their conduct from beginning to end, for such an approach is deeply penetrating and clearly illuminating.

From the Jiayou era to the Zhenghe era, there were nearly a thousand individuals who occupied the seat of the patriarch; yet, only eighty-one entered the ranks of his chapters. His prose is both concise and refined.
It is perfect and vigorous. To express this in the Chahar (Mongolian) language: among all the essential points, there is nothing that is not fully prepared.

What is thus prepared is the Great Universal Way of the Patriarchs, which cannot be altered. Since the time of Master Hong after the Jianyan era, only the two schools of Jue and Dong have propagated their Dharma and transformation throughout the world.
Coinciding with the end of the Ming dynasty, when heroic spirits emerged in great numbers at once, there appeared those who continued the lamp of the lineage.
This recent edition has appeared. Regarding its ancient discrepancies and uncertainties, it seems that they cannot yet be resolved or settled.
Why is this? Is it because [the editors] have not attained a comprehensive understanding of the *Chuán* (Commentary) and a broad mastery of the *Hóng* (Preface)?

Or is it because there is still something further required before they can be definitively settled? For instance, this recent edition takes Haizhou Ci as the primary authority for the *Wàn* (Ten Thousand).

Wanfeng [Wuxue] was in his later years when he finally visited Dongming Xian. It is said that Wanfeng passed away in the *Xinyou* year of the Hongwu era (1381), while Yuci was born in Chengdu, Sichuan, into the Yu family in the *Jiaxu* year of the Hongwu era (1374).
He entered the monastic life at Daisui Mountain, where he was given the name Yongci.
At the age of twenty-eight, he traveled east to visit Xian and received the Dharma. Thereafter, he remained obscure at Niushou Mountain, concealing his traces in Quanjiao.

At forty-four years of age, he opened the Dharma at Dongshan. Three years later, Master Tian passed away. Tian had previously entrusted his robe and verse to Dongming to serve as the abbot of Mingbai An;
he was sent to Dongshan, where he was shortly thereafter given the name Huizhou Puci.
He was born into the Qian clan of Changshu and left the household life at Poshan. It was only when he was over seventy that he met Tian—how clear this is! Or perhaps it is a character for "word."
After three transcriptions, "wu" (烏) became "yan" (焉). Is this perhaps due to a different source that shares the same name?
I submitted this inquiry to the Great Masters, all of whom agreed that the recent edition was correct.
Furthermore, I requested my teacher, the Elder Hongjue Muan of Tiantong, to provide the account of the life and conduct of Chan Master Haizhou Yongci, as established by Zhi Xuan and Zhi Xi.

The stele was shown to me, and my initial doubts were resolved. However, being of dull wit, I have nonetheless compiled a record of the essential facts regarding eminent masters from the Jianyan era of the Song dynasty down to the end of the Ming dynasty—spanning five hundred years—which must not be allowed to perish.
This work, intended to form a complete volume, is now entrusted to my disciple, Xing Lei.

I have commissioned those who had omitted or neglected matters to collect and supplement them; together there are ninety-seven individuals. This work is titled the *Song Dynasty Biographies of the Jewel-like Monks of the Yuan and Ming*.
I await a sage of the age to prune and finalize it—how would I dare to presume such authority myself? This is the preface by the Purple Reed Śramaṇa Zirong.

Volume One of the *Biographies of the Jewel-like Monks of the Chan Forest of the Southern Song, Yuan, and Ming Dynasties*.
Compiled by the śramaṇa Ziruo of Mount Zituo; supplemented by his disciple Xinglei;
edited by Lin You of Min and Fu, and Wang Jiao;
verified by the Chan Master Fodeng Xun.
The Chan Master’s name was Shouchun; his style name was Fodeng. He was born into the Shi clan, a prominent family in Jixian Prefecture.

In his youth, he left the household life and attained the Way under Master Qin of Fotedian at Taiping. Initially, Shouchun consulted Guangjian Ying but did not reach a point of accord, so he went to see Fotedian.
Fotedian was solitary and rigid, difficult to penetrate; Shouchun thereupon sealed his bedding and vowed: "If I do not attain enlightenment in this lifetime, I shall not [leave this place]."

He manifested this realization. Thereupon, he sat during the day and stood through the night for seven weeks. Being utterly exhausted, he happened upon Fojian giving a discourse that said, "The myriad phenomena of the universe are all sealed by a single Dharma.
Xun leapt with joy and immediately left the Dharma Hall, whereupon he went directly to Lingyun.
Upon seeing peach blossoms, he offered this verse: "Throughout the day I gazed at the sky without raising my head; Only when the peach blossoms were in full bloom did I lift my eyes.
Even if you had a net that could cover the heavens, Once you have penetrated the secure barrier, you may simply rest. Fojian asked, "What is the state of Lin Yun where there is no doubt?
He replied, "Right now, even if one sought a place of doubt, it would be utterly unfindable. Fojian said, "Xuan Sha said..."
"He has not yet reached the ultimate point. "Where is it that he has not reached it? [Foguo] replied, "I know deeply that the Master’s heart is filled with a motherly concern.
Fojian was pleased by this. When Foguo arrived, Fojian praised Xun’s insight as stable and substantial, saying, "This man will govern himself;
he is strict and solemn in his private chambers as if he were facing a high guest. In the future, he shall achieve great things. Foguo feigned agreement and then privately invited Xun for a stroll.
At Mount Shan, they happened upon a pond. Fuguo pushed Xun into the water and immediately asked, "What was it like before Niutou saw the Fourth Patriarch?
Xun replied, "The pond is deep, so the fish gather. "And what was it like after he saw him? Xun said, "The tree is tall, so it beckons the wind."
"How is it when seeing and when not yet seeing? Xun replied, "Stretching out one's legs is within the drawing in of one's legs. Foguo then laughed heartily.
In the first year of the Xuanhua era, an imperial edict summoned Fojian to reside at Jiangshan. Foguo sent a letter to Jian, insisting that Xun be appointed as the head of the Jiangshan assembly;
from this, Xun became renowned throughout the world. During the Jianyan era, he resided at Tiansheng. At the time of his opening the hall for formal discourse, the Palace Secretary...
The Prince asked, "When the Three Sages encountered people, they would speak to them. Xun smiled and said, "Have you ever read poetry?
The Prince replied, "In my leisure time from official duties, what is there that I have not perused? Xun said, "A poem says: 'The shimmering lake light is beautiful in the clear weather;
the misty mountain colors are marvelous even in the rain. If one were to compare West Lake to Lady Xi, whether in simple or elaborate makeup, she is always fitting. The Prince [continued].
The Duke then spoke highly of Xun at court. Pan Lianggui, a Palace Attendant, once requested further instruction from Xun regarding the story of Nanquan killing the cat.
Xun said, "Nowadays, when scholars discuss Chan or the Way, they merely rely on intellectual principles and feel satisfied.
This is like buying oil-cakes with money; once eaten, one is no longer hungry. As for everything else, they say it is merely deceiving others."
How laughable! After you received the essential instructions, you propagated the Way of Xun while in the body of a layman. When Xun moved to He Mountain, you later resided at Tianning Monastery.
Every time you saw that the faculties of students were not sharp, you would guide them with painstaking care and skillful means, pouring forth your teachings like an autumn river from a jar.
There have been those who have ventured to offer private criticisms, yet there has been no time to address them. I once raised the story of the Old Lady burning the hermitage, saying:
"In general, to uphold the lineage and establish the teaching, one must be the right person. Look at this old lady: though she was but a woman, she possessed the strategic prowess of a man of honor.
It is well known that for twenty years she had spent oil and soy sauce [on her practice]. One day, from atop a hundred-foot pole..."

Make a show of being at a loss; you must exhaust every ounce of strength in your lifelong skill. Unless one is a common man, one knows when to stop, until finally, when cleverness is exhausted, the clumsy emerges.
Even so, do you all wish to understand? Only after the snowfall does one know the integrity of the pines and cypresses;
only in times of difficulty does one see the heart of a true man. He further cited how one day Muzhou saw a wild fire and said:
He asked Dao Wu, "Do you see the fire? Dao Wu said, "I see it. Miaoyan said, "From where does it arise?
Dao Wu said, "Apart from walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, please ask another question, Master. Miaoyan then desisted and said, "The wild fires reach the heavens, boundless;
as for their place of origin, one must still discern the master. When the film over the pupils of the eyes has vanished, the entire world before one is clear."
Cutting off the flowers in the sky—Old Daowu is truly worthy of praise. But tell me, from where does this ultimately arise? The monk drawing water returns to the temple beneath the forest;
the boatman waiting for passengers stands on the sand at the river’s edge. A monk asked about the "guest within the guest"; Xun replied: "The traveler's road is as vast as heaven;
the gate awaiting him is as deep as the sea. Regarding the "host within the guest," Xun replied: "I often recall, at the places where I saw guests off..."
When receiving guests from another house, the host among the guests replies: "Meeting by chance, there is no need to inquire about one's future path. When the host among the hosts replies:
"In a single morning, I exercise the patriarchal authority; who is the one who emerges? A monk asked: "What of the supreme vehicle above this? Xun said:

"If the great ocean were to know contentment, the myriad rivers would surely flow backward. He also once said to the assembly, "Brothers, if you have a moment of realization, do not be constrained by time or season;
you must come and reveal some sign of it. Once, during a snowy night, a monk came straight to his quarters and knocked.
Xun rose, took up a candle, and with a majestic shout, bellowed: "It is a snowy night at midnight; you seek to resolve your doubts. Why do you act so arrogantly?"

The ritual was incomplete. As the assembly looked toward his robe and satchel, Xun immediately drove him out. In the Jiayin year of the Xiangxing era, he returned from Tianning to Zhangnan and passed away.
His attendant requested a final verse, to which Xun replied, "I have never composed one. He then immediately passed away; after the cremation, his tongue remained intact.
He was interred in a stupa at Baoying Monastery. When Xun was first at Mount Lu, there was a monk named Yanwei who, during the winter months, used...
Daowei was wearing a paper robe made of reed flowers. When Huixun saw this, he became greatly incensed and said, "You, a youth, are already seeking such warmth;
do you have any heart for studying the Way? Daowei was greatly alarmed and withdrew to ask his brothers, who told him that there were those in the hall wearing robes of reed flowers.
There were only three or four people, all over seventy years of age.
Zhan said: "At the end of the seventh week, Fodeng suddenly realized the Great Matter. Why was it that even Yuanwu still had to 'knock at the door' for him?
It is like a coral tree from the bottom of the sea: if it is not raised up by a heavy iron cable, how could its precious brilliance be revealed to people?"
How extraordinary he was for his time! Yet, that the Lamp of the Buddha used a style of clarity and simplicity to shake the world is sufficient evidence of its source;
it is truly beyond reproach.
Thus says Chan Master Zhiji of Yuantong Zhenji.
Master Dezhi was a native of Jinyi in Liyang; he was the younger son of Xu Hongzhong. He inherited the Dharma from Master Chanti Zhao of Baofeng.
Zhao was a native of Jianzhou; in his prime, he traveled to various regions and visited Master Huikai of Furong at Dahong, whereupon he attained realization and departed.
When Master Huikai declined the imperial summons for the Daguan era and encountered difficulties, Zhao—
He hurried from the Three Wu region to follow him, attaining great enlightenment along the way. Master Kai then linked him to the prophecy of Touzi;
thus, this Zhao was a contemporary of Danxia Chun and their peers. As for Chun’s regard for his teacher, he treated him as his own son.
This master was a peer to Zhenxie Liang, Hongzhi Zhengjue, and Dahui Zonggao. When the master was ten years old, he refused to learn to read or write;
instead, he often sat in private at night and took pleasure in watching his father nap during the day. His father jokingly called him the "Dullard.

Nevertheless, the master’s eyes were a deep azure-blue, their divine radiance piercing others, and his speech frequently accorded with the sacred scriptures. Consequently, his father came to cherish him all the more.
He was distinct from his other sons. He once remarked to his guests, "I am both ignorant and not ignorant.
When the Master was in his early twenties, he dreamed that a strange monk bestowed upon him a four-line verse. Shortly thereafter, someone presented him with a statue of the Abbot of Nan'an Rock;
inscribed upon its side was precisely the verse bestowed in his dream. From then on, he maintained it in mind without forgetting, even while studying all the secular classics.
As soon as he saw it, he set it aside. At the age of twenty, while accompanying his father on an official post in Xiluo, he would often sit in meditation with the door closed;
at times, he would not permit food to be brought to him for several days. Everyone marveled at his conduct.

One night, as he was about to blow out the lamp to go to sleep, he suddenly attained great enlightenment and uttered several gāthās in succession. The first said: "Not because of words or phrases, Not because of another person, Not because of external objects."
He was not moved by sounds. At midnight, he extinguished the lamp just as he was about to rest his head upon the pillow; suddenly, it was already daybreak within this very place.

Thereupon, he continued to chant and sing with composure. People marveled at him even more. His father wished to bestow upon the Master the hereditary office of the family, but the Master firmly declined it in favor of his elder brother.
He then told his father, "I am about to cast off the worldly net and dwell no longer within the three realms; how could I again thrust my head into the field of fame and profit?

He thus sought to leave the household life with all his might. His father, knowing that the Master’s resolve was firm and could not be bound by official rank or emoluments, permitted him to shave his head and conferred upon him the bhikṣu precepts.
After wandering through various regions for several years, his reputation resounded throughout the capital during the Zhenghe era.
In the interim, Ji Tou sent Chan Master Zhao to the south of Chu. In the third year of the Xuande era, the *xinchou* year, Emperor Huizong bestowed upon him the title of Chan Master Zhenji.
In the *rentin* year, as the seat at Yuan Tong in Jiangzhou was vacant, an imperial decree appointed Zhao to fill it.
Zhao declined the position of Yuan Tong and instead resided at Letan; the Master (Foyin) consequently responded to the summons and succeeded him as the presiding abbot of Yuan Tong. At Yuan Tong—
When the renowned monastery of Mount Lu was established, the venerable elders of the various mountains had not yet been satisfied with the Master’s reputation.
On the day he took charge of the monastery, they all went to observe him; as he ascended the seat and delivered his discourse, the ears of the assembly were all uplifted.
His words were: "Twenty years ago, this mountain monk was blind in both eyes and could see nothing at all. I only heard people say that above the blue sky there is a Great Sun."
The wheel illuminates the trichiliocosm, leaving no place unpenetrated; yet, despite a myriad of stratagems, one can ultimately never see it.
Twenty years later, the eyes open with a sense of shame, only to encounter continuous overcast skies as thick clouds surge forth in chaos.
He surveyed the four directions and probed upward and downward. When he saw the clouds moving, he made calculations regarding their movement;
when he saw the clouds resting, he established a fixed pattern regarding their stillness.
Just as he was in this state, he suddenly encountered a man of great erudition who asked him, "Do you wish to see the solar disc? Why not go to the summit of a high mountain? The mountain monk—

He then asked, "Where is that dwelling place? He replied, "Atop the peak of a high mountain. [The Master] said, "A place where the red dust of the world does not reach—this is a truly excellent piece of news for you all.
Do you understand? On the long meditation benches, it is *Buddhāya*! He spoke again:

He was called Caizhulu. Caizhen later moved to Longya in Tanzhou. Longya had several hundred followers, yet he handled their coming and going and their lifting and carrying as if with his own left and right hands.

His single bamboo hat was not even complete, yet the Zen disciples were thoroughly steeped in his flavor; he remained lofty and self-possessed, alone enduring wind and rain.
The tongue of a fledgling strikes out the profound mystery; thus he resided there for thirteen years as if it were but a single day. There is a saying:

If you can see this and practice this—when vigorous, walk; when weary, rest. If you have not yet realized it, you are like two cormorants carrying a single turtle. During the Shaoxing era, he retired.

On the twenty-third day, he spoke again: "Nirvana and birth-and-death are both but flowers in the sky; 'Buddha' and 'sentient beings' are merely figurative designations."
"What do you all think of this? After a long silence, he roared and said: "White clouds surge from the earth; the bright moon hangs in the sky. He then passed away.
His body was cremated, and five-colored śarīras were collected and enshrined in a stupa at his native mountain.
The Eulogy says: Master Fojian once said to Master Cai, "There are three essentials for a monastic administrator (zhuchi). First, one must be able to act upon what one perceives;

Thus, he has been publicly renowned for twenty years; the multitude revere him as the flocks of birds follow the phoenix, cherishing its virtue.
At that time, while Sishin was skilled at reviling everyone else until they were silenced, he alone praised Gong with unremitting admiration.
How could this have been in vain?
As for Chan Master Miaopu of Xingkong Puan:
his courtesy name was Xingkong, and he was a native of Hanzhou. By nature, he was seldom adorned with artifice and enjoyed confronting others with blunt candor.

Following this tradition, he traveled to Xiushui and built a thatched hut in the wilds of Qinglong. He amused himself by blowing his iron flute and delighted in composing new melodies. He once sang:
"When the mind and its objects are both forgotten, one is still separated from delusion; When form and dust are non-dual, a trace of defilement remains.
The hundred birds do not come and spring passes once more; I know not who is the person dwelling in this hermitage. He also said: "Studying the Way is like guarding a prohibition."

The city: by day one guards against the six thieves; by night one remains alert. When the commander of the central army can carry out his orders, he governs a time of peace without moving a blade of grass or a single weapon.

Some tried to stop him, citing the dangers, but the Master said, "To respond to conditions as they arise is my vow.

that I am deprived of wealth is because the Five Elements were not in harmony; that I am constrained by my fate is due to the [inappropriate] day and time."
Inauspicious! Alas, how profound it is! Fortunately, there is the Way that transcends the mundane, through which one awakens to one’s own nature and its wondrous mind.
As for this wondrous mind, with what could it be compared? Above, it accords with the true transformation of all Buddhas; below, it harmonizes with the ignorance of ordinary beings.
Not a speck of dust stirs; it is primordially and spontaneously perfected. How wondrous! How wondrous! Even the sun and moon are not sufficient to describe it.
He took this to be his enlightenment. To him, even Heaven and Earth were not sufficient to be considered "Great."磊磊落落 (lěi lěi luò luò)—towering and expansive, without obstruction or hindrance.

as new arrivals could no longer find space to accommodate them, a "Thousand-Monk Hall" was constructed to house them.

The Vice Minister Zhāng Zǐsháo, the Grand Marshal Wāng Shèngxī, and the Junior Minister Fēng Jìyòng were all included among their ranks. It was during this period that Qín Huì held the levers of power.
The Censor-in-Chief, Zhan Dafang, slanted his judgment and said: "Zhang Jiucheng was the leader in inciting groundless rumors and slandering the administration;

the monk Zonggao of Mount Jing followed suit. Consequently, Zhang Jiucheng was sentenced to internal exile, stripped of his clerical robes, and his ordination certificates were burned, while Miaoxi was banished to Hengyang.
From the moment the order was issued, cries of lamentation filled the roads. Those who understood the situation remarked: "The sun and moon have no partiality."
He perfected his brilliance; as for sages and worthies, there is no distinction in their attainment of greatness.

Could it be that Master Gaǒ’s transformation was destined for the south, such that Heaven lent him this manifestation in Hengyang? Furthermore, the orthodox spirit of the Dharma-gate illuminates the ages;

moreover, as he is bound by the vows of the multitude, the Master will surely return with long life—what cause for worry? Though he has been transferred to Mei and Yang for ten years, despite the pestilence and miasma...
In his native village, Miaoxi tirelessly brandished his fly-whisk; monks and laypeople flocked to him in great numbers, amidst a climate of radiant wind and clear sun.
After another five years, by imperial decree, he was granted permission to return to his monastic robes. Monks from all quarters left their seats vacant to welcome him, yet he declined them all.

Finally, there was an imperial edict compelling him to take charge of Yuyang Monastery. Hundreds of *qǐng* of reclaimed fields were built up to provide for the sustenance of the assembly, and a manor was bestowed upon him.
He was named Baizhang. Two years later, he moved to Mount Jing; there, Mount Jing flourished even more.

Although the great masters (the "dragons and elephants") vied with one another for prominence, whenever he ascended the hall, he would invariably praise his adopted son, Ying’an, noting that he had deeply mastered the pedagogical methods of his late master.

Consequently, the world further praised him for his impartiality. As Miaoxi’s years of ordination grew advanced, he repeatedly requested to retire to the Bright Moon Hall (Mingyuetang) to decline all future visitors. However, [he could not do so].
This may be prohibited. Previously, when Emperor Xiaozong was still a prince, he dispatched an eunuch to Jingshan to visit Miaoxi and presented him with a verse.
The Emperor was greatly pleased. Later, while residing in the Prince’s residence, he again sent an attendant to request that Miaoxi ascend the hall for a sermon;

the Emperor personally wrote the plaque for Miaoxi’s hermitage and bestowed upon him a portrait and a eulogy. Upon his accession to the throne, he further conferred upon him the dharma title of Chan Master Dahui.

When he was summoned for an audience, Miaoxi had already manifested signs of illness. One night, a great star suddenly fell to the earth, its radiance scattering in all directions, while birds and beasts all cried out.
He then passed away in the Bright Moon Hall (Mingyuetang). His disciples personally sealed his final testament, and the attendant monks requested that he leave behind a verse of farewell.
Miaoxi said in a stern voice, "If you have no verse, you shall not die. He then wrote in large characters:
"Living is just like this; dying is just like this. Whether there is a verse or no verse—what a fuss it is! He threw down his brush and passed away.
It was the tenth day of the eighth month in the first year of the Longxing era. His worldly lifespan was seventy-five years, and he had spent fifty-eight summer retreats in seclusion.
When the Emperor read his final words, he was deeply moved by grief and composed a verse for the memorial offering, which said: "Birth and extinction are not extinction; permanence is not abiding.
Perfect enlightenment is empty and luminous, manifesting according to all things. By imperial decree, the Mingyue Hall was renamed Miaoxi Hermitage, and his entire body was interred there.

Later, he was posthumously titled Pujue (Universally Awakened), and his stupa was named Puguang (Universal Radiance). His complete recorded teachings in eighty fascicles were included in the Great Canon (*Dazang*).
A eulogy states: Master Duan said, "Having attained awakening, one must surely meet the right person. For several decades, I have spent my time in vain amidst the forest;
yet among all the practitioners I have encountered with my own ears and eyes, there is none who does not occupy a high and broad seat, claiming themselves to be the true successor of Caoxi.
This is the true transmission of the Pulse of the Minor Chamber; it is only a pity that it has not yet met with the Elder Dahui.

Had it met him, there would surely have been a separate "pot-heaven" (a realm of transcendence). How could the words of Master Duan have been mistaken? Alas! A horse meets Bole, and firewood meets Zhonglang.
This is a great fortune for our school! The Chan Master Chanming of Jing Mountain, whose name was Liaoming, was of unknown origin.
He possessed a tall stature and a large belly; wherever he went, he struck awe into the multitude, and all the people...
He was called "Da Chan, Da Chan" (Great Chan, Great Chan). His spiritual acuity was swift and sharp, and his demeanor was noble and radiant;
he was a dragon-elephant among the assembly of Chan Master Miaoxi Gaofeng. When Miaoxi resided at Yuyang Monastery, he did not permit the use of the *he* shout within his quarters.
Whenever Da Chan entered the room, he would invariably let out a loud *he* shout before withdrawing. Consequently, Miaoxi posted a notice stating: "Those who shout *he* shall be punished."
The fee was one *guan*. Dacian, however, secretly tucked a thousand coins into his sleeve, first placed them on the ground, and then departed while shouting a series of loud roars.
Miaoxi said, "What can be done with that fellow? He further issued a proclamation: "One who shouts 'down' shall be fined a single midday meal for that day."
Dachian immediately went to the storehouse and said, "The Master requires ten taels of gold. The administrator, without suspicion, gave it to him.
Dachian tucked it into his sleeve and entered; he then set it down on the floor and let out a loud shout. Miaoxi was greatly startled; when he calmly questioned him, he learned what had happened.
He laughed at this for a moment. One day, Miyō said to Daizen, “You fat fellow, if you understand Zen like this, it will be as long as a donkey’s life before you even dream of it.
Daizen replied, “How is the prophecy given on Vulture Peak any different from today?
Miyō then examined him on the details of the anecdote concerning Deshan’s alms bowl. Daizen responded, “The chilling, hair-piercing blade shines forth.”

One’s gallbladder freezes with cold; there is no room for deliberation, nor can it be transmitted. To lift one's eyes is already to have one's body in three pieces. This is the "Red Iron Ball" of our own house.
Miaoxi sighed and said, "These words will circulate widely in the future. Thereupon, he went to Touzi, where the monastic community was transformed.
Later, he moved to Changlu, where all neglected matters were restored. Once, while passing through Jingshan, he went to visit Miaoxi.
Miaoxi sent this verse in reply: "People say a staff brings forth a filial son; I say out of love for one's child, one does not notice their ugliness.
The Elder of Changlu comes in such a manner; Miaoxi has wasted his mouth in vain. Let the rumors spread through the four seas as they will;
A jackal can indeed let out a lion’s roar. Who says there is nothing to present him on his way? Under a shout, the iron ball turns upside down!"

He walked backward. Since Da Chan became the abbot of Changlu, he manifested many extraordinary traces. Although ten thousand followers attended him, the offerings from donors were as vast as mountains;
thus, people of the time compared him to the Bagua Monk (Puduo Heshang). In his later years, he succeeded to the seat at Jingshan.
In his quarters, he used only the "Old Lady of Mount Tai" koan to test practitioners. Dun’an mocked him with a verse: "One press, and the ox eats grass."
First, he gave the thief a ladder to pass over. "I knew early on that the lamp was fire; the rice has long since been cooked. The Great Chan Master replied:

"Within the midst of war and weapons lies the foundation of great peace; it is not by abandoning war and weapons that one first attains it. If one lacks the strength to lift the cauldron and pull up the mountain..."
"A thousand-li black steed is not easily ridden. Following the passing of Miaoxi at Jingshan, Chan Master Dazhen restored its monastic administration to new heights.
However, as the annual budget was vast, the administrative officers cautioned him that future provisions would be insufficient.

Dazhen alone comforted them with the assurance that the "Dragon and Heaven" permanent endowments would suffice. Prince Yang Wang saw a strange monk in a dream—tall and large, with a long, white beard.
He walked slowly with his chest bare, saying he wished to convert a village in Suzhou. The King found this strange. The following morning, Dàchán arrived with staff and sandals;
the gatekeeper could not stop him and hurriedly informed the King. The King went out at once to see Dàchán, who was magnificent and tall, exactly as described in the dream.
Thereupon, they lit incense and performed the rites of homage. The Great Chan Master said, "The Great King’s estates are exceedingly vast;

you might bestow one location in Suzhou to provide for the Buddha and the Sangha. This would be a benefit that is inexhaustible. The King had not yet given his consent when the Great Chan Master finished the vegetarian feast and departed.

There were no other words. At that time, the news spread far and wide both inside and outside the palace. The Prince-Wang offered his estates in Suzhou as a gift to the Great Chan Master Buidai of Jing Mountain.
When the Prince entered the imperial court, Emperor Xiaozong heard of the Prince’s donation and expressed his congratulations on his behalf.

After the Prince thanked him and returned home, he dispatched an envoy to Jing Mountain to invite the Great Chan Master; however, two days prior, the Great Chan Master had parted from the assembly without illness, manifesting [the signs of passing].

He was transformed. From that time on, whenever King Wang was at leisure—whether awake or asleep, or even when his eyelids closed for a brief moment—he would see the Great Chan Master standing before him.
The Master spoke, saying: "Among the six perfections, the perfection of giving is foremost. To be good in the beginning and good to the end constitutes the ultimate.

The King sighed with admiration and immediately granted a manor and its serfs to Mount Jing. This estate yielded an annual revenue of one hundred thousand [units], and both ships and storehouses were provided; this was all due to the Great Chan Master.

This was the lingering radiance of his legacy. When Miaoxi was first exiled to Meizhou, the guards escorting him were extremely strict; there was even talk that disaster might await him in unforeseen ways.

Yet Dachen exerted all his strength to carry the shackles and accompany him, while the rituals between master and disciple became increasingly solemn day and night. Upon reaching the place of exile, they remained so.

The followers of the patch-robed monk numbered some two or three hundred. Because Miaoxi lacked sufficient provisions for their meals and feared they might raise complaints, he once urged them to leave.
Dacian said, "It must not be so. What these monks carry within is the Way; what they tread upon is righteousness.
Moreover, they have traveled a thousand li through layers of heavy robes, seeking resolution as their primary purpose. Even if they face toil and hardship, or the perils of wind and waves—"

Ding listened to this, and the dragons and devas remained patient while he cast it aside. He then personally took charge of the rice gruel, carrying a wicker basket on his shoulder every day to beg for alms until evening;
at that time, dozens of people would carry the cooked rice for him, returning in a procession. Although there were many monks, none lacked anything.
In this manner for sixteen years, it was as if it were but a single day. Looking back at the flourishing lineage of Miaoxi, it appears even more so during this period of exile.
Those who came into contact with him numbered half [of all visitors]. This was due to the power of Great Chan Master Ming’s clarity.
The eulogy says: When faced with the most difficult and entangled circumstances, Chan Master Master Ming maintained his propriety as sternly as ice and frost; he is worthy of emulation.
Furthermore, upon reading the sayings from his life, they were like a divine blade drawn from its scabbard, cutting through iron as if it were mud.

Examining his deeds, he responded universally to both favorable and adverse circumstances, with miraculous manifestations appearing one after another. At that time, some suspected him to be Maitreya incarnate; how truly divine he was!

The Sūtra says: "It is like the jewel-king of the mind; according to the mind, it manifests all colors. Because the minds of sentient beings are pure, they are able to see pure lands. How true this is!"
Master Yuyang Chanshi, whose name was Duanyu, was a native of Kuaiji and a descendant of the Qian kings of Wuyue.

At the age of fourteen, while driving away crows at Dasha Temple in the district, his gaze shot outward; he possessed extraordinary capacity. Whenever he heard [the words] "lantern," "dew-pillar," or "Buddha"...

When the words regarding the Hall and the Mountain Gate were spoken, [Foyan] was utterly bewildered. While traveling on foot and staying overnight at Jingci Monastery, a monk struck a pillar and asked, "Why do you not speak of Chan?
At this, Yuanwu attained a realization. He visited various renowned masters, all of whom praised him as exceptionally outstanding;
yet, Yuanwu remained ultimately dissatisfied. Later, he met Master Foguo Qin at Zhongfu. Every time Qin blinked his eyes and looked at him, Yuanwu did not understand.
One day, Qin asked, "Who knew that the treasury of the true Dharma-eye would be extinguished at the side of a blind donkey? Is it extinguished right now, or not?
Yuyue replied, "Master, you had better keep your mouth shut. Qin said, "This is still within the realm of ordinary sentiment."
When Fuyou was about to offer a response, Wumen Qin struck him. Fuyou’s mental block was instantly dispelled; from that point on, his responsiveness became peerless.

When the imperial court conferred the honorary title of "Complete Enlightenment" (Yuánwù) upon Qin and appointed him as abbot of Tianning Monastery, Fuyou served as his secretary, recording his words with the brush and ink. His reputation eclipsed that of his contemporaries.
Later, when he first went to reside at Danxia, his assembly numbered over a thousand. Whenever he hung up the plaque to enter the room for instruction, there were few who could grasp his kōan.
Yuyong shed tears and sighed deeply for a long time without ceasing. The assembly were all moved to indignation and resolved to renew themselves.

Later, when he moved to Mount Huqiu and Shuangjing, dozens of people became great vessels of the Dharma. He once addressed the assembly, saying: "Deshan’s 'staff upon entering the gate' mostly leaves its traces buried within the skin-bag [of the body].
Linji’s 'shout upon entering the gate' is entirely a matter of appearing and disappearing amidst the dust of sound. If one is truly a man of heroic spirit..."
"Monks, you must truly let the wind rise from beneath your feet and transcend the tracks of the ancients and the moderns.
Pointing his staff and shouting, he said: 'What is this very thing like? If you call it 'staff and shout,' you are still asleep and have not yet awakened.
If you do not call it 'staff and shout,' you do not yet know Deshan or Linji. Ultimately, how is it? Again, pointing his staff and shouting, he said: 'Do not touch it at all.'"
It is further said: "Movement brings forth shadows; awakening gives rise to ice. Even if one remains unmoving and unawakened, it is still like the ruts of a chariot from the Qin era.
Reaching this point, one must illuminate every subtle distinction and open all ten thousand doors.

One must pivot the wheel of mechanism upon the tip of a hair, so that the life-vein does not sink into the sea of poison. At times, awakening is like still water; at times, movement is like shooting stars.
At times, both movement and awareness are forgotten; at other times, illumination and function are sovereign. Tell me, at such a moment as this, is it movement or awareness?
Is it illumination or function? Can anyone still distinguish between them? An iron ox blocks the ancient road; when touched, one’s very bones and hair grow cold.
It is also said: "When walking, there is no trace of walking; when speaking, there is no mark of speaking. If walking and speaking were to reach their ultimate limit, then—
A single bud arises, beckoning the arrow. If one speaks before reaching the destination, the divine blade will slice it apart.

Even if one’s speech is without leakage and one’s practice does not lose its direction, one still remains stuck within the shell of the husk. Only the Great Garuda, with its golden wings, can soar with such vigor across hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*.
The Ten-Shadow Divine Steed gallops across the four quarters and the eight directions; it does not graze at every opportunity, nor does it bury its body wherever it goes.
Furthermore, it relies on nothing at all. Is there still any portion for it to tread upon? Every moment and every speck of dust is the essential passageway.
It is also said: "The entire earth is the eye of the śramaṇa; throughout the ten directions is one's own light. Why, then, [does one look toward] Pūrvavideha in the east?
When the drum is struck in the west, Jambudvīpa does not hear it; when a lamp is lit in Jambudvīpa, Uttarakuru sits in darkness.
Even if you were to speak with complete mastery regarding this very point, it would still be nothing more than a livelihood based on shadows and light. (He strikes the whisk.)
"It is all broken into a hundred fragments. What is the single path for emerging? He threw down his whisk and said, "Examine!
In the tenth month of the Gengwu year of the Xiangxing era, he manifested slight illness. His exhortations to the assembly were more earnest and urgent than ever before, causing many to weep.

His disciple Fajian requested that he leave behind some final instructions. Yuyi changed his expression and said, "Exhaust this mind and intention; support one another with the Way. Having spoken these words, he passed away.
He passed away. Upon cremation, his eyeballs, teeth, and tongue remained unburnt, and the ground emitted light throughout the entire night.
The śarīra relics obtained were beyond counting and did not cease for over a month. His disciples divided the remains between two locations: Mount Mao and Xihu.

There was a layman named Luo Zhaochang, who had frequently visited Daoyu to inquire about the Way. It happened that when Huiyuan returned, Luo alone had obtained nothing. His longing and remembrance were most sincere.
While he was eating with his guests, as he was chewing, something emerged from his mouth; it was a *śarīra* (relic) the size of a bean, colored like amber.
He then prostrated twice at the site of the cremation. Hearing a sound from within the fragrant casket, he opened the box and obtained [a relic] just as before.

He was exceptionally rosy and lustrous. Yu (Dadao) traveled through ten renowned monasteries and was granted the title Chan Master Fozhi. He passed away at Yuyang Monastery and was posthumously honored with the title Dawu.
[This concludes the biography of] Chan Master Quan of Daochang.
Chan Master Fahuan was a native of Gusu. His surname was Chen, and his style name was Wuan. In his youth, his father took him to see Master Chu’an of Dongzhai.
Chu’an gazed at him intently and said, "If you can follow me? Fahuan joyfully knelt on the ground and requested a name.

His father marveled at this and subsequently shaved his hair. When he traveled to study under various masters, his conduct was consistently upright and dignified; others could not easily approach him.
Relying on Fozhi at Huqiu, whenever Quan entered the room, Fozhi would question him with the koan of the dog having no Buddha-nature. Quan was rendered speechless;
he saw only blows raining down like rain and shouts thundering like lightning, becoming increasingly bewildered and distressed, not knowing what to do.
He repeatedly sought instruction from the assembly, but Fozhi rebuked him. One day, Quan heard a monk cite the verse of the Fifth Patriarch: "Zhaozhou’s exposed blade."

Suddenly startled, he broke into a sweat. He hurried forward to present himself to Zhi, saying: "The drumming and blowing resound as I bare my shoulder; incense mists from the Dragon Tower fill the boat of Yizhou.
At times I go barefoot, playing with the bright moon, treading through the sky beneath the waves of the Five Lakes. Zhi then gave his approval.

However, what Quan harbored was a profound sense of caution that no one knew of. When Fozhi succeeded Lingyin Temple, he appointed Quan to head the assembly, whereupon he became renowned among those in the monastic community.
Some requested that Quan take charge of a major monastery, but he declined. He would often frown and sigh, saying, "In antiquity, one severed an arm to seek peace of mind;
today, people sell themselves to ensure the continuation of ancestral sacrifices. The Way of our school is in peril—this is clear. Thus it remained for a long time.

Because his Buddha-wisdom had matured with advancing age, he returned to his former hermitage at Xihu. He began preaching the Dharma at the Daochang Monastery in Anji, whereupon he held up his staff and said:
"Each and every one of you stands head-to-heaven and feet-on-earth, carrying a *zhuli* staff slung over your shoulders as you travel from place to place to test the various quarters.
What more do you seek by coming here? As soon as you are lightly pressed, you immediately say—"

"Inviting labor at Tiantai; wandering the mountains at Nanyue—I shall ask you: have you ever recovered the great state sword of the kingdom of Mahācīna? Be careful not to bite off a horn of a sheep. He spoke again:
"If you wish to attain what is present before you, do not harbor thoughts of compliance or resistance. Holding his staff horizontally across the table, he said:
"The Great Master of the Third Patriarch transformed himself into a horse-faced yakṣa and traveled throughout the four great continents. Then...
It comes and presents itself in the hands of this mountain monk; it turns out to be nothing but a single black lacquered staff. Do you see it?

Even if you were to see it, you would enter hell as swiftly as an arrow shot. In the autumn of the Jichou year of the Qiandao era, when a physician arrived for his illness, Yuanquan yielded to him, saying:
"To seek a skilled physician and find an excellent prescription for the sake of this illusory body—can this truly be endured? In the end, he passed away.

When Fayan announced his passing, the assembly wept and requested a verse. Fayuan wrote out the two characters "wu wu" (non-being, non-being) in large script, then cast aside his brush and passed away.

His cremated remains produced five-colored *śarīra*, which were enshrined in a stupa on Jindou Peak. Initially, when Fayuan was serving as the head seat at Lingyin Monastery, there was a monk named Quan Dao who had long been a practitioner without realization.
He requested instruction from Fayuan, who challenged him with the principle that all phenomena are established upon the ground of non-abiding (*anālaya*).
Wuquan had a sudden realization. He laughed privately and said, "Sewing a needle in the dark; drawing breath through one's ears. Thereupon, he established the master-disciple relationship.
Chan Master Huazang Wuquan was the son of the Qi family of Lin’an. His style name was Yian. Although his spiritual resonance was in accord with Wunan Quan...
As the Head Seat (*śrāmaṇera*), Yuanqi further disciplined himself; he often sat motionless like wood or stone. Once, while passing through the hall, he forgot to spread his alms bowl.
A neighboring monk touched him with his hand, and [Yuanqi] spoke this verse: "A pitch-black Qilin grasps a fishing rod; The ancient sail is hoisted high as it descends the surging rapids.
Amidst the shadows of reeds, he plays with the bright moon, Drawing the blind turtle onto the fishing boat. Fozhi Da... (text fragment)
He praised him highly. He then summoned Zhiquan and asked, "When the mind encompasses the great void and its capacity spans the sands of the world, what then?
Zhiquan replied, "The great ocean does not harbor a corpse. Zhi patted his seat and said, "This boy shall one day occupy this very place."
Having rebuked the Buddhas and reviled the Patriarchs, he departed. Thereupon, the various mountain monasteries requested that he emerge into the world, but he did not accept.

Carrying only his staff and wooden bowl, he wandered through the lakes and rivers, coming and going within the courtyards of Ying’an and Miaoxi. When Master Quan passed away, the seat at Huazang became vacant;
they sought out Quan by searching for his likeness, but Quan again declined. Someone said, "Is the Dharma-way of the old man Wuan not still here?"
"O Master! You now confine yourself to minor details, delighting in forests and springs. Even if you were as pure as Chao Fu and You Zhuo, or as faithful as Wei Ji, what would be so noble about that?
Quan was moved by these words and went to visit him. Later, he moved to Wannian Temple, where his followers always numbered in the tens of thousands;

yet the atmosphere was as solemn as a government office. Every day, he shared the same labors and rest as the multitude. Someone remarked, "The abbot sits at ease while expounding the Dharma; why do you subject yourself to such hardship?"
Yuequan said, "In the Dharma-ending age, people are arrogant; those who have not attained claim they have attained. They borrow their status to act with self-indulgence.

If even those who lead by example do not follow [the path], how could one dare to indulge oneself? In the autumn of the Gengzi year of the Chongxi era, he manifested parinirvāṇa. Upon cremation, his teeth and tongue remained uncorrupted, and countless śarīras were produced.
His remains were enshrined in a stupa on Mount Heng, and further portions were distributed to various stupas at Wannian Mountain Temple. Yuequan was a person of exceptional character.

He was firm and resolute. The Dharma admits no private interests. Once, when a nobleman entered the monastery to offer wealth, his attire was disheveled; Huiquan refused to accept the gift on that account.

Furthermore, when the monk Chong served as the fundraising director and returned with a large sum of donations, he appeared somewhat self-satisfied; Huiquan rebuked him and sent the funds back. Consequently, it was not easy for those outside the gate to enter or leave.
Both men transformed others through their own integrity and moral character. In Huiquan’s later years, his enforcement of the monastic rules became increasingly rigorous and strict.
There is a saying: "This morning the mouth of the cloth bag is tied shut; O clear-eyed monk, do not wander aimlessly.
Where mental activity ceases, one can turn the body around; even a sneeze becomes the lion’s roar. Roam at will through the sandalwood grove; raise your eyebrows and they grow upon your crown.
To gouge out flesh and create a sore is to expose the family’s shame."
The Eulogy says: The Buddha-intelligence spanned three generations, establishing itself upon a foundation of stability and substance. At that time, the style of Chan underwent a transformation.

Observing the traces left behind in its earlier and later stages, they are like the insect-script and bird-seal characters; though their forms and styles differ, the underlying principle remains one and the same.

Were it not for a Great Being of saintly caliber, how could such a feat have been achieved? This is all the more so when considering that the method of using yellow leaves to stop a child’s crying was employed to sever the flow of criticism.
The Secret of Hanging Sands.

*Biographies of the Jewel-like Monks of the Chan Forest of the Southern Song, Yuan, and Ming Dynasties*, Volume Four.
Chan Master Daochang Bian:

The Chan Master’s name was Mingbian. He was the son of the Yu family from Jixian Prefecture. He preached the Dharma at Mount Daochang in the prefecture and styled himself Zhengtang (Hall of Rectitude).
He was upright and principled in his conduct, never yielding to laxity even in the slightest degree. Whenever monastics or laypeople entered the mountain to request the Dharma, he would receive them.
One must first ensure that incense is prepared and that the guest bows to the Abbot Foyuan; only then may they receive the formal audience. Upon entering, the visitor stands in awe.
When asked, "How can one pass through the realms of speech and silence, and the distinctions of transcendence and immanence, without transgression?

Bian replied, "Transversely situated beyond the triple world, alone liberated from the myriad functions. The former [the questioner] said, "As Xuefeng once said: 'I always remember the third month in Jiangnan, when the partridges cry.'"
"Abiding amidst the fragrance of a hundred flowers—how about that? Bian said, "Why do you speak of this unimpressive fellow?
[The Master] said, "Tender bamboo sways as the golden wind blows fine; a hundred flowers carpet the ground as the sun moves slow. Bian said, "Where did you see Fengxue?
The monk said, "In the ears and eyes, utterly refined and elegant. Bian said, "That is just a mental fabrication; it has nothing to do with it. He asked again.
"What is the Buddha? Bian said, "A fierce fire with no fuel to burn. "What is the Dharma? He said, "A poor man dressed in the finery of a rich man.
"What is the Sangha? He said, "An old woman selling fans shielding her eyes from the sun. "What is one shout like a vajra-king sword?
He said, "A venomous snake in an ancient tomb with horns upon its head. "What is one shout like a crouching lion? He said, [The text here is incomplete in the source].
The Lion said: "The void smiles and nods its head. "How is it that one shout is like a probing rod or a blade of grass? He said: "A stone man claps his hands and laughs 'he-he'.
"How is it that one shout is not used as a shout? He said: "A pig's head inside a cloth bag. "What is the matter that transcends [the ordinary]?
He said: "Sawing apart a weightstone. "What is the Master’s thorny plum? He said: "A saw cutting a weightstone. "What is the Master’s thorny plum? He said: "A saw cutting a weightstone."

Péng said, "I do not answer this question. [The other] asked, "Why do you not answer? Bian laughed loudly and said, "It cannot be swallowed, nor can it be spat out. Bian Ji was essential and vigorous;
every ten days he would retreat into his room, so that even those in close attendance rarely had the opportunity to see him. Nevertheless, his instructions were piercing and absolute.
He did not harbor a reputation for fame, nor did he indulge in playfulness or reckless conduct. Consequently, those who entered his gate numbered only twenty or thirty.
Zai concealed his spirit and hid his brilliance; those renowned throughout the various quarters all heard of him and held him in awe. In his later years, he ascended the hall and said:
"Picking up [the treasure] from the mouth of a fierce tiger, placing it upon the head of a venomous snake; no longer do I stake my pole or ply my oars."
"Turning back, there is another way of life. The old woman has been seen through by me. In the Great Compassion Temple, there is a rustic feast. Again, he ascended the hall.
