Yue. On the day of Guihai, the letter from Danshu arrived again. After Ren finished preaching the Dharma to the assembly, he passed away while still upon his Dharma seat.
The eulogy says: Baojue said, "A single speck of dust flies up and obscures the heavens; a single mustard seed falls and covers the earth.
In the state of peace and bliss, one must strictly avoid all such cluttered trappings; one must simply die the 'thieving heart' of immeasurable kalpas. This was indeed Ren.

The Master was renowned in the world for his mastery of the sutras and śāstras. While his habitual, deluded mind was at its peak, he encountered a master of true substance; with a single blow, his old bones were shattered.

This is nothing other than one’s own family treasure—how could it be a matter of jealousy? Yet, regarding the way he deployed his spiritual pivot before and after that moment, it was not as the saying goes:
"The profligate pities the traveler from home," nor "The wine-seller loves the drunkard. It was something else entirely.
Regarding Chan Master Huxiang Yuan:
his name was Huiyuan, born into the Peng family of Meishan. He was a late disciple of Chan Master Yuanwu.
When Yuanwu again took charge of Zhaojue Temple, he was advanced in years and thus entrusted the leadership of the monastery to this worthy member of his school.
The virtue of that master had already spread throughout the land; thus, the commands of Magadha were once again put into practice at Zhaojue.

Yuan arrived from Lingya, where he had previously resided with Master Huiguo. Having obtained an iron whisk from Huiguo, Yuan served as the head seat (shouzuo) and propagated the essential tenets of the Huanglong school.
Yuan attended him for two years, gaining a general grasp of the teachings under Master Huiguo’s guidance.
However, when Yuan was appointed as the Head Seat (Shouzuo), the Master repeatedly encouraged and guided him, yet Yuan remained indifferent and paid no heed.

He subsequently traveled to Zhaojue, where he waited for ten days before finally being granted an audience with Master Wu. The Master conversed with him and was greatly impressed, remarking with a sigh, "My Way has not yet declined.

He granted Yuan the privilege of entering the inner quarters at his own discretion. Whenever Yuan knelt in formal prostration to request further instruction, the Master would simply smile and say, "I had thought I was old."
"Is that why you are so urgent? I have long held my breath in trepidation and lost my composure, not daring to speak.

One day, hearing the account of Layman Pang’s karmic connection regarding "not being a companion to the myriad dharmas," he attained great enlightenment into its meaning. He stepped forward before the assembly and asked:
"Purely naked, empty, and without a single thing; standing as bare bones, poor and without a single coin. My door is broken and my house ruined; I beg the Master for relief.

The Master said, "The seven treasures and eight jewels are all seized at once. [The monk] said, "Thieves do not enter the doors of a careful household. The Master said, "The pivot does not leave its place;
you have fallen into a sea of poison. Yuan [the monk] then gave a shout. The Master struck the meditation seat with his staff and said:
"Have you finished eating your staff yet? Yuan again shouted. Gong shouted twice in succession. Yuan performed a prostration and hurried away.

From then on, his spiritual spark was unstoppable. The monastic community collectively bestowed upon him the title "Iron-Tongued Yuan," and he subsequently became renowned alongside Yuan Fudai and others.
During the Shaoxing era, the Governor of Mei invited him to reside at Mount Xiang’er, but he did not go. Not long after, Yuanwu Keqin...
Shi Yuan rose abruptly and said, "The noble traces have vanished; who shall succeed him? To recline in high repose at the northern window—how could that be possible?
[He then] set out in a small boat from the gorges, reaching Kaihua and Longpan in Huainan.
He moved to Langye, from Langye to Puji, from Puji to Dingye, and from Dingye to Guangxiao. Over the course of eighteen years, he was honored by the most eminent of his generation.
He returned [to his quarters]. A monk asked, "What is it like when 'this very mind is Buddha'? Yuan said, "A head with a topknot. The monk asked, "What is it like when 'neither mind nor Buddha'?
Yuan said, "Ears adorned with golden rings. The monk asked, "When it is neither mind, nor Buddha, nor a thing—how then?
Yuan said, "A bald-headed asura dancing the *zhazhi*. He asked again, "In the midst of the vast dust of the world, how does one discern the host?"
Yuan said, "A wooden ladle at the edge of the chopping block slicing vegetables—is this not where you, Master, act for others?
Dongshan said, "A pestle stirring up noodles. Again he asked, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as his companion? Yuan said, "Feet treading upon a waterwheel.
He asked, "Why does the person inside the hermitage not know what is outside the hermitage? Yuan said, "Carrying a staff slung across my shoulder."

"Spiked Iron Fetters. He asked again, "In the past, there was a scholar who composed a 'Treatise on the Non-existence of Ghosts. Once the treatise was finished, a ghost rebuked him, saying, 'What can you do about me? What did you think of this?

Yuan made a gesture with his hand, slashing at his forehead, and said, "'How does it fare? [The Master] asked, "'As for Wuzu making the shape of a magpie's beak with his hand and saying, "Gu-gu," how would you handle that?
Yuan said, "'I take it upon myself.'"** *Note: The term "self-leads-out" (zì lǐng chū) is a Zen idiom indicating taking full personal responsibility for one’s own realization.*
He departed. [Dongshan] said, "The mountain flows upon the water. Yuan said, "The third and the first, the eleventh—no need to choose a day.
[Dongshan] asked, "How should one apply the mind throughout the twelve hours? Yuan said, "Dipping into the snow to eat a winter melon.

His spiritual mechanism was as boundless as the sea; Yuexi’s teachings were mostly like this. Furthermore, he passed through Nanyue and stayed at Nantai. At that time, Chan Master Lian was residing at Long...
Wang and Fang Guangxing were both eminent disciples of Yue’an, whose reputation for the Way had spread throughout Huxiang.
They privately remarked to one another, "This place is as steep and inaccessible as ten-thousand-fathom cliffs; what footing can one find here for those who come from afar?

Therefore, they requested him to ascend the seat and posed more than thirty questions, all concerning the difficult passages and critical junctures of the patriarchs' teachings. Yuan answered them all completely, his words and meaning transcending the ordinary; Lia and the others...

He submitted to his summons, intending to station Yuanyuan at Mingcha Temple; however, Yuanyuan disregarded this and went into seclusion on Mount Tiantai. He traveled between the three temples of Guoqing, Huguo, and Hongfu.
In the *dinghai* year of the Qiandao era, the Governor of Pingjiang welcomed Yuanyuan to Huqiu. Furthermore, by imperial decree, he visited both Chongguang and Lingyin Temples.
Emperor Xiaozong frequently summoned him for audiences to inquire about the essentials of the Dharma, and subsequently conferred upon him the honorary title "Fohai" (Ocean of Buddha).
Scholarly Confucians flocked daily to the Chan Master’s seat. Among those who succeeded him in the Dharma while remaining laymen were the Palace Secretary Zeng Kai and Prefect Ge Tan;
Tan, styled Xinzhai (Hall of Faith), heard from Yuan how he expounded the principle that "mind is Buddha."
He had a realization and presented this verse: "Neither mind, nor Buddha, nor yet a thing; Before the Five-Phoenix Pavilion, the mountain looms high.
In the midst of the radiant sun, he turns his body upside down; The wild fox leaps into the golden-haired lion’s den. Yuan said, "Your insight can only enter the realm of the Buddhas;
it is difficult for you to enter the realm of the Maras. Tan asked in astonishment, "Why? Yuan replied, "Why not say, 'The golden-haired lion leaps into the wild fox's den'?"
He entered the wild fox den. Tan then grasped the essential meaning. Zeng Kai, whose courtesy name was Tianyou, had long ascended the hall of Yuanwu and Dahui;
hearing of his reputation, he came to visit and asked, "What is a good spiritual friend? Yuan replied, "The pillar and the lantern."
"Cat, dog," [Wumen] said. "Why is it that praise brings joy and disparagement brings affliction? Yuan said, "Have you, Minister, ever met a true teacher (shanzhishi)?
Kai changed color and said, "I have traveled to various places for thirty years; how can you say I have not seen one? Yuan said, "Look where there is affliction;
look where there is joy. As Kai hesitated, Yuan shouted at him. Kai again prepared to offer further words.
Xuansha waved his hand and said, "The one who opens his mouth is not [the truth]. Guankai was so overcome with shame that sweat broke out through his layered robes.
Xuansha called to him, "Where have you been, Minister? Guankai was suddenly enlightened and leaped for joy. He spoke a verse, saying: "Alas, blind donkey! A pestilence to the monastic groves.
With a single sound that shakes the earth, the celestial mechanism has been leaked. If anyone further asks what the meaning is, I pick up my whisk."
Pikou Ce said, "I have only obtained one peg. Yuanxiao laughed and said, "Even so, you have gained one peg.
When Miaoxi was in Lingnan, he read Yuanxiao’s *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings) and was greatly astonished, exclaiming, "Does the Master have such a son in his later years?

He then sent the Dharma robe originally bestowed upon him by Yuanwu to present to Yuanxiao. Consequently, those throughout the Jianghu region considered that Master Yuanxiao had surpassed Miaoxi in subtlety. One day, suddenly...
He addressed the assembly, saying: "In the second year of the Chunxi era, on the first day of the ninth month of the intercalary autumn, do not show your head in the midst of clamor;

fix your gaze where it is cold. Brightness and darkness do not interfere with one another; each is divided into its own half. If everyone were made a nobleman, who would be left to sell firewood and charcoal?
I tell you: it cannot be disparaged, nor can it be praised. Its substance is like empty space, without shore or limit. [The text ends with the character for "appearance" (xiàng).]

"Call out to one another; let us go back home. The Lantern Festival is surely on the fifteenth day of the first month. At that time, this was rumored throughout the capital, leading many to harbor doubts.

Consequently, the matter reached the imperial ear. On the appointed day, he ascended the seat as usual without any ailment. Nevertheless, officials and commoners gathered in great numbers, and the Emperor also secretly dispatched an imperial messenger to observe his well-being.
He even issued a distant command for his attendants to all proceed to the hall. When the meal was finished, the meditation chamber fell into profound silence.
However, a white vapor swirled about. An attendant entered the curtain and saw the ascetic-monk Yuanxing standing before the couch, holding a scroll in his hands;
Yüan had already passed away. The attendant hurriedly took the scroll from the monk’s hand to examine it; it was a verse of farewell at the end of his life. The verse said:

"Breaking the scale-weight, overturning the public proclamation, Suddenly emerging before the trigger-mechanism, Where even a crow’s flight cannot pass. The fourfold assembly earnestly requested him to remain for ten days.
On that day, he received his final offering from the imperial court; his countenance did not change in the least.

At the age of seventy-four, having sat in meditation for fifty-nine summers, Master Huiyuan, who had long kept a black monkey that was so well-trained it understood human speech—whom he named "The Monkey Practitioner" (Yuan Xingzhe)—also departed peacefully.
His junior disciple Daoji, along with the monastics and laypeople, enshrined Master Huiyuan’s stupa at the Wuyou Temple.
Feng also buried the Ascetic Ape (Yuanxing) at his side.
He offered this eulogy: "The Lady Ji was one of supreme integrity. I have examined the proclamations of Fohai;

like the Son of the Red Emperor severing the snake while the Goddess of the Night wailed, his appearances and disappearances were unrestrained and pervasive, similar to those of the Fifth Patriarch, Master Yan. This is marvelous."
Xi Ning was not startled by the mere sound of the wind.
Regarding the monk Jidian Shuji of Huye:
he was born into the noble Li clan of Tiantai in eastern Zhejiang; his name was Daoji. His mother dreamed of swallowing the sun.
She became pregnant. At the time of her delivery, a crimson light illuminated the chamber. National Master Bencheng of Lingyin Monastery considered her a treasure among the Dharma;
he rubbed her head and offered a prophecy. When Fojian was eighteen, he went to Lingyin to see Master Xiatang Yuan. Yuan immediately shaved Fojian’s hair for him.

Not more than a year had passed before his spiritual realization surpassed all others, and Yuan granted him formal certification (*inka*). However, Fojian was by nature wild and simple, and he moved about—
In the Sangha hall, he would frequently speak out loud in defiance of the assembly. The assembly reported that Huiji had violated the monastic rules to Master Yuan.
Yuan said, "The Chan school is vast and expansive; how could it not tolerate one eccentric monk?

Thereafter, he often went to Cold Spring Pavilion to wrestle with young men, or sang wildly in wine shops, or went to Call the Monkeys Cave to lead the monkeys in performing somersaults together. At times, he would carry meat and wine, defiling [the monastery].
At the place where he was reading the sutras, the administrator again spoke to Yuan. Yuan considered only that this eccentric monk should be protected; thus, he was called Jidian (Crazy Ji).
After Master Yuan passed away, Ji’s eccentricity and drinking became even more extreme. The temple could no longer tolerate his presence, so he subsequently took up residence at Jingci Temple.
The Elder Dehui of Jingci marveled at Ji’s conduct and invited him to serve as the Secretary. Nevertheless, in the end, he could not [contain Ji].
Jiǔrěn (Tolerant of Alcohol) of Jìngcí Monastery also fell short of Huī in his generosity. Huī’s biased protection was likewise like that of Xiètáng.

The monastery secretary frequently visited the residences of the sixteen court officials in private; the two Grand Commanders Máo and Chén daily provided him with fragrant wine, such that no one dared to criticize him.
When the secretary was intoxicated, he would compose poems of several thousand words, whose expressions transcended conventional thought.

Those who understood him revered him. One evening, while intoxicated, he lay down at Shili Song Temple (Ten-Li Pine Temple). The abbot had someone help him back to his quarters, where he fell into a deep sleep beneath the kitchen.

During the first watch of the night, he suddenly rose and paced along the corridors, shouting wildly that a fire had broken out. The assembly took him for a madman. At midnight, a glass-like fire erupted from the Hall of the Arhats;
the flames caught the ends of the banners and the temple was destroyed. Master Hui then left behind a verse and passed away amidst the light. [This was recorded by] the Secretary.
He subsequently requested that [Falin] become the abbot of the main hall at Shaolin Temple on Mount Song. Falin’s worthy secretary was also like Master Huī;

through his skillful deployment of spiritual mechanisms, he moved the imperial court in a dream, and within less than two years, ten thousand pillars and a thousand beams were restored to their former splendor.
Furthermore, as the shadow-walls (*yingbi*) for the two corridors had not yet been completed, he wished to reach his new post as the Warden of Peace (*Anfu*) in Lin’an to have them finished.

Chongsheng stopped him, saying, "It must not be so. I have heard that when Lord Wang was in his humble days, he frequently sought alms at a monastery where monks were being fed. He was subsequently betrayed and sold by the monks of that temple.
Lord Wang was enraged and inscribed upon the temple wall: 'When meeting a guest, [the monk's] head is like a turtle; when encountering a meal, his neck is like a goose. Now..."
"Whenever anyone sees a monk, they all resent him. How could you possibly gain access by interfering with them? The assembly will surely obstruct you.

The secretary smiled and agreed, then went straight to the front of the government office. He happened upon the Duke as he was ascending the hall; the secretary then poked his head out and gazed toward him. The Duke was greatly incensed.
He ordered Yin to seize him and prepare to flog him. The Secretary said, "I am the secretary of Jingci Monastery, the monk Jidian.
I have a certain karmic connection that only you, Excellency, can understand; I have come specifically to deliberate with you.

The official had also heard something of Jidian’s reputation for poetry and wine, so his mind was somewhat eased. The secretary then composed an eloquent verse concerning Prince Wang’s past inscription on the wall.
He recited it for him. The Duke laughed heartily and invited Master Ji to stay overnight in his private quarters. As Master Ji was about to leave, he gently alluded to the meaning of the shadow-wall.
The Duke then donated three thousand strings of cash to repent for his previous transgressions. Thus, Master Ji’s propagation of the Dharma was unhindered.

The general categories are as described above. As for his unraveling of karmic knots, the quelling of calamities, his playful mastery of *samādhi*, and his manifold extraordinary traces, they are so numerous that they cannot all be recounted.
One day, he entered the city to visit old friends; after drinking wine and composing poetry with Director Zhang, he returned home and lay down ill.
At Anle Hall below Mount Song, he asked the Master [Zhaoqing]. The Master smoothed his mat and declined, saying, "I am ashamed. Thereupon, he requested that the Master shave the head of Shen Wafan.
Wafan was a man of great sincerity and integrity who had served the Master for many years. The Master immediately ordered Wafan to inform his former patrons of his poetry and wine.
Wafan then bathed, sat in the lotus posture, wrote a verse, closed his eyes, and passed away. The Grand Marshal and the court officials were all present.
He proceeded to Jingci Temple, where all the venerable elders from the various mountains had assembled; the funeral procession numbered in the thousands.

Upon reaching the front of Hupao Temple, he was cremated, and countless *śarīra* relics were recovered. As they returned to the front of Jingci Temple, two itinerant monks came to pay their respects to [Zhao]song, saying:
"We just passed by the Six Harmonies Pagoda and encountered Master Ji Gong, who entrusted us with this letter and a pair of monk’s sandals."
Sung was greatly startled and said, "When Ji Gong was passing away, I exchanged these shoes for his worn-out sandals.

Opening the sealed package before the assembly, its words were most earnest and sincere, totaling two hundred and nine characters. On the back of the paper, there was further attached a verse which says:
'Cannot see it; mistaking a colander for a wooden ladle. Last night at the third watch, the moon was due west. The Qilin shook loose the golden tether.'"
In my youth, I once went to Yanmen Pass; with eyes blurred by intoxication, I could clearly distinguish the old from the young.
Recalling how an arrow once struck me before my face, even now my hair stands on end and my bones shiver with cold. Because no one recognized my true face, I traveled once more to Tiantai.
After another ten-odd days, a messenger from Qiantang passed beneath the foot of Mount Tiantai and met Master Ji, who again sent [this message].
There are two poems that follow. Furthermore, fifty years later, a man from Fan Village delivered timber to Jingci Temple, stating that it had recently been procured through the efforts of Master Ji.
The eulogy says: Master Ji penetrated the essential pivot beneath the words of Xiatang; he then employed the mysterious mechanism beyond the ordinary, mingling with the world and sharing in its dust.

Sometimes he would mock the wind and play with the moon, revealing the heart-source of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. At that time, people did not find him strange, but rather looked upon him as a "mad monk"—how fortunate!
When his manifestation ended and he passed away, the world began to honor him as the "Master," an unfathomable man. Was this not the case? At the end...
Later, the true efficacy of his illumination upon all things was indeed vast. Alas! To examine Master Jian’s life:
had it not been for a sage responding to the world, one could not have sought out such a person who exhausted skill through simplicity; even to be born as such would have been impossible.
*Biographies of the Jewel-like Monks of the Southern Song, Yuan, and Ming Dynasties*, Scroll Four;
*Biographies of the Jewel-like Monks of the Chan Forest of the Southern Song, Yuan, and Ming Dynasties*, Scroll Five: Chan Master Mianjie.
The Chan Master’s name was Xianjie; his style name was Mian. His ancestors were a prominent clan from Fuzhou, and his surname was Zheng.

His mother dreamed that a white-haired *dhūta* entered her chamber and she gave birth to him. On the night of his birth, celestial music was heard throughout the region, though no one knew what auspicious omen it portended;
his parents kept this secret. From childhood, the Master was exceptionally brilliant and perceptive, possessing a profound and dignified bearing, and he served his parents with filial piety.

He heard that his parents possessed virtuous conduct and exhorted him to travel far away. Consequently, he was able to receive the full ordination. Without seeking companions and without preparing bedding, he wore but a single robe through both cold and heat as he traveled to knock at the doors of various regions.
The masters of those regions held him in high esteem. In his later years, he relied upon Ying’an, whom he frequently encountered with harsh rebukes and scoldings.
Without needing a single word, Master Mo silently grasped his karmic potential. One day, during a late-evening formal inquiry (wanshan), Ying’an asked: "What is the True Dharma Eye?
Master [Muzhou] immediately stepped forward and replied: "A broken sand pot. Ying’an nodded in approval and ordered him to enter his service. He became immensely popular among the assembly.
When he took his leave to return home and visit his parents, Ying’an sent him off with this verse: "Having attained great penetration through the opportune phrase," [The rest of the verse follows.]

Yangkuo’s crown has been opened for four years now; though interrogated, he remains utterly traceless. Although the bowl and robe have not yet been entrusted to him, his spirit and bearing swallow the heavens and earth.
Yet he takes the Eye of the True Dharma and calls it a broken sand pot. On this journey to pay his respects, take care not to simply follow in his footsteps.
I have a final word; when you return, I require that you abide by it. When the Master returned from Min, Ying’an then—
Ascending the hall, the Master took his seat and said: "One blow leaves a scar; one slap leaves a hand of blood. Yet the old blind donkey Linji has not been seen through to this very day.
At the summit of Mount Sumeru, waves lap against the sky; yet in the waters of the great ocean, there is not a single drop.
How magnificent is the man of true substance! With three eyes upon his brow, he discerns dragons from snakes; at the tips of the hundred grasses, he captures tigers and rhinoceroses."
With the strength of a single hair, he pierces the nostrils of all people on earth; sitting firmly, he cuts off the tongues of the monks.
Nevertheless, he has not yet stirred the upper orifice. But what is this upper orifice? Go ask the Head Seat Jie in the hall.
Not long after, he went to teach at Wugu in Quzhou; his integrity and bearing were much like those of Ying’an, and his manner of receiving others was entirely so.
Just as with Miaoxi, those who had long grown weary of the monastic forests all rose up and returned to him.

Zhang Zi of the Secretariat, who was dedicated to the ancestral style, converted his residence into Huiyun Temple and invited the Master to occupy the abbot’s quarters. Moved by his sincere faith, the Master showed him the "Mu" (No) koan of Zhaozhou.
Having grasped its essential meaning, when the Master traveled from Xiangfu to Jiangshan, and subsequently through Huazang and Shuangjing, [Zhang followed].

Yang Qi served him as an attendant. Later, when he moved to Lingyin Monastery, there was no space to accommodate his bedding and calendar, so he invited the late Pōān to share the seat and receive disciples.
The Master was once summoned to the imperial court and sometimes stayed overnight in the Neiguang Hall.

Although the Emperor repeatedly wished to bestow gifts upon him, the Master repeatedly declined on the grounds of illness. His teacher, Yan Kangchao, said: "When in straits, one perfects oneself; when in prosperity..."
Thus, to provide universal relief for the world is the natural order of things. Moreover, a golden age does not recur, and a sagely sovereign is difficult to encounter.

Yet my Dharma-brother constantly employs the strategy of "concealing the six," disregarding the vital pulse of the lineage that has been suspended from above. He does not grasp it even in the morning. The Master said:
What you have observed was originally intended as a general discourse; however, the propagation of the Way and the establishment of teachings must accord with the times.
At this juncture, while the palaces and monasteries of the capital region shimmer with gold and green glaze, the lofty spirit of the ancient masters is nowhere to be heard.

It is hoped that those who are mature and steadfast may be able to remedy the maladies of rash advancement and recklessness. Furthermore, I am currently crossing the Huating River on my way to seclude myself in the Western Mountains.

Is this not precisely the way to provide universal salvation for the world? He earnestly requested retirement to Pingjiang. In the spring of the Jiachen year of the Chunxi era, a messenger from Tiantong arrived.
The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "Last August, I received an imperial decree granting me leisure and ease.

Casting off my nature as a wandering cloud and water, I strolled freely to Mount Yang. My disciples from the Yuan residence joyfully pursued me with great effort; thus I have resided in this hermitage for three [years]."
This month, my heart opened wide as the universe. Suddenly, I received a letter from Sīmāng (Sì Míng). The meaning of your correspondence was profound and lingering.
Tiantóng’s Dharma seat is vacant; your Excellency’s words remain upright. From afar, you dispatched a special messenger, regardless of the hardships of the journey.
This mountain monk, approaching the twilight of his years, dares not deceive himself. Beating the drum to welcome him, the fourfold assembly also rejoices. The former Master has not yet...
"If it were already understood, there would surely be waves stirred. I venture to ask the assembly: what was it that the former master had not yet understood?
'Each time one drinks water, one swallows it; Linji and Deshan both turned red with shame. Entering the monastery, he established the retreat according to the legacy of Ying’an.
Ascending the seat, he said: 'An old case from several decades past; today I bring it forth once more to analyze and judge. Let [it be]..."
"Those with iron eyes and copper pupils must also be dragged into the red furnace to be smelted.
If someone among the assembly were suddenly to emerge, unfooled, and say, "The entire great earth is this very red furnace; even it could not smelt me through," you should simply say to him:
"I know you are making your living inside a ghost cave. In the year of Bingwu, during the Chunxi era, he passed away peacefully without illness.
The stupa was erected to the east of the monastery. Those who succeeded him in the Dharma were twelve people, including Po’an Xian and others;
while Chengzhao took Zhenjing as his model, he himself resided at Tiantong.
The commentary states: Ying’an Kuang emulated the style of Huqiu; those who entered his courtyard were numerous indeed.

Because he discarded the guiding line and compass to determine right and wrong, I privately took offense at him. However, when Mian opened the way for transformation, the mountain was no longer constrained by its peaks.
That the sea does not restrain its surging waves—is this not because its wisdom surpasses that of its masters? Is it not different from those who merely walk alongside it, eye-to-eye?
Otherwise, how could the spirit of the Linji school have spread to the four and seven patriarchs in the West and reached the two and three patriarchs in the East?

Chan Master Yuwang Kan was born into the Mao family of Siming; his name was Miaokan and his style name was Xiaoweng. At the age of ten, he was taught secular classics, which he could recite from memory after reading them once, yet he took no pleasure in them.
He subsequently followed Master Yan’an Qin to devote himself to the study of Buddhist teachings, eventually becoming a fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*). He received [the precepts].

He did not disregard the instructions of Chan Master Quan Wuyou. After taking up residence there, he maintained the fundamental principles with unyielding integrity, and his reputation reached the imperial court.
The court repeatedly offered him prestigious mountain monasteries, yet Wukan remained composed and indifferent to such honors. At that time, everyone vied to admire him.
Initially, Wukan had studied under Songyuan at Lingyin Monastery but found no resonance; it was only by chance that a practitioner read Wuyou’s own eulogy, which began: "The ladle..."
He cannot be ranked even among common villagers; there is not a single trace of literary refinement within his breast.

He once attempted to fathom the very bones of empty space, yet he has earned only a reputation for foul-mouthed talk that fills the rivers and lakes. Kān was so struck with awe that he longed to see the Master in his entirety.

Before he could act upon this thought, Master Quan visited Lingyin Monastery. Kān felt fortunate at this encounter. As Songyuan led the assembly, Quan said: "Just now, Master Songyuan raised [the case]..."
The Story of the Bamboo Whisk. This caused Tiantong to suffer defeat. Do you all wish to know? Listen to this verse:
Gripping the black-lacquered bamboo whisk, A thunderclap leaves no time to cover one’s ears. Deshan and Linji stare blankly; How can those who are muddled insert a word?
If you can gain faith and entry here, then follow me to Tiantong. There, you shall offer incense and enter the room. Master Quan, regarding Zhao...

Zhou Wuzi invited Fukan to respond to a challenge. Quan suddenly struck him, whereupon Fukan attained great enlightenment and said, "The great poison-drum resounds through heaven and shakes the earth;

it turns one's head and brain, leaving a corpse strewn across ten thousand *li*. Quan approved of this. Later, Fukan appeared in the world at Miaosheng Temple, was transferred to Jinwen, and then to Guangxiao.
From beginning to end, he never practiced leniency. His sincerity moved the spirits, resulting in miraculous responses. The year was the Yihai of the Shaoxing era.

In the tenth month, prayers were offered for rain. The local officials wished to follow the precedent set during the reign of Emperor Huizong, placing the Daoist master to the left of the Buddhist monk and thereby honoring his arts of medicinal water and talismans.
Zhi can strongly argued that this was improper, whereupon he retired to Xuedou. Heaven ultimately did not send rain, and children and elders sang a rhyme:
"To place the right on the left—Heaven said it could not be. In the fourth and fifth months, fires broke out in the ponds and pools; the news spread abroad.
In the morning, the old order was restored, and the rain subsequently ceased entirely. The Prince of Wei then requested that Huikuan take charge of Bao’en Temple on Mount Tai.
Since Mount Tai had previously lacked the Vinaya school, Huikuan deliberated upon establishing ten temples as ordination platforms to widely propagate the *vinaya*.

Thereupon, the fourfold assembly gathered like clouds, and his transformative teachings spread throughout the southern regions. Consequently, even a butcher’s father practiced compassion, and the thieving dog ceased its depredations. By imperial decree, he resided at Huqiu Mountain.
Not long after, Qiu was promoted to Lingyin Monastery. Prince Wei specially constructed Daci Temple and invited him to serve as its founding patriarch.
Subsequently, he retired to Upper Bai. There, Chen, the Magistrate of Tai Prefecture, invited him to reside at Ruiyan.
After a short time, he moved again to Jiangxin Temple; this was the year of Renyin in the Chunxi era. At that time, Emperor Xiaozong was deeply devoted to the Buddhist scriptures and frequently...

Suddenly, a memorial was presented ordering monks and Daoists to purchase purple robes and honorary titles to serve as abbots of major monasteries. [The Emperor] remarked with great astonishment: "Upon careful examination..."

"In that case, could merchants and traders all preside over the Dharma? My Way would be in peril. He then went to the palace gate to submit a memorial, offering several thousand words of urgent and direct admonition;

the proposal was subsequently shelved. In the *Guichou* year of the Shaoxi era (1193), Fozhao again responded to the summons of Emperor Shouhuang, and as the seat of Yuyuan Temple remained vacant, he appointed Kan to fill it.
Having served as the abbot of many famous monasteries, Kan’s spiritual power never failed to strike its mark; he deeply understood that the capacities of sentient beings vary.
[He was] dull-witted. Yet, the Dharma has neither small nor large. He once showed this verse to the assembly of students:

"The carriage and oxen ache behind their heads, yet the whip is pressed harder; One casts away the gold and embraces a common brick. Chasing evil and following the heterodox until this day— This is not the Buddha of the Mind, but a mistaken transmission.
He further said: "At the eastern edge of the city of Awakening, there is an old woman with hair white and disheveled, yet full of spirit. She [is] with the Buddha..."
Those born together loathe seeing the Buddha; as for the wicked, what can be done about the wicked? It is further said: "Liuyi’s delivery of the letter was known only to himself;
gaining an advantage is actually falling into a disadvantage. One abandons one's own flesh-and-blood son, yet cherishes and deeply pities an adopted child.

Nowadays, people have fallen into decline; there is no one worthy of mention. You, Master, have now manifested your traces at Lingyin, benefiting sentient beings and engaging with all things.

Your coming and going should be like autumn leaves or spring clouds—letting them gather and disperse according to conditions. Whenever you meet with high officials or men of noble rank, you must strive to overturn their habitual patterns and sever their thieving minds.
If even the slightest thought of a private residence lingers in your breast, you will become muddled and indistinct.

If one merely conforms to worldly standards, they become a master of the common run; though they may preside over ten thousand followers, what is there to be esteemed? His words were exceedingly earnest and poignant.

In the spring of the Gengshen year of the Qingyuan era, he wrote his final testament for submission to the throne and composed a brief verse to request Vice Director Zhang to oversee his funeral affairs.
Then, sitting cross-legged, he addressed the assembly, saying: "The mirror of karma hangs high. For seventy-two years, with a single blow, I have reduced it to powder."
[The stone] shattered. The Great Way was thus made level. He bid farewell once more to Governor Cao Tong and passed away with his eyes closed;

Who could achieve greater merit than this? Is it not right to call him the "Great Fruit"? Yet one must realize that his vast and majestic principles remain intact.
Furthermore, it is originally stated in the *Miaoxi*:
"Chan Master Min of Huazang was born into the Zhu family in Jiading Prefecture; his name was Anmin, and his courtesy name was Miyin. He possessed extraordinary features, and his voice was like—"

He occupied the first seat; amidst a cluster of a hundred flowers, the udumbara flower appeared. When Chonggu initially began his lectures in Chengdu, he was widely praised as being peerless in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
While visiting a friend at Zhaojue Temple, he happened upon Yuanwu’s informal sermon (*xiaocan*). Yuanwu raised the story of Zhaozhou’s use of Nanquan’s three calls to the attendant, saying:
"It is like a person writing characters in the dark; though the characters are not yet formed, the traces of the brushstrokes..."

The next day, he prepared to depart but hesitated, unable to decide. A friend said to him, "Since you have already taken charge of disciples and led the assembly, your reputation for literary brilliance is daily increasing.

"Is it not possible? he asked. "To harbor such thoughts within your breast—would that not be a sickness? The layman replied, "Yes, sir. He then lit incense and entered the room.
Yuanwu slowly raised the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and questioned him as to where his mind was located. The layman presented many interpretations of the meaning.

Yuanwu laughed and said, "Master of the Tripitaka, when you enter hell in the future, do not resent this old monk for not having told you. The layman was struck dumb with astonishment and humbled himself. Hu...
He knelt and begged to be told the former meaning. Wù laughed again and said, "The literary brilliance has already been revealed.

Míngmín bowed his head and departed, sighing, "The Chan school truly possesses its own strengths; the 'dragon' of Duke Yè is not worthy of esteem. He then dispersed from the lecture hall and took refuge under him.
One day, Riyue said to Yuanwu, "Master, please stop citing these stories. Wait until I speak of them myself.

When you shout and strike the meditation seat, is this not 'reversing the hearing to hear the self-nature,' whereby that nature achieves the unsurpassed?"
Dowu said, "So you have been making your living right here all along! Upon hearing this, Min attained realization. He then asked again, "What is it like when the ancient sail has not yet been raised?

Leaping up with joy, he stepped forward and said, "The ancients said, 'A single drop falls into a vast abyss,' but they did not realize that the abyss itself..."

When Fojian heard of this, he laughed and said, "When will it blow to the gates of Jiangshan? There is another matter to be discussed. Later, Min went to visit Jian, who asked him:
Foguo has a phrase that he has never once spoken to anyone in confusion. Has he ever spoken it to you? [The monk] replied, "Shut your dog’s mouth!
Foguo changed his expression, shook his voice, and said, "This is not the principle. [The monk] said, "No one is snatching away your salt and tea bag; why are you shouting?
Foguo said, "If Foguo does not speak for you, I shall speak for you. [The monk] said, "..."
When the Abbot hesitated, Min withdrew from the monastery to seek instruction elsewhere. Master Jian laughed heartily and received him with exceptional courtesy.
Min subsequently began teaching at Baoning. Thereupon, the monastics and laypeople of Jiankang forcibly invited Min to Huazang;

once he had ascended the seat, they entrusted the seals and keys to him and each departed from beneath the dais. Realizing he had fallen for a trap, Min sighed and said, "For thirty years I have been playing with horse-riders."
Today, I have instead been kicked by a donkey. At that time, the patriarchal style of the school flourished greatly within the realm;

even the smallest monasteries gathered a thousand monks. Yet, Master Min alone maintained a strict standard of conduct, never allowing miscellaneous guests to perform the duties of the kitchen. He would personally attend to these tasks himself.
When the Dharma drum sounded and dragons and snakes vied for their positions, he did not attempt to restrain them. Addressing the assembly, he said: "The multitude sells..."
The flowers alone sell the pines; though their green hue is not as red as the blossoms, when one calculates it, they ultimately do not harmonize with the times.

"Return, return! Into the midst of the verdant mists. It is laughable that the ancients spoke thus; it is much like fleeing from a peak to fall into a ravine, or avoiding drowning only to throw oneself into fire.
How can this compare to following one's lot and seeking out one or two [disciples] at the edge of the eight-foot or five-foot mattock?
"Even so, this mountain monk does not want even half of it. Why? Because the wealthy lament that a thousand mouths are too few, while the poor resent having even one body too many.
Furthermore, he retired from Huazang to Zhongfeng in his native village, where he took up Yuanwu’s white whisk.

Yuanwu asked, "How do the sages of the past receive people? Yin held up his fist. Yuanwu said, "This is what this old monk uses;
what about that which the sages of the past use? Yin struck him with his fist, and Yuanwu also raised his fist. As their fists met, they laughed heartily. One.
The public’s perception was transformed, and Master Min’s reputation grew even more esteemed. Ultimately, he passed away without illness at his native mountain.

Upon cremation, his heart and tongue remained unburnt, and countless *śarīra* relics were found. Commoners dug the earth about a foot deep and obtained them all; they were particularly radiant, brilliant, and pure.
Chan Master Binyin of Mount Jing was a native of Jiazhou. His style name was Biéfēng. Initially, he pursued the study of Confucianism; later, he abandoned Confucianism to become a monk.

He studied the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, but subsequently abandoned that as well to follow Chan Master Huázhàng Mín, from whom he attained realization of the essentials of the mind. His master, Yuánwù, would often...
This was called "Praising Him. Because Yinyuan possessed strategies that surpassed his master, his reputation soon became widely known.
He then went to pay his respects at Miaoxi, introducing himself as a "Dharma nephew from Xichuan. At that time, the many scholars at Jingshan secretly laughed at him.
Miaoxi asked, "Before you have even left Jianmen Pass, I have already given you thirty blows! Yinyuan then prostrated himself, saying, "It was not right for me to trouble you, Master."

Shang, Miaoxi was delighted and looked to his left and right, saying, "You all will not be able to keep up on horseback. That day, ten thousand people gathered, causing the monastic forests to tremble.
Thereupon, he returned west to propagate the Dharma; those who were long renowned as the "Tigers of Meaning" from the two river regions all followed Yinyuan.
Yinyuan further comforted them regarding the commencement of the lectures, saying: "The teachings of Chan and the scriptures are of one essence, yet you..."
"Bai Qi'er, you have expounded the teachings with a heart free from deception; this is the essence within the teachings. I shall propagate the essence with a heart free from deception;
this is the teaching within the essence. When our Buddha first turned the Wheel of the Four Truths at the Deer Park, Kauṇḍinya was the foremost among those free from deception.
Later, when he held up the flower at Vulture Peak, Kāśyapa was likewise..."

Deception is the ultimate end [of all things]. Therefore, during the more than three hundred assemblies in which I discussed the sutras, I did so entirely through the method of non-deception, thereby benefiting the assembly through non-deception.
You gentlemen, simply reflect upon yourselves: are you able to be free from deception?

Once you are free from deception, if you employ a tongue of non-deception to disseminate teachings of non-deception, then are these teachings and the [original] school one or two? I urge you all, sirs, to strive in this. Furthermore, Yin—
He left the Gorges and resided at Baoning. Next, he moved to Jingshan. From Jingshan, he transferred to Xuedou, and from Xuedou, he was appointed to the dual peaks of Tiantong (Shuangjing).

His assembly was vast and flourishing. He once addressed the assembly, saying: "When the World-Honored One first attained perfect enlightenment in the Deer Park, he turned the Dharma wheel of the Four Noble Truths, and the bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya was the first to realize the Way. Zhenjing [Huichao] held up his staff and said: 'Now...'"
Inside the Cave of New Riches, he simply turns this staff. He then picks up the staff and strikes it on the left side, saying:
"Is there anyone here who attained enlightenment at the very beginning? If there is no man of substance, one must have the will to pierce the heavens.
Do not walk where the Tathāgata has walked. He then lets out a shout and descends from his seat. If it were Master Yin, it would not be so; today, at Feng...
In the mountains of Phoenix, there was originally no effort; turning the Dharma wheel of the Four Truths likewise required no exertion.

He turned his staff and merely instructed all people: "Walk with slow steps; speak with a low voice. Why? "If you wish not to incur the karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata.
He also said: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time expound hundreds of thousands [of teachings] from a single phrase."
Ten trillion phrases—though hundreds of thousands of millions of phrases may be gathered, they are contained within a single phrase. In the gate of the Patriarchs, there is not even half a phrase.
Just as it is, how many painful blows must you endure? O virtuous ones, tell me: who are the Buddhas, and who are the Patriarchs?
If you say that the Patriarch is the Buddha but not the Buddha, or that the Buddha is the Patriarch but not the Patriarch, you have not yet forgotten the duality of acceptance and rejection.

If you say that the Patriarch and the Buddha are both simultaneously "is," or that the Buddhas and Patriarchs are simultaneously "is not," your recklessness is no small matter. Now, provide a single phrase that cuts off this entanglement.
"How would you say it? he asked. "A tiger wearing a paper hat; it is both laughable and startling. He added, "To take the mind and eliminate delusion—delusion is difficult to eliminate.
To clarify the mind through delusion, the path becomes circuitous. Kick away the bottom of the bucket; without inhibition or hesitation, every step is a lotus.
As he grew old, he remained in constant meditative seclusion, his simple couch worn and sagging—a venerable elder monk indeed.
Whenever he visited and prostrated himself at the foot of his teacher’s bed, his affection and devotion were twice that shown to his own parents. Emperor Xiaozong, aware of this, summoned him;
however, because Zhipin suffered from a foot ailment, he declined the imperial decree. The Emperor granted him a palanquin and had him welcomed into Xuande Hall through the inner Donghua Gate.

Initially, the ritual officials had deliberated on the court protocol for the audience, but when Zhipin ascended the dais directly and sat cross-legged, the assembled ministers all turned pale with alarm.

The Emperor was pleased by his sincerity and forthrightness, and thus inquired about the essential meaning of the *Awakening of Faith*. Zhenyin responded to each question according to the occasion, and the Emperor felt a silent resonance with him.

He subsequently composed a commentary on the *Awakening of Faith Sutra* and commissioned Zhenyin to write the preface for it. From that time on, a sedan chair for Chan masters was stationed at the East Flower Gate (Donghua Men) to attend to imperial consultations.
In the winter of the fifteenth year, Zhenyin earnestly requested permission to live in seclusion in a mountain hermitage. In the first year of the Shaoxi era, he went to visit Zhixian.

Master Ce also bid him farewell with these words. Ce asked for the date of his departure, and Yìn replied, "When the water arrives, the channel will be completed. Upon returning, he sought paper and wrote:

"On the seventh night of the twelfth month, at the hour of the rooster's crow, I shall pass away according to this schedule. His remains were escorted back to the Dharma Hall of the monastery and remained there for seven days;
his complexion remained bright and lustrous, his hair grew longer, and the crown of his head remained warm. After another seven days, they selected a secluded dwelling for his interment.
He was interred to the west of the mountain, and his posthumous title was bestowed as Chan Master Ciben; his stupa was named Zhiguang.
The eulogy says: "Chan Master Min was a tiger among the wings of the Dharma altar. Once he entered the gate of Zhaojue, he suddenly changed his course.
Possessing a nature of brilliant acuity and bearing a dignified, lofty appearance, he was like a monkey reaching for the moon, rushing toward [the truth]."
As for Yang’s *Deer*, is it not the case that days and kalpas increase exponentially? Master [Yang] applied his own methods of healing to Biefeng Yin;
naturally, they merged like water and milk, meeting like a needle and its eye-pin. This serves as the true mirror for the arrogance of ten thousand ages.
This is indeed the brilliance of Xishan; how could it be considered much?

As for Chan Master Yuanyuan of Daolin, his native place and clan name are unknown. He was plain-spoken and possessed little literary talent, being a man free from competitiveness. He once pointed to his chest and said of himself: [text continues]
The official said, "Those who travel to study under masters must possess the eye that discerns the Dharma; otherwise, what benefit is there in treading through iron shoes?
At that time, among the Dharma seats of Wu and Chu, they vied with one another in their outward appearance, yet only Master Guo of Yue’an at Daopei was exceptionally austere.

In his quarters, he kept nothing but a single wooden platform upon which he sat upright like an iron stake, never shedding his robes even amidst frost and snow. He frequently admonished the administrative officers:"
One may use gentle words to entice people, but when they encounter the flow of study, they are immediately led away. Only Yuan remained steadfastly relying on definitive discernment;
though he was frequently subjected to rebukes, he stood firm like a tree-root and did not avoid them. Every time, Yue’an would gnash his teeth and stare at him intently before finally ceasing.
Once, when a donor entered the mountain seeking the Dharma, Yue’an rose and said to the assembly: "When Zhongxi built a chariot, it had one hundred spokes; remove both ends."
He removed the axle-pin, struck a circle, and said, "Do not mistake the mark on the scale-pan;
it is deep. Here, all subtle attachments are completely cast off. Later, Yuan appeared in the world at Daolin in Tanzhou as a Dharma heir of Yuean.
Yuean was the successor of Kaifeng Ning, who had entered the furnace of Wuzu Yan Chan Master. Thus, Yuan was a grandson of Yan who truly captured his likeness. They were of the same lineage.
Under the gate of Yue’an, there were eight disciples, each converting people in a different region. Only Yuan alone was humble and self-effacing in his conduct.
Because the other eminent men vied with one another to rise to prominence, their reputations were often diminished; thus, Daolin’s fame and prestige surpassed them all.
Qionggu Lián once remarked, "There is a 'rebellious scale' beneath Daolin’s chin; it must not be provoked. A monk stepped forward boldly and asked, "What would happen if one were to provoke it? Lián—
He said, "A corpse lies across ten thousand *li*. The monk conveyed this message to Daolin. Yuan said, "The blind shaven-headed one in the deep valley has wrongly applied these words of renown.
The monk requested another response. Yuan said, "I only fear it is not jade; if it were jade, it would be truly marvelous.
Thereupon, those in the Chan lineage came and went, being deeply influenced by his words. A monk asked, "When Xuefeng posed a question, Deshan lowered his head immediately—"
[The Master] asked, "What is the meaning of 'returning to the abbot's quarters'? Yuan said, "A rushing thunderclap and bursting flames.
[The Master] asked, "When Yantou said that he had not yet realized the final word, what did he mean by that? Yuan said, "He came along with me. [The Master] asked, "I do not understand;
where was it that Yantou secretly revealed his meaning? Yuan said, "The ten-thousand-year-old pine stands on Mount Zhurong. [The Master] said, "Three years later, the fruit indeed appeared."
Regarding the transition of life and death: is there not, in truth, anything at all? Yuan said: "Maṇidhāri hūṃ phaṭ. Yuan’s command was such that it could not be issued;
yet once issued, it was like the wind blowing through the grass, causing everyone to submit. However, this led to the decline of indolence, as people turned toward it with ease.

Furthermore, they did not frequent the homes of patrons, but instead made their daily work with hoes and spades their Buddhist practice. When the time came for the communal labor to end and they were returning home, Yuan suddenly took up his staff and addressed the assembly, saying:

Setting aside form, sound, and speech, bring forth a single phrase. The assembly was unable to respond. Yuan said, "Beyond movement and stillness, beyond form and sound, people of this age are unwilling to respond.
As for the mundane and the supramundane, after all, who can truly comprehend them? Having spoken, he leaned on his staff.
He stood solemnly facing the window and passed away.
The eulogy says: "When I read the *Recorded Sayings* of the Patriarch Dongshan, I saw that green mountains and white clouds were free to open and close at will.
Since then, how many venerable masters have emulated him? Is it only when one tries to grasp the bright moon in the blue pool that one realizes its nature? Now, Jian... [text ends].
Master Daolin’s several remarks were quite similar to his; they must not fail to be transmitted. However, Yue’an was unrestrained in his solitary rigidity, yet Daolin followed him.
When the ice melts in Qingyang, it has never happened that the myriad species did not attain their flourishing. This is what one might hope for.
As for Chan Master Baifeng Shun:

Chan Master Shun was a native of the Wen family in Mianzhou. Having abandoned his secular life to travel as a wandering monk, he observed the precious wheel-treasury (ratnacakrakośa) spinning rapidly and suddenly attained a thorough penetration of the principle of the "separate transmission outside the teachings.
He received a prediction of enlightenment from Longmen Fuyan and emerged together with him from the Buddha’s [teachings].
Regarding the Gate of the Eye (the lineage of Chan masters): there were those such as Gao’an Wu, Zhuan’an Gui, and Xuetang Xing.

When Shun resided at Baifang, his fellow disciples all spread their reputations far and wide. Yet Baifang alone was but a few dilapidated rooms, leaning to the east and collapsing to the west, propped up by forked branches.
Day after day, Shun would take his bowl and bag and travel to the local towns and cities; by evening, he might return carrying a peck of grain on his back.
He returned home. When he reached the gate, several dozen people were delighted to join him. Every night they attended the assembly; [Zhao] Shun would invariably sit upright upon a wooden bed.

His followers sometimes stood with bared feet, leaning their ears toward him to listen to his every nuance. Shun said: "Good things come piling up one after another; there is no need for fabrication or contrivance.
Yellow leaves falling in the forest are swept away by the water; white clouds drifting across the valley are rolled back by the wind."
A single cry from the cold wild geese severs all worldly thoughts; as soon as the frost-bell tolls, my mountain crumbles. Yet the white poplar tree has something even more extraordinary:
throughout the night, it stirs the dead embers in the cold hearth. Suddenly, if a monk were to come forth and say, "Old man, you are selling your wares too cheaply! [the master would strike him.]
Reduced to such a state of destitute mendicancy, I, this mountain monk, simply said to him: "Yet you have hit upon it. He further said:

"The rooster crows at the dawn moon; the dog barks at the withered stump. This can only be realized through silent understanding; it is difficult to enter through discursive thought. It is where one cannot see."
The earth shook and light was emitted; where words cannot reach, heaven and earth are dark and yellow. A six-foot-tall man from Fuzhou; the quality of the paper originally comes from Qingjiang.
The assembly clearly hears it spoken, yet it is difficult for people to see. Last night at the third watch, the moon shone through the window.
It is also said: "The wind blows through the thatched roof, leaking from the ridge; the rain beats upon the *kalyāṇamitra*’s eyes, making them wet.
Though it is so clear, you do not realize it; instead, you come here and stand with your head bowed. Having resided at Sūnzhu Bǎiyáng for a long time, he thus exhorted his students.
He possessed subtle and effective strategies. Although he was austere and plain to the point of being unbearable, he had disciples such as Qingyuan Shaodeng who attended him from beginning to end;
later, they all appeared in the world and greatly manifested his reputation. When Shun was afflicted by illness, one day the masters of various mountains hurried to inquire after him.

Shun rose and addressed the assembly, saying: "I have been ill for a long time and have never left my wooden pillow. Whenever people come, they mostly ask, 'How is it? As a mountain monk, I answer according to their questions."
"Facing conditions: outside the window, the yellow oriole has even more to say. As for this seven-foot frame, where exactly does it contract its illness?
You who possess the eye among the assembly, try to point out the source of the ailment for this mountain monk. The assembly vied with one another to offer words of response.
Then Shun clapped his hands once, made a sound of retching, and said, "What a fine wooden pillow! He then passed away. He was cremated according to the prescribed rites.
He collected five-colored śarīra relics, along with various uncorrupted remains—namely, eyes, teeth, tongues, and prayer beads—and buried them to the west of the temple.
Previously, while Shun was at Longmen, the seat of Yunju was vacant. Hearing that Gao’an’s realization was profound and his character upright and firm, he went to Longmen to invite him there.
Gao’an firmly declined. Foyan urged him to go and take up residence, but Gao’an still would not accept. Shun then informed Gao’an [of his intention].
He said, "The wise of former times awaken those who know later; the enlightened of former times awaken those who are enlightened later. This is simply one's natural lot.

He went first to visit Guoqing’s Guang. Guang pointed him toward Wanshou’s Yuan, who asked, "Where have you come from?

One day, hearing the sound of the wooden board signaling the meal, he attained great enlightenment. Without waiting for the weather to clear, he reached Wuning. Just as he arrived, Dongshan was sitting in the courtyard. Then—
Youzhicai said, "Where have you seen gods or ghosts come from? Cai said, "Having shattered empty space, there is no handle at all.
You shook his hand and said, "Not yet. Cai said, "The neighbor to the east sits in the dark; the neighbor to the west curses one another. You was greatly pleased and said:
"In the future, when you establish a monastic community, one capable disciple will suffice. Thereupon, [Fayun] attended him personally for a long time before taking his leave to go to Shuangjing.
Xuyou said to Chai: "To propagate the timely teachings of a single era, one must possess both merit and wisdom in equal measure.
Your merit does not equal your wisdom; this is what I worry about for you. Chai replied: "I only fear that my own eyes are not clear. If my own eyes were clear, I would face the Sage alone."
"A monk eats his meal; what cause for regret is there? You thought him a man of virtue. Shortly thereafter, he indeed guided one person to loudly proclaim the Way of Huanglong.
Originally, You had been a Confucian scholar who felt no inclination toward the imperial examination system; having renounced fame, he left Chengdu. On the road, he met Huang Shan谷 (Shangu).
Seeing that You’s bearing was extraordinary, Shangu traveled with him by boat down to Jiangling, where they eventually donned monastic robes and lived together.
He lived in a thatched hut and found his opportunity under Zhantang Zhun. Zhun’s master was Zhenjing Wen; Master Wen was the disciple of Huanglong Nan.
Thus, Nan was the fourth-generation ancestor of You. At the age of ninety-three, You retired to Wuning and named his dwelling "Tending Oxen" (Dianiu).
The door of Dianu was never free of frequent visitors. He composed a harmonious verse on "Herding the Ox" and sent it to the layman Zhang Wujin. Its [text follows].
The verse says: Two horns point toward heaven; four hooves tread upon the earth. Dragging and snapping the nose-rope, he grazes on dung and excrement.

Wujin burst out laughing and said, "This is the old habit of that mad old man. As for Chai’s presiding over the monastic assembly, his manner of seizing and upholding [the Dharma] was largely similar to that of Tanzhang;
yet his bearing was grave, firm, and resilient, much like Huanglong. Thus, the principle of Huanglong’s Three Barriers reached its renewal through Chai.
I once cited the teaching on the Middle Way: "If one sees me by means of form, or seeks me by means of sound, such a person follows a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata.
Although this is so, it is precisely like catching a mouse and breaking an oil jar.
Master Huai said, "Where are your eyes? While this indeed exposes the old Śākyamuni, what can be done about the fact that he still holds [the whisk] up?

"Those who lick their fingers [of hunger] do so in vain. At Jingshan, it is not so: seeing forms and seeking sounds is perfectly fine. Amidst the shadows of a hundred flowers, one embroiders mandarin ducks;
since one has recognized the golden needle, let the wind blow as it will—the fragrance fills one’s sleeves.

He further said: "To see at once—this is still separated by the Iron Ring Mountains. The old fellow Xuansha’s 'painful awl behind the head' is renowned for its loftiness; how could its fame depend on stubborn obstinacy?"
On a stony path, the traveler’s mouth is like a stone monument. In the autumn of the Gengshen year of the Qingyuan era, he ascended the hall and, stroking the Dharma-seat, said:
"I shall not sit upon this seat again. You should offer me a written memorial. The next day, he bathed, changed his robes, and sat upright.

He commanded the *gongtou* (attendant) to prepare a sacrifice, and the disciples followed his instructions, prostrating themselves with full devotion and kneeling to proclaim the text. As they leaned forward in their exertion, [the Master passed away].
"Listen! May you enjoy this until the end. He gave a smile and then raised his voice, saying: "The four elements have already parted and flown; smoke and clouds return as they please.
On an autumn night, amidst the frost and the moon, a brilliance turns and shines across ten thousand li. He then passed away.

The eulogy says: To look far into the conditions of karmic retribution, one must rely solely on the supreme Dharma-eye. What need is there to concern oneself with the traces of prosperity and decline?

This is, in brief, the life story of Master Zhongfeng. Some may wonder why this master so freely released the "ox-herding" spirit, while his disciples were as numerous as clouds and he would not grant them his seal of approval at all.
Was it that the King’s blade was exceptional? Or was it that the refined gold leaped from the forge? Nevertheless...

That which was not initially accepted or affirmed is precisely what is accepted and affirmed [in truth]. In the Dharma-ending age, seeking someone who can accept and affirm [the truth] begins with the application of "vermilion and yellow" (i.e., biased and superficial judgments).
How lamentable! *Song Yuan Ming Sengbao Zhuan*, Volume Five;
*Song Yuan Ming Chanlin Sengbao Zhuan*, Volume Six.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Ziruo of Zituo Mountain and supplemented by his disciple Xinglei.
Regarding Chan Master Songyuan Yue:
the master’s name was Chongyue, his style name was Songyuan, and he was the son of the Wu family of Longquan. He served under Mian and attained [realization].
After the Master’s passing, seven pagoda-poles were erected in total. There were twelve successors, each with their own name. Yuezhou was highly esteemed by people;
whenever he saw a distinguished guest, he would ask, "A person of great power—why do you not lift your foot?
When seeing a member of the Chan lineage, he would ask, "An enlightened-eyed monk—why is the red thread at your heels never severed? Some would respond.
[Daowei] would frequently smile and look back at him. At that time, it was said that Xue had attained the "pivot" (ji) of Ying’an and the "function" (yong) of Mi’an.
Indeed, in his youth, Xue grew weary of the mundane world and left home; as a layman, he went to study under Lingshi Miaoxi, but failing to reach accord, he immediately ascended Mount Jing.
At Mount Jing, ten thousand monks were flourishing. Yue followed the assembly to listen to Master Miaoxi Gaofeng preach the Dharma;
he was ignorant of anything beyond this, yet he heard Gaofeng highly extol Ying’an as one who had truly received the orthodox transmission of Linji.

Yue then hurried off to visit Ying’an. However, Ying’an became increasingly difficult to approach. Yue therefore exerted himself with renewed vigor, washing his face and exposing his arms, heedless of any discomfort.
Yuanwu Anlan showed it to Yuanwu Yue, saying, "The World-Honored One has a secret teaching; Kāśyapa did not conceal it.

As soon as Yue heard these words, he stepped forward and said, "This leaves the Master at a loss. Anlan shouted at him. Yue had an awakening. Anlan laughed and said, "What has this worldly fellow accomplished?
Yue then requested to have his head shaved; he was thirty years old at the time. Having received full ordination, he entered Min.
He met Mudan Yong. Yong gazed at him intently and said, "The tree has fallen and the vines have withered; do you know where they have gone? He replied, "It is shattered.
Yong said, "Langye said, 'What a pile of firewood! Do you understand? He replied, "Adding a point to an arrow. Yong then let the matter rest. Thereupon, Yue became increasingly self-important.
Yong said, "Whenever you offer a word of response, I cannot surpass you, yet it remains that you have not yet reached the ultimate. He [Yue] departed.
Jirō held the handle of his whisk in his hand. When asked by a person, he could not provide an answer; when testing someone, he could not find anyone who passed.
Jaku said, "For one who acts as a teacher, to cause an ordinary person of this broad world to leap directly into the state of a sage is indeed difficult.

But for one who tests others, if they strike [the student] as he passes right before him, even before the student has opened his mouth, the very marrow of their being is already known—how could that be difficult? Yō raised his hand and turned it over, saying, "I have told you clearly."

"The opening of the mouth does not reside on the tongue. Fenyang went away from him. Upon crossing the mountain pass, he encountered two practitioners sitting side by side discussing the various masters of the different quarters.
Whatever Fenyang praised as being "consonant with his heart," the practitioners would both dismiss it. Fenyang asked, "If this is so, then who accords with your own views?
One of the practitioners took a finger and wrote the four characters: "Mimian Bufan" (Mimian is extraordinary). Fenyang already knew that Mimian was [the one].
The man eventually went to Xishan in Quzhou, where he humbled himself to serve him. As they were about to advance to discuss the profound teachings, Miyuan laughed at him.
Yue remained suspicious in his heart until Miyuan moved to Shuangjing, where he finally attained full realization upon entering the inner chamber.
Muduan said, "Opening one's mouth is not a matter of the tongue. After a long time, he emerged into the world at Chengzhao to propagate the Dharma of the Zen school, thereby repaying [his teacher].
Mimian Huhai was known for his integrity and conduct free from deception; many followed him. He later moved to Guangxiao Temple, where he attained great renown.

During the Qianyuan era, an imperial decree ordered him to transfer to Lingyin Temple, which occurred during his final years. At that time, disciples such as Wenli and others had already begun to propagate the teachings in major centers.
Despite this, Huaiyue continued to ascend the hall and enter the inner chamber, never failing to engage in formal inquiry even on windy mornings or snowy evenings.
Zhong once used the words "Bimao holding a trident" to receive the head-dhūta Xian; he used the words "There is a thief but no stolen goods" to receive the practitioner Zhao;
and he used the words "The study of mind has not been heard of" to receive the Grand Councilor Lu You. After You attained realization, he lived in seclusion at Mirror Lake.
He styled himself Fanglong (Fang-ung). In the autumn of the *Renxu* year of the Jiatai era, when he was seventy-one years old, he suddenly summoned his assembly to bid them farewell.

He spoke a verse which said: "Coming, there is no place from which one comes; Going, there is no place to which one goes. A sudden pivot turns at the profound gate— Even Buddhas and Patriarchs are at a loss.
He sat in the full lotus posture and passed away. His stupa was enshrined on North Peak (*Beifeng*). While Yue resided at Lingyin, he was in no way inferior to Mian Zhongyan.
Initially, Miman resided at Lingyin. Among the assembly of monks on Mount Yue, Miman frequently feigned illness, keeping his door closed and refusing to grant audiences.
Upasaya Qian discussed this privately with Mount Yue, who said, "Not so. A teacher is revered and the Way is honored throughout the ages; one must be a clear mirror for the present age.

Those who recruit the powerful and noble do so thinking their hearts are set on practicing the Way and establishing it, yet they fail to realize that if propriety is slighted, [the Way will not flourish]."
Arrogance arises easily; words may be numerous, yet the capacity for understanding remains shallow. Amidst the calculations of worldly toil, how can there ever be an end?

Since both monastics and laypeople have come for the sake of the Way, they must reveal their true hearts with utmost sincerity and urgency; only then will a single word enter their ears and become a seed of the Way forever.
This is how Maitreya [the Bodhisattva] of Tuṣita awaited Zhang Wujin, and how Xuefeng Chengyuan of Xian County received Fushan Yuan. This is it.
If it were merely the "old woman’s Zen" of narrow-minded practitioners, how could it be worth valuing?
The eulogy says: Master Yue attained realization while still a layman under the words of Ying’an; this was certainly no trivial matter.
Yet he ultimately devoted his life to Miman, penetrating the profound depths of his ancestral lineage. It was like General Fan, clutching his shield, charging into the Hongmen Gate.
Who could have resisted him? Thus, when he was assigned to Lingyin Monastery, his driving away of those who tilled the fields and his seizing of their sustenance were widely known and witnessed.
Otherwise, how could those such as Tianmu Li and his peers—each harboring extraordinary ambitions—have so willingly entered into his sphere of influence?

As for Chan Master Yiyun of Jingci: his style name was Tuigou. He was the son of the Huang family of Minqing, Fuzhou. The Huang family had for generations maintained their lineage through the study of poetry and the *Book of Rites*.

Yiyun possessed extraordinary features; he could read several lines at once. Nevertheless, he was a man of independent spirit who did not know how to compromise or sink into worldly obscurity. Whenever...

Their schools were in decline because they failed to grasp the ultimate source of the sages; each adhered to partial doctrines, thereby misleading later students. Consequently, [Hui]yun—who had thoroughly mastered the principles of nature—was highly esteemed by his predecessors.

At that time, there was an old woman from Hu who lived on Mount Wushi; she was nearly a hundred years old and was proficient in the arts of divination and calculation, possessing a subtle and far-reaching insight that left nothing unnoticed.
People vied with one another to seek her audience, and Yun also went to visit her. The woman was greatly pleased and entertained him cordially for several days, after which she said:
Fayun said, "You are a person of merit who is destined for great fortune. You shall soon return to your own country;

I have a worn-out fur robe which I offer to you as a token of my sincere affection. Fayun accepted it and returned home, but finding it heavy, he opened the seams and discovered that they were filled with pearls and fragments of gold.
Yun lost his footing and lamented, saying, "Alas! A man of seven feet tall has been bought by a barbarian old woman.
He then cast his fur robe into the river and traveled north. There, the scholars of the National Academy were all surpassed by him; consequently, he expounded upon the *Zhongyong*.
Having attained some realization, he tore open his scholar’s robe and departed to seek the Way from Chan Master Shantang Chun.

Chun said, “You, with your intelligent nature, have come to visit this mountain hermitage. This mountain hermit has no great talent; let us try to discuss your point of view so that I may provide you with verification.
Yun then discoursed on the practice of stillness and concentration for over a thousand words. Chun said, “As for what you have... [continued]”

To explain the principle: it seems not to contradict [the teaching]. Yet there is another question: suppose there is a person running forward, with hundreds of thousands of tigers and wolves pursuing from behind.
Another person seizes him and wishes to question him regarding his practice of meditative stillness (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*).
If he answers, the tigers and wolves will close in from behind and he will lose his body and life; if he does not answer, then [he maintains] his practice of meditative stillness.
"Where are you now? At this moment, how exactly do you establish yourself? Yun was utterly bewildered. Master Chun laughed heartily and rose.
For the entire night, Yun was filled with shame and remorse; he beat his breast and sighed, saying, "The study of the road is ultimately not a matter of true realization.
Thereupon, he sought to shave his hair and beard, choosing coarse clothing to urge himself on, practicing with vigor yet without self-conceit. He traveled on foot as far as Wu, where he met Tie...
At An, Tie’an spoke with him and marveled greatly at him. Yun then took his leave again. Tie’an said, “A monastic who embraces the Way must judge others by his own standard;
he must not act with artificial intensity. By remaining in a state of pure integrity, he may startle the deaf and worldly folk as he departs on this path.
When one’s form is divined by its shadow, not even a hair’s breadth of shame arises—only such a person can serve as a model for others. Yun wrote: [The text continues with Yun’s verse.]

The words reached Yun’s ears, and he subsequently visited Lingyin Temple. There, his spiritual resonance met with that of Fozhao. When Fozhao moved to reside at Yuwang Temple, Yun served as the head of the assembly.
Fozhao commanded him to hold the whisk (to preside over the Dharma hall), remarking, "He is truly like Xuetang; it is a pity that our late teacher Miaoxi did not live to see him.
Consequently, Yun donned the *kāṣāya* robe entrusted to him by Miaoxi and went forth into the world at Xiangshan Temple, where he succeeded [Fozhao] in turn.
Regarding Master Yun: Master Yun took the legacy of Emperor Yaoxian’s Buddhist illumination as his model; its scale was vast and its annual expenditures immense.
Yun alone prioritized simplicity and frugality, which caused many to depart. Chan Master Zongyin visited Yun;
beyond serving him vegetarian food, they sat together before an incense burner, engaging in quiet conversation through the long night. Zongyin smiled inwardly and remarked to Yun: "Ice..."

The traditions of the Dàn family have been a source of beauty for a thousand autumns. When it comes to venerable elders or gentlemen who visit our mountain gate, the protocols of ceremony seem impossible to simplify.
After a long silence, Yúnlǎo apologized, saying: "It is not that I am unaware. The Elder’s presence in this world commands such reverence that his virtue is honored throughout the universe;

his annual expenditures alone amount to many millions. In all quarters, people have grown accustomed to these customs, and it is not the case that unless one uses brocade screens and large bowls, [the host will not be satisfied]."

Regarding the reception of guests: Yun once privately marveled at this, considering it excessive. According to my humble view, when a venerable elder comes to our mountain gate out of compassionate kindness, and the abbot happens to be fortunate enough to host him, he should lead the assembly with diligent devotion to respectfully invite [the guest] and universally bestow the benefit of the Dharma;

this is the proper ritual and substance for treating a venerable elder. As for a layman visiting the abbot for the sake of the Way, his face should show no expression of flattery, and his heart should harbor no seeking.
He spoke directly to guide him, enabling the nobleman to recognize the "atmosphere beneath the forest" (the life of a recluse). Was his manner not truly excellent?
Otherwise, as ancient customs decline, one would surely be ridiculed by those with clear vision. Yinyuan greatly approved of this.

During the Qingyuan era, he was summoned to Yunju and Jingci; carrying his staff and traveling across the river, he was accompanied by dozens of fellow monks, all dressed in simple yet dignified robes.
His demeanor was serene and detached. The officials and subordinates of Lin’an, along with the gentry, met him on the road and privately comforted one another;
