they changed his fine robes and honored him as if a Buddha had appeared in the world. Once he took charge of Jingci Monastery, its regulations were standardized and remained no different from those during the time of Yuyang.
He maintained that the true offering consisted solely in the proclamation of the fundamental tenets. On ascending the hall, he said: "The rushing torrent..."
Crossing the blade; swift flames surpassing the wind; the simultaneous act of pecking and hatching; ten thousand *li* from Yaizhou. Some say: "It is like a person learning archery;
through long practice one becomes skillful. But they fail to realize that even before the bow is drawn, hitting the mark has already involved a circuitous detour.
When Zhaozhou arrived at Zhuyou, he leaned his staff against [the wall]. Setting that aside for a moment, consider this:

when Elder Fu said, "The holy arrow has been broken," how could one respond? [Zhaozhou] shouted: "If you do not sleep in the same bed, how can you know there is a hole in the bottom of the quilt? He also said:
Formerly, a monk asked Yunmen: "If one kills one's father and mother, one repents before the Buddha; but where does one repent for killing the Buddhas and the Patriarchs?
Yunmen said: "Exposed! Do you understand? The heavens revolve and wind and thunder roar; the stars shift and the mountains and seas grow dark.
Who knows that beneath this scholar’s cap lies none other than the man of former sorrows? In the second year of the Kaiming era (1206), he fell ill. His attendant monks spread a mat over his bed.

Yun shouted at him to leave, saying, "I am but a man of old bones; what use have I for this? He then planted his staff upright, took his leave of the assembly, and said, "The mind is in a state of frantic agitation;

the spirit of ten thousand people is withered. As for that which lies beyond the Buddha-dharma, when has it ever been stepped upon? At the moment of death, the karmic consciousness is vast and boundless—leave it as it is.
While others were still deliberating, he threw down his staff, closed his eyes, and passed away in silence.
The Eulogy states: In the past, when Gao’an heard that Cheng had resided at Jinshan Monastery in great splendor, he sighed, saying, "The dharma of a bhikṣu prizes purity and frugality;
how could such excess be appropriate? How does this differ from those of later generations who habituate themselves to lightness and fatness?
Will they not feel shame before the ancients? According to the records, even when Tàigǔ was in his prime, he was able to be so simple and austere. His integrity was truly...
Sufficient. This serves as a mirror for those to come.
Chan Master Shan of Lingyin—Master Shan’s name was Shan;
he was a native of Wuxing. His ancestors were surnamed Liu, and his family had held high office through successive generations. As for Shan himself...
At the age of thirteen, his resolve to transcend the mundane world was firm. His parents said to him, "In our family, we spit upon the heights of the blue clouds;
what more do you long for that you wish to pursue this? He replied skillfully, "I wish only to become a Buddha.

His parents were moved by this extraordinary response and, knowing he could not be restrained, permitted him to receive instruction from the śramaṇa Qizheng. His inner conduct was pure and refined, and all people revered him.

He cherished the study of the sutras and śāstras, yet he harbored no settled understanding within his breast. Consequently, he visited various Chan monasteries, but failed to attain ultimate realization.

Later, he went to pay his respects to Chan Master Fozhao Guang and engaged in a debate regarding the koan of the wind and the banner. Guang would not grant him approval. Shanshu earnestly sought clarification and resolution.
Guangshi said, "The dialogue concerning the wind and the banner reveals the total functioning [of the mind]. For a thousand ages, the monastic communities have given rise to disputes over it.
*Tu!* This wood-seller from Xinzhou—gaining the advantage is losing the advantage. Shan raised his voice and said, "Aha! But it is just like this.
Guangshi struck him with his staff and said, "Today I shall open a single thread for you; cut through the nails and sever the iron to revive our school."

From that time on, for several months, Guang did not descend from his hall. When asked the reason, Guang said, "I have fortunately laid down the burden upon my shoulders that my late master Miaoxi entrusted to me.
He then traveled through Heng and Xiang, visited Mount Lu, and nurtured his "sacred embryo" beneath Mount Miaogao.
He stacked firewood to make a dwelling and did not plan for overnight grain stores. He remained there for ten years and was known at the time as the Venerable Master Miaofeng.
He once composed a verse: "The price of rice in Luling—I tell you to know: Amidst the vast expanse of dust, those who recognize it are rare.
Turning my head, I do not know where I have gone; White clouds and flowing waters remain intertwined. He also said: "At times I laugh, and at times I weep."

The melody was high and harmonious, its few notes difficult to restrain; a single stream of pure sound pierced the nine heavens. Before the wind, who could understand the traces of this fragrant legacy?

On a neighboring mountain there was a presiding master (*śāstrin*) who prided himself on his subtle realization of the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra*. He brought several disciples to visit [the master], and after exchanging polite greetings and sitting down, they gazed at one another for some time.
The presiding master said, "Yesterday I saw Dahuì, who had an eight-part verse on the 'eight returns' which says: 'When spring arrives, of itself...'"
The flowers bloom; when autumn comes, the leaves fall again. Old Gautama with the yellow face—cease wagging that three-inch tongue!
Though his words are clever and elegant, they have not yet captured the true meaning of the sutras. Shan suddenly called out, "Head Lecturer! The Head Lecturer responded, "Yes?
Shan said, "Let us set aside the meaning of the sutras for a moment. Can you express the meaning of the Elder Dahui? The Head Lecturer stammered and was at a loss for words. Shan laughed heartily.

He laughed loudly and rose from his seat. The presiding master (zuozhu) withdrew and avoided him for several months. Later, when the formal relationship of teacher and disciple was re-established, [the master] again requested further instruction.
Shan Shan showed him this verse: "On the stringless lute, there is no private melody; When one tune is played, it rolls on and on.
By the flowing water at the broken cliff, few are those who understand; Six times six does not make thirty-six. Shan then traveled east to Mount Yan, where he propagated the Dharma.

At Linhai, Huixin visited Hongfu and subsequently moved to Wannian. There, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Those who have long attended eminent masters look upon the four seas with eyes of emptiness;
their nostrils reach toward heaven. They see what is to be seen; they speak what is to be spoken; they practice what is to be practiced; they employ what is to be employed.
Yet, though they have attained this, they still do not recognize it—namely, that the old monk’s staff is right here. Why then do you [fail to realize] what is already accomplished?"

"A mountain nine *ren* high would not be completed without the addition of a single basket of earth. At that time, Huishan’s reputation filled the region south of the Yangtze River; he eventually retired to Gaoting Mountain.
Both monastics and laypeople subsequently requested him to reside at Ruiyan in Mingzhou. After Huishan had lived there for some time, invitations from Pingjiang and Jinling arrived one after another.
Huishan responded according to the conditions presented, without clinging to notions of acceptability or refusal. Having long presided over the affairs of the assembly, his Dharma...
He instructed Yi-lüe; his disciple Yi-xin followed him. Later, when he retired from Tiantong to Lingyin, it was already his later years.
Although offerings from donors arrived incessantly, his quarters remained desolate, with only a single quilt within the room. His only personal effects were a bamboo rattle and a Zen staff.
In the second year of the Duanping era, he inscribed his own portrait and left it to Longji Zongmao, further admonishing his disciples, saying: "The Semblance Dharma..."

As autumn approaches, the roots of fame and profit run deep, like an elephant submerged in thick mud or a pearl sunk in the vast ocean. The waves of consciousness and the conditions of worldly dust will never reach their end.
Throughout my seventy-odd years as a monk, in all that I have seen with my eyes and heard with my ears, there have been those who protected the Dharma and endured defilement with patience;
yet, when seeking those who do not obey the imperial edicts or receive official summons, they are few and far between.
My lord, those who are like withered trees on a cold cliff—firm and impossible to turn back—are rare indeed. People know only that the Dharma-gate flourishes from its manifestation;

they do not realize that it declines from its flourishing. Thus, the merit of one who has a karmic affinity for the Dharma-gate is of a single moment, while the merit of one who lacks such affinity for the Dharma-gate lasts for ten thousand ages. As the proverb says: "In front of the courtyard..."
Auspicious grasses sprouted. "Better not to have had such good fortune. How could this be mistaken?

On the twenty-eighth day of the ninth month, he wrote a verse, sat cross-legged, closed his eyes, and passed away peacefully. He was eighty-four years old; he had spent seventy-one summer retreats as a monk.
After cremation, countless śarīra relics were found. His disciple Shan-zhen, styled Cang-sou, requested Zheng Gong Qingzhi to compose an inscription for the stupa at Lingyin.
On the western ridge [of this mountain] was Chan Master Longji Jiu.

As for Chan Master Jiu, his style name was Youyun; his secular surname was Wang, and he was a native of Luling. From childhood, he abstained from meat and pungent vegetables. At the age of... [text fragment ends].
19. He took leave of his parents to cultivate the affairs of the Great Sangha. The elder was largely impressed by him.

Subsequently, he traveled everywhere to see those who possessed the Way, yet he did not attend to the chapters and sentences of the *Zongcheng* (the Vehicle of the Lineage). He relied solely on sleep and dreams, often feeling distressed that he could not act as a spiritual director (*zai*).

When Master Hua Zang Shan of Jinling moved to Lingyin, Jue crossed the river to rely upon him; however, after more than a year, their spiritual resonance did not harmonize, and he prepared to seek out another teacher.
Before he had set out, he happened to see a monk reading the self-portrait eulogy written by Zangcengsou. Jue also followed along to examine it, chewing over its words;
he was then struck with awe that the worthy men of Lingyin Monastery were no ordinary folk. The text read: "Chanting Chan has no awakening; knowing characters has a fixed number.
His eyes are triangular like the sorrow of Mount Yan; his face is wrinkled a hundred times like Zhao Po drinking vinegar. One stroke is high."
He departed. In all directions, people dared to say, "Rice is made from grain. Daogu then resolved to seek further instruction from Zhanshan Shanhui, regarding him as his elder brother.

Only after a long time did he finally grasp the essential meaning, whereupon he took his leave. On his way down from Foding Peak, he grew weary from the journey and rested at a mountain villa on a flat rock.

Admiring the lush density of the surrounding woods and mountains, he pointed and asked the villa’s owner about them. The owner informed him, "Within these mountains lies the ancient temple of Longji."
Formerly, this was the site of the hermitage of Master Xiuxi; it had now fallen into ruin. [Master] Miu said, "May I dwell here?

Zhuangzi replied, "There are many wolves and tigers there. If you, Master, can dwell there, why should it not be possible? Miu eventually cleared away the thorns and bound together thatch to live in. He ate from the trees and drank from the mountain streams.

Sometimes, when the snow was cold and he had no lodging, he would eat nothing for days, consuming only a few inches of sweet flag (*achillea*) at a time. At other times, he would go for long periods...
He smiled and chanted: "This mountain monk has his lot dwelling among the misty vines; lacking both rice and coin, I need concern myself with naught.
The waters are like lapis lazuli, the mountains like jade; before my very eyes, there is more than enough. When Master Shan of Lingyin learned of this, he was greatly delighted.
He inscribed his own portrait and presented it to Miao, saying: "On the solitary peak of the Wondrous Summit, the grass grows lush;
across my chest, I rest a bamboo staff of three feet of iron. Only the Buddhas and Longji may know this; the true wondrous secret is not transmitted from father to son.
Thereupon, those of noble aspiration who "ate the wind" and turned toward him established monastic communities based on his example. Miao once wrote upon his gate: "Except for..."
"Turn away from the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue; which of these is your own self? If you can speak thus, I grant that you have personally seen Longji.
If not, then stay outside the gate. Whenever someone came forward to respond, Baozhe would scold and drive them away.
Upon hearing this, the Elder Zhenchang laughed and said, "To provide for others in such a manner—is it not like the miraculous tortoise dragging its tail? Nevertheless, it was indeed the sixth month.
Shuanghua then sent a monk to ask, "How many people has the Master ever received? Zhaomou replied, "This mountain monk has lost his advantage.
The monk returned and reported this to Zangshou. Zangshou merely nodded in agreement. He then drafted a letter of resignation from Mount Jing and recommended Zhaomou to take his place.
Zhaomou said, "The soil over my late master’s grave is not yet dry, and his final instructions remain in my ears. Furthermore, I am a decrepit and unworthy man; what else could I do?"

Those who plotted against him used sweet words and gentle speech, yet he remained a neighbor to the "vermilion and purple" (the high officials). Claiming illness as an excuse, he did not rise from his seat until the age of eighty.
Day and night he never ceased his duties; at night, reclining upon a simple wooden bed, he gathered the assembly around him to listen as he bestowed his instructions, diligent and tireless.
One day he addressed the assembly, saying: "The former master was eighty-four years of age. Although my own age has reached that mark, as for the Dharma..."
"My fortune has declined; the fault lies with my own person. Having spoken these words, his tears fell. He then snapped his fingers once and said, "This alone is the parting word for the assembly.
A monk asked, "What will it be like at the time of the thirtieth day of the twelfth month? Daomou replied, "At the gate, there is no one to collect debts.
The assembly was moved to sorrow and requested him to provide a final expedient means. Daomou said, "A single lamp remains in sight; there is nothing further to say."
He said, "The great earth will sink level and the void will split asunder; [the body] will transform in stillness. He enshrined the stupa atop Mount Foding.

Initially, when the monastics and laity requested that a longevity stupa be built, Baotou firmly refused them, saying, "Why should this old monk die in the morning and be buried by evening, defiling a single patch of earth at Longji alone?
There is no need to search for mountains or select sites. I have always laughed at those who are submerged in their belief in geomancy (xingjia)."

The tomb site flourishes and prospers. Thus, the karmic affinity for the Sage and the Sages is favored by the yellow earth; to look upon it and act accordingly—how could this be the original aspiration?
The eulogy says:

The lineage of Miaofeng, father and son, from beginning to end, whether in action or concealment, did not meet as a mere coincidence, but were in perfect accord. This is what is meant by "the waters and the moon interlacing."
Mirrors and lamps reflect one another; how can this be faulted as being too solitary or steep? The *I Ching* says: "After ten years, she bears a child; this is a return to the norm.
This was said by Chan Master Zide Hui of Jingci Temple.

Master Zide, whose name was Huīhuī, was the beloved son of the Zhang family of Kuaiji. From his youth, he severed worldly attachments and took leave of his kin to receive ordination at Chengzhao Temple.
Carrying his solitary staff, he traveled like a cloud until he met Zhenxie of Changlu, under whom he realized there was something to be verified.
Yet, beneath the "lightning-like" catalyst, he ultimately returned south; the monastic communities he encountered were like inns, which he passed through after a single visit.
He abandoned them and went to pay his respects to Master Jue Hongzhi. Hongzhi’s majestic virtue was sovereign and his reputation for the Way was preeminent in the age;
those who saw him at that time were all struck with awe and trepidation. Yet Daohui alone harbored what he possessed within his heart and did not rely on intermediaries to introduce himself.
He specifically requested an audience. While at the master’s seat, Hongzhi gazed intently at Huì and accepted him.
Huì was slightly suspicious as to why this was so, and thus he volunteered to recite the "Treasure Mirror" verse. Hongzhi summoned Huì to his bedside and interrogated him on the verse.
Huì spoke abruptly, whereupon Hongzhi assumed a stern expression and sent him away. Huì then humbled himself in repentance, casting aside all his previous precious attachments.

"Let it go. One night, while he was going before the Sacred Monk (Śākyamuni) to burn incense, Hongzhi happened to come forward. Upon seeing him, Daohui suddenly attained realization of the Great Principle;
from that time on, his questions and answers were unhindered, and he received the transmission of the seal of approval (*kaji*).

In the Ding-si year of the Shaoxing era, he began teaching at Putuo Shan. He sent word of his proclamations to Hongzhi, who was greatly pleased. His words were as follows: "The north wind is piercingly cold..."
Sweeping the cold forest, fallen leaves return to their root, revealing the bare heart. Myriad streams flow toward the source; the boat has reached the shore.
The six windows reflect into emptiness; a mustard seed meets the needle. This is the original manifestation—do not seek it elsewhere. The nature-ground shines idly through ancient and modern times.
The frost outside the door melts away; spring colors stir the four mountains. All together they form the song of the wooden dragon. It is also said: "The Old Śākyamuni exhausted the principle."

Exhausting one's nature: the Buddha’s golden mouth proclaimed the teachings for the various periods of his lifetime; like pearls rolling and jade turning, yet people called him "the rag used to wipe away filth.
Master Bodhidharma, using the Dharma of the One Vehicle, pointed directly and transmitted alone, facing the wall for nine years without establishing written words;
yet people called him "the Brahmin who gazes at the wall. Tell me, how should one practice so as to avoid [such labels]?
Pointed out by bystanders: "The patched robe covers the head, and all matters come to rest. At this moment, the mountain monk understands nothing.
He also said: "The nest knows the wind; the burrow knows the rain. What is sweet is sweet; what is bitter is bitter.

There is no need for calculation or deliberation. Five times five is always twenty-five; myriad arrangements reach the state of the ordinary. This is being fully satisfied within the monastic community."

A phrase for investigation: Do you all understand this thoroughly? The rustic elder knows nothing of the labors of Yao and Shun; he beats the drum with a deep *dong-dong* sound to sacrifice to the River God.
Within the mystery of the valley and the pivot of the gate, one must investigate from the side. Upon returning to the path, one attains the wondrous: though the clouds move, they are ever at ease;
though the moon is obscured, it shines all the more clearly. Guest and host intersect; the direct and the indirect are both reached. The spring has ended on the Ten Islands.
The flowers withered away. The coral groves were bright under the blazing sun. Thus, the style of Potalaka stood shoulder to shoulder with that of Tiantong.
His relocation to Wanshou, followed by Jixiang and Xuedou, was all undertaken through the earnest exhortations of renowned officials and high-ranking dignitaries.

In the *Chunxi* era, the year *Bingshen*, an imperial decree was issued appointing him to Jingci Monastery. He ascended the hall and said: "Skin and flesh have fallen away, severed from all counterparts;
Mind and body are clearly understood—there is not a single thing. Wondrously entering the profound and tranquil realm of the Way, The jade person uprightly drives the white ox-cart."

Those who reach the stage of wondrous clarity are rare; it is not reached by the conscious mind, but only known through direct realization. Only then does one know that the child of white clouds is truly spiritual—spiritual!
The father of the green mountains shines by himself, his majestic presence ever-present. When the faculty of discernment aligns with the light atop the crown, the eye prior to the kalpas is realized.
Therefore it is said: "The road of Xinfeng is steep and rugged; the cave of Xinfeng is profound and lush. Those who ascend, ascend."

Ah, unmoving and unshaken. The traveler wanders, yet never in haste. Though pavilions and halls exist, those who enter are rare; though groves and springs abound, they do not grow with ordinary trees.
O practitioners of Zen, as for that "one step beyond," its nobility is difficult to clarify. In the palace of lapis lazuli, the sovereign is not merely titled "Honored One";
before the emerald curtain, he must join his companions—precisely thus. At such a time, the needle and thread penetrate the True Principle.
Without falling [into error], how can one establish [the teaching]? With a head full of white hair, he leaves the mountain crags and valleys;
at midnight, he pierces the clouds to enter the marketplace. At that time, those who greatly propagated the tradition of the Caodong school mostly emerged from the gate of Hongzhi.
Among them were Shichuang Gong of Ruiyan, Liutang Che of Guangxiao, Fazhi of Shenquan in Changzhou, and Wen’an.
Cuiyan was his residence; Fazhen resided at Qingliang, and even Dahong and Changlu were all under his jurisdiction.

Consequently, half of those who held official positions in the monastic hierarchy at Jingci were disciples and nephews from various quarters. Their poetic exchanges were so harmonious that they were hailed as the "New Fengcheng Orthoepic.
In the autumn of the Gengzi year, he retired to Xuedou. With white hair falling to his shoulders, he lived in leisure and joy, fondly carrying [his belongings] with him.
The Chan guest spent his days in empty discourse and smiled as the green mountains fell away. He often composed a verse which said: "Layer upon layer, all gone, returning to the ordinary;
The spring is warm, the breeze gentle, and the days grow longer. Outside the door, the birds’ calls are soft and fragmented; Rock-flowers lie in profusion across the mountain hut.
On the twenty-ninth day of the winter month in the year of Gui-mao, he bathed and passed away. He was interred at Mingjue Pagoda.
Commentary:

Master Hui possessed a rare and brilliant disposition, his spirit soaring with sharp acumen. Upon witnessing the shadow and echo within a flash of lightning, he was immediately willing to take up the burden.
When he entered the furnace of Tiantong to be forged into a great vessel, he was able to immediately raise a great voice.
Having reached the ninefold gates, how could his realm not be harmonious? Examining the present and the past in detail, were they not either flowing or stagnant?

You, however, tread upon the full without overflowing; you follow the Way while being able to exercise restraint. How profoundly humble and retiring you are! Your fragrant model stands before our eyes, and we cannot help but feel the longing to look up to you as one gazes upon a lofty mountain.
Chan Master Beijian Jian:

The Chan Master’s name was Ju Jian; he was a native of Tongchuan. His courtesy name was Jingsou, and he was also called Beijian, a title derived from the fact that he resided at Beijian for a long period.
Jian possessed a refined appearance and was accomplished in literature, earning the esteem of his contemporaries. While traveling to Guangfu Temple, he read the *Chushi* (The World Beyond).
Dian immediately cast off his crown and received full ordination. He then went to visit Bie-feng, who directed him toward Tu-du (Poisoned Coating).

Tu-du showed him the essential point of the mind, stating that what he had previously studied could not serve as a point of entry. His state of doubt became fierce and urgent; he often remained standing until dawn.
Once, while passing by Ze-mu Liao, he read the words of Wan-an: "If you wish to know the mind of all Buddhas, simply look toward the mental activities of sentient beings."
He took up the middle consciousness, seeking the nature of the eternal and undecaying mind. He sought realization only within the realm of the shifting and changing of all phenomena.

Suddenly, through this discernment, he realized that Wan’an and Fozhao were of the same lineage. He then set out separately for Lingyin Monastery, where his spiritual faculties harmonized with those of Chan Master Fozhao Guang.
Thereupon, he traveled back and forth among the venerable masters under Miaoxi for fifteen years, exerting himself.
He exerted great power in upholding the fundamental tenets. He then took leave of Fozhao, traveled through the regions of Wuyue and Min, passed through Jiangxi, and went to Luohu to visit Zhongwen.
When they discussed the Dharma, Zhongwen was greatly pleased and said, "You are the one person who follows after Miaoxi.

He then presented him with a bamboo cane—the very same one used by Miaoxi while he resided at the Yangyu Hermitage—and said, "Your lineage will surely flourish. Not long after, he left to take up residence [at a monastery].
Zituo of Tiantai moved to Bao’en and then to Guangxiao, where his reputation grew immensely. He retired to the shaded slopes of Feilai Peak in Wulin;

even high officials sought him out, yet he paid them no heed. At that time, among those who had emerged from the school of Foyin were Lingyin’s Shan, Jingshan’s Yan, Tiantong’s Dong, and Chanshan’s Guan and Shangfang’s Xian. They submitted joint memorials urging the Emperor to appoint him.
He disregarded the summons to serve as Prefect of Xujiang; nor did he heed the envoys from Jiangzhou who earnestly urged him to take up positions at Donglin and Yunju.
Zujian then compiled the *Beijian ji* (The Collected Works of North Gorge) for circulation among the world. Later scholars appended their commentaries to it. Ye Shuxin remarked:
"Master Jian’s teaching handles are truly startling: 'Six times he leaped about, yet his body remained unmoved. Tell this to the neighbor's child."
"Children and grandchildren—applying blue and dyeing green does not prohibit spring. Jian sighed and said: "The harm caused by wolves and tigers is easily understood by the people of the world;
however, the harm caused by literary works to the world is difficult to perceive. When wolves and tigers are on the mountain, the wild herbs and greens are not gathered;

yet when literature deceives the world, the ears and eyes become mired in it. Recently, I have observed that the conduct of contemporary followers is lax and negligent; they do not fail to acknowledge the words of the former sages."

I say: it is not that the traces of the ancient sages are not upheld. However, when the winds of external circumstances suddenly blow, and honor and disgrace have no master, one may seek momentary gratification at the cost of sweeping one's reputation and integrity off the ground.
If this occurs, then all that was previously said and upheld becomes mere ornamented rhetoric used to deceive the world.
The harm of deceiving the world is worse than that of wolves and tigers. My own failing body cannot measure up; I am deeply afraid of this. What I have observed—

What I have heard has been casually recorded in pen and compiled into this collection. If one were to harbor even slight ambition for fame through poetry and prose, they would be a sinner against our Teaching.

Consequently, I destroyed the printing blocks. Later, while residing at Jingci Monastery, his disciple Daguan requested a brief elucidation of the essential meaning of Ga’ān’s *Verses on the Essentials of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Since Jian had long admired Ga’ān’s character, he then composed these verses in response.
He wrote this preface. In the spring of the *Chunyou* cycle year of *Bingwu*, he addressed the assembly, saying: "If one recognizes the One, ten thousand matters are resolved.

Yet even a patch-robed monk who does not recognize a single character—even if he were to act in such a way—it would still not be called the 'Full Manifestation. Where the power of Yu did not reach, the sound of the river flows toward the west.
He returned to his quarters and inscribed the six characters: "The First Day of the Fourth Month—Take Care. When the appointed time arrived, he spoke these words.
After some time, he closed his eyes and passed away. When Jian was first at Zituo, two clans in Weiyu were contending over Mount Bamboo, exhausting their resources without end.
Jian, serving as the Assistant Magistrate of Xianju, exhorted them to cease; he presented them with his "Rhapsody on Planting Bamboo," and the dispute between the two clans was finally settled.
The people of Tiantai sang this folk song: "The brush of Master Jian is as sweet as honey."
The commentary states: When Marquis Huan of Qi fell ill, he neglected Bian Que while the disease was still in the *qīlǐ* (the superficial tissues).

By the time it reached the marrow, even the Lord of Fate could do nothing for him. Yet, for sentient beings in this final age, the discrepancy between their words and deeds is a malady far more grievous than one residing in the marrow.
Therefore, throughout his life, Bei Jian traveled with the constant apprehension that his acupuncture and moxibustion might fail to reach the mark; thus, by means of his writings...
Regarding those who attained liberation through their names, such as the Dharma transformation of Beijian—how could there be any need for further discussion?
Is it not so? *Song Yuan Ming Sengbao Zhuan*, Scroll Six;
*Song Yuan Ming Chanlin Sengbao Zhuan*, Scroll Seven.
Chan Master Wuzhun Shan of Mount Jing:
Chan Master Wuzhun, whose secular name was Shifan, was the son of the Yang family from the capital of Shu. At the age of nine, he relied upon a śramaṇa at Mount Yinping;

when he underwent the examination on the scriptures, his memory was so sharp that nothing escaped his sight. In the fifth year of the Xihé era, he received full ordination and went forth to seek the Way, whereupon he sought to practice seated meditation.
Having received the final instructions from the venerable master Yao-gong, he departed for the gorges with a deep sense of faith. He went to pay his respects to Chan Master Fozhao Guang.

The Master asked, "Where is your place of birth? The Master replied, "Jianzhou. The Master asked, "Have you brought your sword with you? The Master [Daowei] then gave a shout. The Master Guang laughed and said:
This was Wutouzi, who acted recklessly. He then went to Lingyin and visited Chan Master Miman.

Since Miman was not easily met, he entered the quarters of the former Head Seat, Poyan. When Poyan spoke with him, he secretly marveled at him. One day, Poyan invited the Master to visit Shishun Temple.
A practitioner asked, "What is it like when a wild monkey cannot be caught? Poyan replied: "It is like..."
As the wind blew across the water, ripples naturally formed. The Master was suddenly enlightened; he cried out in a startled voice, "Yes! First, he returned home in great joy.

He then entered the service of Master Xian and went to Qionglong. This was because Master Xian deeply recognized that the Master had thoroughly grasped the essential principles of the profound and the pivotal, as well as the roles of host and guest, and deemed him a reliable successor to the True Lineage.
When Master Xian moved his residence to Wolong, the Master took his leave and traveled to Tiantai, where he subsequently established [his teaching].
Famingzhou Qingliang repaid his debt to the late Master Po’an with incense; thus he became renowned throughout Wuyue.

When the Master first stayed at Ruiyan, he dreamed of a person in magnificent robes and cap who presented him with a bundle of thatch. Upon arriving at Qingliang, he saw the image of the monastery’s guardian deity.
This was precisely the one he had dreamed of. Mao was thus the divine surname [of the lineage]. After three years, he moved to Mount Jiao; after another three years, he moved to Xuedou.
Those of great renown all came to join him. He then addressed the assembly, saying: "Face to face, they gaze at one another; eye to eye, they stare at each other.
As for that which is transmitted apart from the robes, what evidence is there? When you reach the gate, set up the bannerpole. Fengxi did not... [continue as requested].
At the Wutong tree, it was said again: "To deliberate upon [the character for] 'earth' (地) with each stroke of the brush—there is nothing to be deliberated upon.

In the place where there is nothing to be deliberated upon, true deliberation truly flourishes. At the head of Dayu Ridge one meets the Sixth Patriarch; at the inn of Aoshan one encounters Master Zeng."

It is also said: "When the thieves' fires meet at the fifth watch, the manifest plunder need not be contested; in the darkness, all is divided according to share, yet at daybreak, each departs as they were.
It is further said: "The face of the sun and the face of the moon are so abruptly manifest that they are difficult to distinguish."
He seemed about to lift his eyes toward two fragments in the sky. The Master resided at Xuedou for three years; by imperial decree, he was appointed to Yuyang.

After another three years, he took up residence at Jingshan. Not long after, Jingshan was destroyed by fire. The administrators were terrified, but the Master took the blame upon himself and returned to them, whereupon the entire community was set at ease.
The Master restored the ruined foundations and preached the Dharma as before. He further requested Hixiu to serve as Deputy Abbot, and then retired.
Geng served as the *jianyuan* (superintendent), Bieshan Zhi as the *huazhu* (fund-raiser), and Xueyan Qin as the *zuoyuan* (head of the assembly). Before long, the temple was completed.
By imperial decree, the Master was summoned to enter the Ciming Hall to ascend the seat. There, he recounted the karmic occasion of Venerable Piṇḍola proceeding to King Aśoka’s palace, saying:
"When the Sovereign utters a single word, it is like the issuing of a silken mandate; the Venerable One’s eyebrows split into eight strands."
The sea breeze was clear and the smoke and waves were stilled; the azure sky was boundless and the waters were limitless.
The Emperor was greatly pleased and bestowed upon him a golden-patterned *kāṣāya* robe, granting him the title Chan Master Fojian. In the sixth year, Mount Jing again suffered a fire.

On the night of the conflagration, a violent storm broke out, yet the Master sat upright in a separate dwelling, remaining indifferent and asking no questions. Smiling and chanting, he said: "After the rain has dispersed and the clouds have cleared, the towering peaks..."

There are several hundred peaks; though Wang Wei possessed a masterful hand, it would have been difficult for him to capture their traces with his brush. He then thatched a cottage to settle the assembly, and the temple was restored.
Furthermore, forty *li* away, he separately constructed Wannian Temple as a place for regular rest.

Not far from this "cloud-and-water" retreat, he again built a vihāra as a repository for sacred texts, wherein to enshrine the imperial calligraphies bestowed upon him in the past and present. On both sides of his humble quarters, he enshrined the portraits of the Patriarchs.
On anniversaries of his ancestors' deaths or birthdays, he invariably performed Buddhist rites of feeding the monastic community to assist their posthumous merit.

For, during the chaos in Shu, the ancestral sacrifices of the Master’s lineage had been severed; thus, upon the shrine, he heard a voice of praise and was granted the name Yuanzhao-an (Clergyman Illumination).
In the Wushen year of the Chunyou era, he again built a small dwelling by the Mingyuechi Pond as a plan for retirement.

As the Master’s years since his full ordination had advanced, imperial edicts followed one after another, and inquiries from the court were constant. The Master merely recorded the karmic encounters of ancient worthies in writing and declined all further audiences.
Once, when a high-ranking guest passed by the mountain, the Master alone revealed the essential core of the mind’s principle (*citta-tattva*).

When the guest inquired about the political fortunes of the Southern Pyeongju Kingdom, the Master merely lowered his head and remained silent. On the full moon of the third month in the year of Jihyou (1309), he ascended the seat and said: "This mountain monk is both old and ill;
I lack the strength to engage in idle chatter with you all here and there. Today, I have come forth with some effort. What I have previously taught..."
He has, after all, fully shaken out [his burden] before everyone’s eyes. Then he rose and shook his robes, saying, "How much is there?
He subsequently gave instructions for his final affairs and wrote a letter by hand to bid farewell to the Emperor. The Emperor dispatched an imperial messenger to inquire about his final matters.
The Master said, "When I came, I was empty and bare; when I go, I am naked and stripped. If you wish to ask for the definitive truth, it is at Tiantai."
There was a stone bridge; after a short while, he passed away in silence. His stupa was enshrined at Yuanzhao Hermitage. His direct successor was Chan Master Xueyan Qin, who offered this eulogy:
"Nantang said that when the Master resided at Wufeng, the prosperity of his Dharma assembly was no less than during the time of Miaoxi.

Although the congregation was large and provisions scarce, they suffered again from the calamity of fire, which inevitably involved the toil of traveling in all directions. One can well imagine the hardships he endured."
Folded. Had it not been for his making the upholding of the orthodox lineage his primary concern, how could he have been as upright as this?
Alas! Nantang truly knew how to speak.
—Chan Master Bieshan Zhi.
Master Chuzhi of Bieshan was a native of Shu. His ancestors bore the surname Yang, and for generations they held prominent official positions.

Having been born into a family of right faith, Zhi severed all worldly ties from his youth. At the age of seven, he succeeded the śramaṇa Yin Hua as a novice, and upon being given the *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* by Guifeng, he could recite it fluently from memory.
In the year Jiyou of the Jiading era of the Song dynasty, he underwent an examination on his studies and received ordination.
He was fourteen years old at that time. Five years later, he went to Zhaojue to study under Chan Master Ren'ou Quan. For two years, he underwent rigorous training through the *huatou* method;

he did not dare to spread his bedding, often remaining awake until the final watch of the night, occasionally only taking brief naps. It happened that he heard a monk from Gusu reciting the Dharma talks of Shaliyan;
every word struck directly at his own karmic afflictions in Zen. At that time, Yan was residing in Gusu.

He went to Mount Qiunglong. Zhi hurried there to see him and sought guidance based on his past karmic conditions. Yanyuan sat upright with his eyes closed; he simply extended his palms to show them to Zhi.
When Zhi did not receive a definitive answer and requested further instruction, Yanyuan remained as before without saying anything else. Two more years passed at this point.
Zhizhou sought further instruction out of compassion, yet Yankong ultimately did not change his fundamental approach. He then intended to edit the Tripitaka and harmonize the original teachings.
While reading the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he encountered the passage where Sudhana enters Maitreya’s tower and beholds within it the infinite and inconceivable realms of all Buddhas;
at this, he attained a realization. He silently brought up various ancestral cases (gong'an), finding that they all converged upon the essential points. He presented these insights to [Yankong].
Yuanran was about to open his mouth when Zhi said, "As for Lingyun seeing the peach, where does the meaning lie?
Yuanran replied, "A single red dot amidst ten thousand greens; how many rejoice, and how many resent? Yuanran took this to be correct and approved of him.
Zhi then traveled extensively through famous monastic seats, gaining renown everywhere. He crossed the Qiantang River and visited Mount Tiantai, befriending Jue'an Lun and meeting Wuzhun.
At Xuedou, Master Fanzhi’s staff and shouts flew like the wind; Master Zhi was rendered speechless and could not respond to him.
Whenever Fanzhi received inquiries from his disciples, Zhi would attempt to match his responses, yet as he gazed upon Master Fanzhi, he could not utter a single word.
He sighed to himself, saying, "Everything I have investigated and realized throughout my life is but dead dharma. How can dead dharma be of any help?"
He then completely cast aside his former burdens and remained steadfastly under Master Fan. After a long time, through Master Fan’s blows and shouts, he thoroughly penetrated the wondrous principle.
He subsequently presented a verse, saying: "Exhausting my efforts as night draws to a close, Picking east and west, it remains difficult to see.
Unexpectedly, beans burst from within the cold ashes; I take this very piece of firewood to be the flame. Master Fan later moved to Yuyang and then to Jingshan.
Zhì carried his bundles with him. When Jingshan was destroyed by fire, many of the administrators were fearful and urged Fǎn to abandon them.

Zhì said, "It must not be so. In the past, when Master Nán resided at Guījōng, Guījōng was consumed by fire. The authorities held him accountable for the fault, yet Nán remained there in accordance with the circumstances.
For this reason, Master Nán’s reputation became greatly esteemed. Although Jingshan has now been burned, the times are peaceful."
The Way flourishes. Furthermore, the Abbot has returned the blame to himself and harbors no intention of abandoning [the temple].

As we are his sons and subjects, we ought to look up to and embody the heart of our father and sovereign. When the Way of father-son and sovereign-subject is in harmony, what need is there to discard the old for the new?
Thus, Zhì took charge as the presiding master (*huàzhǔ*), and the halls, pavilions, and terraces emerged from amidst the joyful celebration.
He established Wufeng Monastery. In the second year of the Jiaxi era, he went to reside at Tiangwang Temple on Mount Dongting.

Through the practical application of Mantra (Shingon), he welcomed practitioners from all quarters; however, he was fond of disparaging other schools, for which he was ridiculed by the "Tianwang of Wisdom" throughout the Jianghu region.
Chijue Chong once asked him, "Has any monk who has come from Dongting ever seen the Tianwang of Wisdom? He replied, "The student has just come from..."
The Heavenly King arrived and asked, "What kind of sayings do you usually have? The monk cited the words with which the Heavenly King had addressed the assembly:

"Wearing shackles and carrying a cangue, one invites crime and guilt; settling in meditation and entering samādhi, one sits in a deep pit. When both ends are kicked off and there is no dependence, one is a free man in the world.
Chongxiao said, "If that is so, then the wisdom of the Heavenly King involves no small measure of transgression. The Minister [Zhang Shangying] said, "Indeed."
When Xiangyou’s public assembly was left vacant by Xiyu, he invited Zhizhubuzhi to fill the seat. Not long after, Zhizhu departed from Xiyu;
carrying his staff, he moved to Jiangshan in Jinling. Disciples gathered there like ants, and his fame filled Huainan. There was a practitioner named Yuetang Yin.

When he first traveled to Wu, he heard that Huizhi was habitually prone to anger and would spray others with spittle without restraint. While residing at Tianwang Monastery, he went to pay his respects to Huizhi.
Huizhi asked, "What is your dharma-name? He replied, "Zu Yun. "Where have you recently come from?
He replied, "Jiangxi. "Is Master Ma well? He replied, "I ask after the health of the Monk. Huizhi then pulled up his staff and rose; Yun stepped on his sandals and likewise rose.
As he was departing, an attendant monk asked, "I do not know whether that monk who came earlier will stay or not. Zhi smiled and said, "He will certainly leave.

The attendant went out to inquire at the Danguo Hall; indeed, he had already departed. Later, after Yuan was residing there, he remarked, "At that time, I only approved of Bieshan’s taking [the monk] in, but I did not approve of Bieshan letting him go.
In the fourth year of the Baoyu era (1256), Tiantong was destroyed by fire, leaving nothing remaining. The provincial commander...
Wu Gongqian reported this in a memorial to the Emperor. The Emperor [bestowed the name] Zhi upon him;
Zhi said, "I shall take my white bones to accompany the green mountains—that is enough for me. The task of restoration is not within my expectations.
He then constructed a thatched hut amidst the ruins to settle the community. Within three years, at the very end of the pine-gated valley, the green mountains revealed a Buddhist temple.
Zhuangjia was in the southeast. His wisdom dwelt among the multitude, and he was able to endure minor matters, gaining the hearts of the monastics (*nàzǐ*) profoundly.

The monastics praised one another, saying: "Our Master’s name is Zuzhi; he is the reincarnation of Hongzhi. On the first day of the ninth month of the first year of the Jingding era, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"The clouds are thin and the moonlight is fresh; the trees have shed their leaves, and the mountains reveal their bones. Since the beginning of heaven and earth..."
"Each and every one possesses a living eye. Thereupon he closed his room and further sent a message saying, "We shall not meet again; each of you must exert yourselves.
Ten days later, he gave final instructions regarding his affairs, then joined his palms and passed away. He was sixty-one years old and had spent forty-seven summer retreats in meditation.
His stupa was enshrined at Zhongfeng.
The eulogy states: When my late teacher, Elder Wulu, was newly at Tiantong, he compiled the stone inscriptions for the successive patriarchs.

I was able to see Master Zhi’s stupa, which had collapsed amidst a thicket of brambles. Upon examining the *Tiantong Zhongxing Tuzhi* (Illustrated Gazetteer of the Restoration of Tiantong), it is clear that Master Zhi performed great service for Tiantong.
Initially, Master Zhi served Wuzhun while residing at Mount Jing, where he upheld the Great Dharma.
With such encouragement, the five-peak pavilions were suddenly completed. Later, when the Master resided at Tiantong, he restored that most magnificent monastery within less than three years;
this was also because there were capable individuals among his disciples whom he inspired and encouraged. Alas!
Were it not for loyalty toward those above and sincerity in dealing with those below, how could such achievements have been possible?
Chan Master Duanqiao Lun of Jingci:
The Venerable Duanqiao, named Miaolun, was surnamed Xu and was a native of Huangyan in Tai prefecture.

When he reached the age of twenty, he wished to enter Mount Ruiyan to leave the household life, but his father and elder brother would not permit it. They compelled him to manage their agricultural production; however, Lun took no pleasure in such work.
He then fled to Yongjia and shaved his head at Guangci Temple. After receiving the precepts, he returned home to visit his family, where he sought the Way from Chan Master Guyuan of Ruiyan.
Guyuan showed him the koan of "Three pounds of flax," which left Yunmen in great doubt, as if facing a thousand-foot iron wall.
Later, because a neighboring monk was reading the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, [Yunmen heard it said]: "Mosquitoes, gadflies, and ants have no speech, yet they are able to..."

When Bian Shilun had a moment of realization, he encountered Master Wuzhun Shanfeng, who was reviving the tradition at Xuedou. Because Xuedou’s style was rigorous, Zen practitioners did not easily venture to pay their respects.
Shilun, however, cast aside his outer robe and went straight to the abbot’s quarters; his attendants were unable to stop him. Master Shanfeng said in anger:
"Where have you come from? he asked. [Zhao] Lun replied, "Ruiguan. He said, "What is the purpose of your coming here so abruptly?
Lun spoke with composure, saying, "In truth, it is because my own personal matter is urgent; I have come to present it to you. He said, "What 'donkey business' or 'horse business' do you have?"
"Try to bring it forth and see," he said. Yun-lun then set forth what he had attained. Zhao-fan said, "Why does a dog have karmic consciousness?
Yun-lun offered a response, but Zhao-fan paid him no mind. This continued in such a relentless stream that Yun-lun offered thirty consecutive statements, yet Zhao-fan ignored them all.
As he was about to offer another statement, he found nothing upon which to land. He then knelt and wept, pleading, "Master, do you have no skillful means? Zhao-fan—
Master Gong took pity on him and showed him an ancient verse, saying: "Though words may end, the karmic consciousness remains; who says that the meaning is not profound?

When the ocean dries up, its bottom will finally be seen; when a person dies, their mind is not known. Lun was struck with awe and stood there in deep reflection. Suddenly, he heard the sound of a wooden board being struck, and his entire body broke into a sweat.
He prostrated himself repeatedly at the feet of Master Fan. Fan laughed and said, "I did not deceive you. Lun, however, could utter not a single word.
Chusheng then departed. Master Fan moved his residence to Yuwang and Jingshan, and Chulun followed them both to assist them.
At that time, those who emerged from Chusheng’s lineage—such as Xueyan Qin and Bieshan Zhi—each transformed a region and were renowned for their realization of the Way.
Chulun also took charge of the small monastery of Zhiyuan; presiding over his quarters and burning incense, he maintained a truly dignified bearing. Prominent monks of the era flocked to his seat.
The monastery was so cramped that there was no room to accommodate him, so he moved to Ruiyan and later to Guoqing. Faling was a man of straightforward character who spoke without reservation;

he delighted in gathering various sayings and weighing the merits of past and present. Once his arguments were set forth, they were like bundles of damp firewood—yet all were supported by citations from the scriptures and historical records, appearing as clear as looking into a bright mirror.
People regarded him as a master craftsman of broad learning; whether wise or foolish, everyone vied to recognize his excellence.
He simply faced them and then ceased speaking. Later, he resided at Jingci Monastery. He once said to the assembly: "In the mountains of Jing there is jade;

those who obtain it do not find it within the mountains of Jing. In the waters of Chi there are pearls; those who pick them up do not find them within the waters of Chi. Zen monks have the 'True Person of No Rank';
those who realize him do not encounter him through the gate of the face. Holding his staff horizontally across his chest, he asked: "Do you understand? The Yangzi River flows from Youzhou."
"A stone man crouches in his mouth. He also said: "Deshan lowers his head; Jia Shan nods his head. Guishan holds up a finger;
Xuansha strikes and breaks a toe. Taking up his staff, he said: 'All of this does not go beyond the tip of my staff.
Why is this so? He struck the ground once and said: 'A single leaf falls, and the world turns autumn. He also said: 'Daguan Ying.'"
He said: "The seven Buddhas are the slaves of nature; the myriad dharmas are the servants of the mind. But tell me, where is the master? He then gave a shout himself and said:
"From the seven Buddhas downward, they have all shown their heads. He then nodded to himself and said: "Each attends to his own duties.
To call the seven Buddhas "slaves of nature" and to point to the myriad dharmas as "servants of the mind"—Daguan claimed for himself that he had a way to emerge from this, yet when it came to him...
"Ha! Self! "Yes. Furthermore, as a slave, one serves one's master; when was it ever seen in a dream? Do you understand the essential point?
[He brandishes his whisk. He said: "In the morning, a spring breeze arises, causing the hundred trees in the gardens to bloom everywhere.

Later in life, after he had ceased ascending the hall for formal sermons, one day he suddenly hung up the notice for entering the room. Afterward, he said to the assembly: "This is the final [instruction] of this old monk."
This was another instance of his playful maneuvering. He again asked the Venerable Yin, "Is it true that Linji received three severe blows from Huangbo?
He replied, "It is. Yun said, "Why did he then strike Danyuan three times under the ribs? He replied, "When one receives an ox from another, one returns a horse to them.
Yun smiled contentedly, tapped the table, and said, "In the future, there will surely be someone who will rely on this to bear witness for you."
Mingzai (whose style name was Yuetang; later succeeded by Jishi Peng) subsequently entrusted his final affairs to his disciples Fangshan Bao and Zhuyue Jian.
Jian also composed a letter bidding farewell to his acquaintances from all quarters. When Duke Wei Guo read this letter, he was greatly astonished and immediately dispatched a messenger to inquire:
"The Master studied at Tiantai; why did you die in Hangzhou? Mingzai smiled and pointed with his finger to his left and right.
It is said: "The sun rises in the east and sets in the west at night. While he was preparing to prostrate, Huilun had already passed away. Zhan said:
"Master Duqiao, with his heroic and magnificent bearing, entered the gate of Master Fan of Xuedou; there he first learned the 'elbow' [of Zen].
Later, the divine tally could not be obtained from others. When he appeared in the world to sift and refine [the teachings], he may truly be called one who is consummate."
He found the right person. For this reason, Fangshan Bao and his successors were able to perpetuate the lineage for generations.

People of all quarters say that this is due to the fact that the single stream of Duanqiao was truly effective; otherwise, it would have been like the worldly torrential flow, overflowing one morning and drying up by evening.
How could the fine reputation of the Duanqiao lineage have been drawn from such a source?

Chan Master Chong of Mount Jing: The master’s name was Daochong, and his style name was Chijue. He was born into the Xun family of Wuxin. In his youth, he was a scholar who achieved renown for his profound mastery of the Six Arts;
yet, he repeatedly failed the imperial examinations. Chong explained this to himself, saying, "There is no cause for worry. This is not to frustrate me, but rather to bring me forth."
Chen’s resolve was firm; he eventually shaved his head at Miaoyin Monastery in Zizhou and received full ordination.
Leaving Sichuan, he wandered through the regions of Wu and Chu, looking down upon the various patriarchs and having no desire to meet them.

At that time, Chan Master Caoyuan Sheng was propagating the teachings of Mian at Miaoguo Monastery; Chongji intended to go and pay his respects, but again desisted and remained lingering among the lecture halls.

Furthermore, I observed that the Chan practitioners would come and go, prostrating at the feet of Miaoguo. Moreover, I praised the spiritual capacity and function of Miaoguo, and in my heart, I reckoned that Master Daosheng must possess some exceptional merit;
for if he had no such excellence, how could the hearts of people be so devoted to him? Thereupon, I rose up and went to see him.
After exchanging several words with Daosheng, I felt a deep sense of awe toward him. I requested to attend upon him, and did not leave his side for one year. Daosheng’s school...
Xuanzhi and Chong both attained realization of the profound principle; however, when they engaged in a contest of fists and staffs, it seemed as though there were some lingering obstruction.
Although Chong repeatedly displayed his skills, Xuanzhi repeatedly brushed them aside. Chong departed in resentment, saying, "I still have a pair of hands from my days of poverty;

I intend to go to various quarters to scratch at the places that itch. He traveled through various monasteries, staying for only one or two nights before departing. Later, he visited Lingyin Monastery to see [Zhao]yue.
Mount Yue again did not grant his request, and Hui-chong intended to depart. Just then, he encountered an old friend who entreated him to stay; he remained for over eight months.
Someone told Mount Yue, "Master Chong’s talent and brilliance are not easily found. If you do not receive him with skillful means, will this not be a failure in winning over a worthy man?

Mount Yue replied, "I have already opened wide the eight characters [of my face]; he passed me by right before my eyes. Whom shall I blame? When Hui-chong heard this, he said: [Note: The final sentence is left as a placeholder for the missing text.]

His mouth and ears were both lost [to understanding]. Only when he clearly perceived Master Sheng’s wondrous function did he turn north toward Miaoguo and bow to him, saying, "How nearly have I failed my teacher!

How nearly have I failed my teacher! After he took up residence, he succeeded Cao Yuan in the Dharma lineage. Initially, the monastics of the Jianghu region had looked on with indifference and would not return;
however, once he opened the hall for teaching, they flocked to him like shooting stars and rolling lightning, and veteran masters and long-established virtuous ones praised his excellence.
Thereupon, the assembly gathered like clouds. He ascended the hall, and a monk asked: "Regarding the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.
What is the past? Xinxin said: "Let it go; wait until it has cooled, then look. "What is the present? Xinxin said: [Let it go; wait until it has cooled, then look.]
"You ask me and I answer: what is the future? Xincheng said, "I will tell you when I ascend the hall next time.
"What is the wisdom of differentiation regarding the past? Chong struck the left side of the meditation seat with his whisk. "What is the wisdom of differentiation regarding the present?
Chong struck the right side of the meditation seat. "What is the wisdom of differentiation regarding the future? Chong struck the center.
The monk then prostrated and said: "Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings have no turning away from one another; the ocean of lands in the ten directions is contained within a single hair.
Chong replied: "The past mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended."
Since the three minds cannot be apprehended, what can be called "discriminating wisdom"?
If one sees through to the bottom, there is not a single moment when the Buddhas of the three periods of time are not atop the crowns of everyone’s heads, turning the Great Dharma Wheel.
What more is there to seek here by jostling shoulders and standing toe-to-toe? [The Master] drives them all away at once with his staff. (Chongchu arrived while Jia was in residence.)

He Guangxiao succeeded him. He subsequently moved to Jiangshan. Being situated near the river, Jiangshan frequently suffered from bad harvests, making it difficult to beg for alms; consequently, the entire community showed signs of malnutrition.
Xuanzhong Zhenqi said to them, "In the tradition of our Buddhas and Patriarchs, we dwell in opposition to the mundane and accord with the extraordinary.
Furthermore, is hunger, cold, and deprivation not themselves acts of Buddha-work? Moreover, the food of Dharma-joy is inexhaustible. Having said this, he personally took up [his bowl]...

Buddhagupta traveled daily through the streets and neighborhoods, never letting wind or rain hinder him. Each time he returned, he would invariably order drums to be beaten to assemble the congregation, carrying out his duties with tireless dedication.

For thirteen years, he remained as constant as a single day. The monastic community was never in want. When an imperial decree arrived for him to move to Tiantong, the seat at Yuyang Monastery became vacant once again;
as Chongshan bore the burden of the great assembly, they requested that he take charge of its administration.
He then gave a small-scale sermon (xiaochan), saying: "What Tian Tong used, Yuyang does not use; what Yuyang uses, Tian Tong does not use.
In the place where neither is used, there is a surplus of utility—a single arrow, and the two eagles fall from one's hand.
Later, he moved to Mount Jing. One day, he ascended the hall and said: "Throughout his life, the World-Honored One exhausted every skill and artifice, yet when it came to rubbing his chest..."
He addressed the assembly: "Those who seek life cannot find it; those who seek death cannot find it. I, this mountain monk, am not like that.
When I wish to walk, I walk; when I wish to go, I go. Even the eight-armed Nala could not stop me. Having spoken, he sat in silent meditation for a period of time. Recorded by Chongshan.
In his later years, he was particularly fond of this practice. However, all that he wrote were verses and hymns of admonition by ancient sages and realized masters;
there were no mundane words among them. When a scholar requested that he write some poetry composed by himself, Hui-chong consented.
He immediately ordered paper to be brought and boldly inscribed the seven characters: *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. The scholar laughed and said, "This is still just the old stuff. Hui-chong—
He waved his hand and said, "I do not dare to treat you with contempt; you shall all become Buddhas.
The commentary states: Tian Dan maintained an undivided heart to uphold his integrity;

within less than a year, Ji-nan fell to him, and he recaptured more than seventy cities for Qi—this may be called truly magnificent. Master Chong, in his youth, maintained an undivided heart to enter the Way.
Suddenly, Master Sheng resumed the single lineage of Master [Dao]sheng at a moment when it was on the verge of extinction yet not yet severed.

Furthermore, amidst circumstances contrary to the norm, the assembly of Mount Jiangshan performed the funeral rites with devotion. In the midst of wind and rain, they caused the Way of Master Sheng of Caoyuan to be revived once more in this age—is this not truly magnificent?
Chan Master Wenli of Tianmu:
Chan Master Wenli of Tianmu was styled Mie’ung. He was born into the Ruan clan and was registered in the Lin’an jurisdiction.
He received the full precepts from the śramaṇa Zhimue of Zhenxiang Temple and attained the Way under Chan Master Songyuan Yue of Jianfu Temple. He subsequently emerged into the world [to teach].
He resided at Guangshou in the prefecture; next, at Nengren on Mount Yan; and was again summoned by imperial decree to dwell at Jingci on Nanping.
His final years were spent at Tiantong, which was where he went in response to the summons of his later life. He held dharma assemblies four times and twice attended imperial decrees.
At Xiqiu Fiquan, this was his place of retirement. When he lived at Yan-shan according to the rites, the officials and gentry of the southern regions...
His disciples followed him in great numbers. His demeanor with the ceremonial staff and fly-whisk was serene and detached; a pure wind seemed to press upon one.

Amidst the pines and clouds, the sound of the spring and the color of the rocks were perceived simply through the eyes, regardless of rank. Yet he ultimately found no pleasure there, and so retired to live at Xiqiu on Liangzhu.
He wrote of himself: "Since I retired from my seat at Nanshan, I have been too indolent to take up my rattan staff and come forth.
Only when I occasionally lean it against a sunny slope do I pause to examine how many branches of plum blossoms are in bloom.

At that time, the layman Zhu Xi, known as Huicang, was establishing a hall for Daoxue (Learning of the Way) in Tainan. Although local officials urged him to accept the invitation to reside again at Nengren Monastery, he did not rise to the occasion.
He composed a verse, addressing the senior monks of Mount Yan: "I cast a single phrase into the Dragon Pool; It struck the rocks and pierced the clouds through many autumns.
How could one with white hair fail to see its penetration? The moon hangs high and cold, making the lonely monkey sigh.

After his formal ceremonies had ceased, he rested at Liangzhu. Monastics and laypeople sought him out without ceasing. For the most part, he sat motionless upon his meditation seat, gazing intently at visitors and shaking his head.

Thus it was. Their mutual affinity transcended conventional boundaries; they would attend to the ritual of washing the water-jar and kettle, conversing with laughter from morning until night without ever growing weary.
When Lord Jiezhai Zhao visited him in humble attire, drawn by his reputation for lofty conduct, they sat and spoke together all day long.
After Jiezhai departed, Zeli never once asked his name. It so happened that the seat at Jingci Monastery was vacant; when Jiezhai proposed that Zeli take up the position, he did not accept. Jiezhai—

He then reported this to the Emperor. The Emperor insisted that he enter the monastery. The ritual text says: "When a decree descends from the Nine Palaces, all within the Four Seas hold it in reverence;
the mountains and peaks cry out in joy, and even birds and fish dance. Furthermore, why would even a man of the Way beyond the mundane world be turned by such a command?

Yet to comply is itself Bodhi. The fourfold assembly praised him highly. Not long after, he again took up his staff and fled under the cover of night, retiring to Fiquan. The Emperor regretted [his departure].

He further commanded Tiantong Ju to reside there. While Ju resided at Tiantong, he would constantly test visitors with the kōan regarding the *shu* bamboo shoots of the Southern Mountains and the black bream of the Eastern Sea.
As soon as someone attempted to offer a response, Ju would invariably strike him three times with his toothpick. Those who understood this were startled.
At that time, among those who entered his gate, unless their wisdom surpassed that of the master, it was not easy to gain passage. Thus, he wrote for himself: "No one from Shaoyang shall come."
Knocking at the gate, he never pressed anyone until their feet were broken. Only when Deshan arrived and began his interrogation did he finally blow out the paper candle.
Alas for this fox-like guile and delusion! How can one ensure the succession of the lineage? Let it be that weeds fill the Dharma Hall and moss seals the ancient halls.
If Yangqi had not obtained Baoning, Baiyun, and Huitang, then all others would have been merely mediocre and unable to carry on the tradition.

He prostrated at the feet of Master Zhu Li and paid his respects to him while he was staying as a celestial youth; however, not long after, he abandoned this state and returned to his former seclusion on West Hill.
Yet, Zhu Li’s excellence continued to flourish. Once, when Zhu Xi (Hui-an) went to pay him a visit, Zhu Li displayed a spirit of extraordinary carefree elegance toward him.

Zhu Xi, however, maintained a refined and composed demeanor; he adjusted his cap and stepped forward to inquire after his mother’s health. Zhu Li suddenly rose and folded his hands. Upon withdrawing, Zhu Xi remarked to others: [The text ends here.]
The *Biluo Stele* (Beiluo bei) indeed has no counterfeit versions. Yang Cihu also asked about the power of non-deception. Zongli replied:
"One must clarify the phrase of the 'complete presentation of the hare and the elephant'; look at the moment he ascends the steps with his ritual tablet held upright.

Zongli served as abbot four times for only eight or nine years in total, yet during the periods when he retired from office, his demeanor was so lofty and ancient that those who saw him were struck with solemnity. Thus it is recorded.

Reflecting upon the essential nature and momentum of the Dharma-path, he sighed with profound emotion, sometimes even shedding tears. Consequently, those who inherited his resolve all achieved great renown in their time.
In the winter month of the tenth year of the Chunyou era, he suddenly rose at dawn and said to his assembly, "Who will build a seamless stupa for me?
An attendant asked, "Please, Master, show us the model for the stupa. Lianchi smiled and said, "Draw it with all your might."

He did not emerge from his meditation and immediately cast off his body; he was eighty-four years old. When his remains were cremated, his cranial bone and teeth remained uncorrupted, and his *śarīra* relics were as brilliant as shimmering pearls.
They were enshrined to the left of the ancestral pagoda of the Patriarch Ying’an at Tiantong.
The Eulogy states: I have examined Master Gōng’s conduct; for over thirty years he has extended his hand [in teaching].

Having been promoted four times and demoted five times, he is like a divine immortal within the shadows of white clouds—worthy of veneration yet impossible to grasp. Upon further savoring his preaching, it was as if Master Zhìgōng were being playful;
even the monk Xiū would have found it difficult to capture it in a portrait. At that time, the gentlemen of the age held Master Gōng’s reputation equal to that of MIAOXI (Yunmen Wenyan).
"An" (the hermitage) is indeed not in error.

As for Chan Master Rujing of Tiantong—Chan Master Rujing, whose courtesy name was Chang’ung, was extraordinary and possessed far-reaching ambitions. He received the seal of transmission from Zu’an Ke. Not...
He was worthy of a grand retirement. He expanded upon the various *upāya* (expedient means) sūtras; those who mocked or reviled him were all liberated and brought to maturity.
Thus, he frequently convened assemblies on both sides of the Zhejiang River, occupying six famous monasteries, among which Jingci and Tiantong were his longest stays.

When ascending the seat, he would say: "Where there is a question, there is an answer; though dung and urine may be scattered in disarray, the eyebrows are joyful and the nostrils stand tall. Directly...
The great earth sinks level and empty space bursts asunder. At this very moment, meet with the ancient Buddha Hongzhi.
(He raises his whisk. Having met, what should we discuss? "From of old, no one has recognized the merit of those who have sweated in battle."
It is simply a matter of re-examining it. Thus, opening the furnace for a transformative achievement, he drew a perfect circle and called to the assembly, saying:

"This is the Tiantong fire-pot. Approach and you will be burned to death; retreat and you will freeze to death. Suddenly, if someone were to come forward and ask, "What about this? [the Master would strike him.]
The furnace stirs. It is also said: "When the larvae of the *mínglíng* are killed and encountered by the *guǒzhù*, it exclaims, 'Be like me!
Be like me! Is there anyone under the gate of the Celestial Youth who is like me? Ten thousand miles without a single speck of cloud;
heaven and earth are one mass of fierce fire. It is also said: "Liu Xujing, Tao Yuanming, Mañjuśrī, and Samantabhadra—making a circle, they say: 'Ei!'"
This one point is presented for your inspection. But tell me, by whose authority is this judged? If it were Confucius, he would have said, "I have nothing hidden from you.
As for the Chan practitioner Jue, he had relied upon Master Jing for a long time. One night at the hour of midnight, he requested a resolution regarding his practice.

Jing said, "I am weary; go now. I will explain it for you tomorrow. Jue thought to himself that the days and months were slipping away, so he departed with tears in his eyes and stood in the dew waiting for dawn.
He adjusted his deportment and entered the room. Jing took pity on him and ascended the hall, saying: "A single black plum resembles its original form;
A spider weaves a web to catch a dragonfly. The dragonfly loses both its wings— How laughable, that the black plum bites an iron nail!"
Jue cried out beside him in a startled voice, "Had I known earlier that the lamp was fire, the rice would have been cooked long ago. Jing then shouted.

Those who understood it praised Jing as being both perilous and essential; he was somewhat similar to Yunmen, yet his subtlety and density were truly like Dongshan’s. However, it has not yet been seen whose lineage he inherited.
Someone once asked in passing, "Master, you have preached the Way for many years, your fame fills the monastic community, and your eminent disciples have already spread the teachings."

Only then can one grasp the source and course of the Dharma. I beg for clear instruction. Jìng remained silent for a long while and then smiled, saying, “I will tell you in the Nirvāṇa Hall” (some versions read:
“Look in the Nirvāṇa Hall”). He further addressed the assembly, saying: “The ancients said, ‘Great snow fills Chang’an. Tiantong sells off that heart and liver.
A Bodhisattva without supernatural powers strikes with a fierce blow; the Great Compassionate One of a Thousand Hands and Eyes squeezes and twists many strange things.”
Do you understand? This is the "Puzzle for the Deluded Child" taught by the Lion to its cub; with a grandmotherly heart, I shall not deceive you.
In my sixty-sixth year, I suddenly ordered my attendant to prepare an incense altar, sounded the drum to assemble the assembly, and offered incense to succeed Zu’an.
The inscription reads: "I, the Pure Practitioner, having wandered for over forty years, first arrived at Nanyue Lufeng. There, I lost my footing and fell into a pit.
This incense now cannot help but be brought forth, though it serves only to embarrass my late Great Master Zu’an.
Zu’an’s name was Zhijian; Jian was a Dharma heir of Tiantong Juexian; Juexian was a Dharma heir of Changlu Qingliao; Liao’s style name was Zhenxie, and he was a descendant of Danxia."
Master Zhen was a入室 (入室) disciple [of Master Jing]. This Jing was a direct descendant in the seventeenth generation under Qingyuan.

Initially, when Master Zu’an Jian was a child, his mother washed his hand-wound (a skin ailment). Holding Jian’s hand, she asked, “What does this resemble? Jian replied, “It resembles a Buddha’s hand.
After his parents passed away, he immediately received ordination from Chan Master Zhenxie of Changlu. Master Jue was his preceptor.
As for his sitting posture and movements, they were dignified and composed. Using skillful means, he manifested the mirror; the mirror is Mount Xiang, hidden and secluded.

He cut off all external conditions and took a single hoe as his companion. Having thoroughly realized the profound principle, he returned to Jue. Jue approved of his state of realization. After Jue passed away, [Jian] remained there.
Having gathered [disciples] through his austere and simple lifestyle, in his later years he moved to reside under Xuedou. Bright-eyed monks with white hair relied upon him.
Jing requested instruction on the "Pine Tree" kōan from Jian. Jian prodded him with a direct, authentic challenge. Jing then attained realization, saying:
"The ancestral meaning of the West is the pine tree in the courtyard; the nostrils are vast and empty, facing the eyes. A withered branch that has fallen to the ground—"
He leaped up; Song Luo laughed with a bright and spirited air. Jue said, "An elder of mature gravity who serves as a celestial eye for humanity;

his reputation and brilliance are so radiant that they are beyond what I could have hoped for. Once Jing had received the transmission of the Dharma, he honored his teacher’s instructions and spent half his life enlightening others without seeking empty fame.
Furthermore, because he detested his contemporaries who falsely claimed to have transcended their predecessors, he only revealed the Dharma at the very end of his life.
Yuan then summoned the assembly and said: "For sixty-six years, my transgressions have filled the heavens. With one leap, I fall alive into the Yellow Springs. Aha!
From the beginning, life and death have been unrelated. He then passed away suddenly.
The eulogy states: After the great flourishing of the Dongzong (Cave School) under Danxia, the malpractice of reckless imitation has gradually crept in.
Yet Chang’eng’s conduct and standards were such that he was like a "poison-drum" from which one could not bear to listen. Is this not because those who recognize the Dharma are filled with dread?

Yet, his entry into principle was profound and his discourse did not stagnate in the subtle mysteries; he was truly a fierce dragon of the Dongxia lineage, whose movement like clouds and dispensation of rain is beyond measure.
Chan Master Wen Quan-yi of Huayan, Capital City.
The Chan Master’s name was Zhiwen, with the style name Quan-yi. He was the son of the Hao family of Xingzhou and an eighth-generation descendant of Chan Master Rutong Ru-jing.
By nature he was quick-witted and did not speak easily; when he did speak, his words were always measured and appropriate.

He buried his nails and hair at Liji. Thirty-seven days later, he enshrined his entire body at Siguan. He sat in meditation for forty-three summer retreats and lived through fifty-eight successive generations.
In the Wuma year of Emperor Renzong’s reign, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Puming Guangji.
The eulogy states: In antiquity, the strategic application of the Hutuo [River] was like a "poisoned drum"—those who heard it all died on the spot.

The lingering echoes still cause mutual ruin. Alas, how magnificent this is! Were it not for the Master’s essential and profound weapons and armor—the true mandate of Wu and Yue—how could such a state have been reached?
