National Teacher Zhongfeng Puying, whose name was Mingben, was a descendant of Linji Xuanshi. From Xuanshi, the lineage passed through seven generations to Yangqi Hui;
from Hui, it passed through eight generations to Wuzhun Shanfeng; Shanfeng transmitted it to Xueyan Qingyuan; and Qingyuan transmitted it to Gaofeng Yuanmiao.
Among the four dharma-heirs of Gaofeng, the Master was the foremost. Counting from Linji, eighteen generations had passed. Counting from Shaolin, [the lineage continued further].
The World’s Eleventh. This Master was the direct successor of the twenty-ninth generation of Shaolin.
The Master was born into the Sun clan of Qiantang; his mother was Lady Li. She dreamed that the Wayman Wumen arrived at her home carrying a lamp, and from that she gave birth to him.
At the time of the Master’s birth, a five-colored radiance filled the inner chamber for three days and nights. From infancy, he possessed the marks of a great man. He sat...
He sat in the full lotus posture; even his playful activities became acts of Buddha-work.

Upon reaching adulthood, he read the *Transmission of the Lamp* (*Chuan deng lu*) and, arriving at the principle that "knowing birth is non-birth," he pondered why he was nonetheless still transmigrating within birth and death.

Great doubt arose within him, and he sought instruction from Chan Master Miaogao of Shizi Monastery. Master Miaogao joyfully ordained him. After three years of contemplating a flowing spring, he attained realization and requested [instruction].
Master Miaogong certified [his realization], yet he was beaten and driven out. From then on, he served day and night, never leaving until the morning bell rang.

Master Miaogong paid him no heed. After a long time, however, he thoroughly penetrated the profound essence. Master Miaogong was greatly pleased and wrote a self-portrait with a eulogy for the Master, saying:
"My own form is inconceivable; even Buddhas and patriarchs cannot behold it. I alone grant that this unworthy child has been able to see half of it."
Biān-bì served for ten years. When Miao-gong passed away, he entrusted Da-jue Temple to the Master. The Master recommended the Head Seat, Zu-yōng, to preside over it.
Thereupon, carrying only a single straw hat, he traveled through the regions of Wú and Chǔ, heading west as far as Mount Huán and Mount Kāṅ-lú, before returning east.

He established the Huàn-zhù Hermitage at Yàn-dàng in Wú, which subsequently became a major monastic center. When Gū Gong, known as Tíng-fā, invited him to preside over Da-jue Temple, he did not accept.
Juding raised the matter, and Taishou Ying responded. Taishou had once received an office from Yishan Wenyi and now wished to change his lineage succession to that of his current master.

The Master strongly disagreed and declined him with a letter, saying: "Yesterday, when we sat together in conversation, we did not reach any other discussion before you first questioned me regarding the succession of this monastery.
I feared only that you might be following worldly conventions. This is fundamentally..."
My dear friend, for sixteen years we have maintained a close bond, and our mutual intentions have been perfectly clear to one another.
How could I have imagined that you would fail to understand my humble sentiments and instead seek to supplant me? Why do you act with such duplicity when it comes to a matter of consequence?

That the ancients were so meticulous in clarifying the lineage of dharma heirs and the direct transmission was because the source and course of the Great Dharma must not be misrepresented. The world has grown turbid and customs have declined...
I am humbled. There have been those who offered gold to request a whisk and exchanged their monasteries for the succession. I have long felt deep pain over this matter.

Although Dajue was the founder of this mountain, there were many venerable elders in the monastic communities throughout the ten directions; yet, you rejected them all and insisted that I must assume the post.
How narrow is your perspective! It is not that I fear being the abbot; it is truly that I fear the succession of the Dharma.
Regarding the founding of this mountain, I therefore declined and withdrew, declining the offer with all my might. Yet, you have been appointed as its presiding master;
since you yourself take Master Yishan as your teacher, how could you merely follow worldly custom and change the one you serve?

Speaking from this perspective, I originally did not wish for those who were disciples under my late master to successively occupy the seat of the Great Enlightenment, let alone those who are but branches extending from him.
"Leading the vine—do you intend to be the successor to the Founder? Upon hearing your command, I was struck with alarm. I have ventured to trouble you by going against the current;
the Abbot of the Pagoda has already informed me of this, and I hope you will directly bring forth the voice of the Jade Gorge.

If you wish instead to follow worldly custom and appoint a successor, then I, Ben, shall most certainly not associate with you for even a single day. I beg your earnest consideration, I beg your earnest consideration. The Master returned to Tianmu.

At the Pagoda of Gaofeng on Mount Lu, during the Wushen year of the Dà period, when Emperor Rénzōng was still in the Prince’s residence (Qīnggōng), he invited [the Master] to serve him, but the Master did not accept.

The Emperor bestowed upon him a robe of gold-patterned silk and conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Fǎhuì. The Master withdrew to Yízhēn; in the Jìyǒu year, he took up residence on a boat and composed this verse:
"Too lazy to debate the 'three threes' of past and future, It is truly superior to dwell on a boat than in a hermitage. This is the true practice of non-abiding."
The Master’s chamber is a monastery where no fixed abode remains. Smoke from villages and waterside lands open for morning offerings; moonlit bays and flowering marshes host evening assemblies.
When a guest knocks on the boat’s railing to seek the Way, the *dhūta* practitioner does not use his mouth, yet he speaks incessantly.
In the year Gengxu, he returned to Tianmu; in Xinhai, he once again resided upon his boat. Chen Zicong of Wujiang built the Huanzhu Hermitage for the Master. The Master—
He departed once more and went north to hide in Bianliang. He composed this verse: "Living at ease in the marketplace, I am entirely free; The myriad things are manifest, with nothing left to seek.
Green cabbages and purple mustard are sold by the street; White rice and green firewood are gathered by the door. My livelihood is sufficient throughout the twelve hours of the day;
The karmic conditions for my path have been fulfilled over thousands of years. If one persists in holding views apart from the mind, I dare say..."
In the year of the donkey, our heads met; the following year, he again established Huanzhu Hermitage on Mount Liuan.
He composed this verse: "What is there to love and what to hate within my breast? I am ashamed before others for being incapable of a hundred things.
I gather scattered clouds to mend my tattered robe, And climb steep steps to hang my withered vine. A single room amidst a thousand circling peaks, A solitary monk within ten thousand empty realms."

Apart from this present case of realization, there was no further transmission of the Buddha-dharma to carry on the lamp. Prime Minister Tuohan, whose reputation was renowned, sought out the Master upon hearing of his fame.
The Master, however, abandoned his hermitage and departed for Donghae-ju, where he composed this verse: "The practitioner dwells in solitude, resigned to his lingering stay;

The low bridge is struck by surging waves, manifesting birth and extinction; the still waters reflect the void, revealing awakening and delusion. When the myriad phenomena subside into stillness, the mind illuminates itself;
the ripples of the water are ever level with the lunar disc. Master Huan commanded the local officials to escort the Master to his private residence.
Thereupon, he consulted with the Secretariat and various mountain abbots to insist that the Master take up residence at Lingyin. The Master firmly declined, saying:

and third, the power of wisdom. The Way is the essence; conditions and wisdom are its functions. It may still be possible to undertake the role if the essence is present even if the functions are lacking; however—"
The power of transformation is not all-pervasive, and the ritual protocols are incomplete. If the essence of the Way is thus deficient, then its spiritual wonders will be beyond reckoning;
even if there were conditions and wisdom, what would they avail? Or, if both essence and function are lacking, yet one presumes to occupy that position, speaking of cause and effect—what can be said?
"Would it not be a source of regret within oneself? This poor monk possesses no such reality; therefore, I dare not assume its name. Ultimately, he feigned illness and returned to Tianmu.
In the year of Bingchen during the Yanʼyou era, the Emperor issued an edict to the Xuanzheng Yuan, instructing them to select and report upon those of profound virtue from renowned mountains.

In the year Wuwu, he returned to Tianmu once more. In the ninth month of the following year, by imperial decree, he was honored with the title Chan Master Foci Yuanzhao Guanghui.

He brought imperial incense and purple robes and paid his respects and expressed his admiration while remaining at his own residence. Later, during the Xuánzhèng era, the Abbot of Jìngshān again invited the Master, but the Master did not accept.

He then established Huànzhù Ān on Zhōngjuī Mountain. Zhōngjuī is thirty *lǐ* from Xīfēng; the rocky paths are perilous and steep, making it extremely difficult for both monastics and laypeople to travel there.
When seekers came to request the Master’s presence so he could return to the monastery, this occurred in the year Wūhài of the Zhìzhì era (1323). West...

The mountain peaks were frozen and parched; great trees were broken and shattered. The Master recounted his own experience, saying: "In my early resolve to leave the household life, my aspiration was to wear robes of grass and practice the dhūta austerities with a soiled face.

Yet, I donned the monastic robes of the fields, for which I have carried shame until the end of my days. My habitual inclination toward withdrawal and retreat was not intended to be a pretension to transcend the world or sever ties with the mundane;
rather, it was because in the realm of words and texts I failed in scholarly inquiry, and in the practice of investigation I lacked clear realization."
Ordinarily, he was praised by those who sought what is good; yet this was merely a coincidence of karmic conditions. In the autumn, he manifested a slight illness.
To those who came to inquire after his health, the Master would always say: "The Huanzhu Hermitage is leaky and dilapidated; I cannot remain here for long."

There was a monk who announced his departure for Wumen. The Master said, "Why have you not yet left? On the thirteenth day after the Mid-Autumn Festival, he wrote by hand and entrusted instructions to his disciples, saying:

The following day, a white rainbow pierced the mountain. At its peak, the Master sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), wrote a verse, and—
After his passing, the reliquary remained for three days; his countenance became increasingly serene and joyful. Monastics and laypeople flocked there in numbers exceeding ten thousand.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at the West River Stone near the temple. He lived for sixty-one years and spent thirty-seven summer retreats in seclusion.

In the *jisi* year of the Mingzong era, he was posthumously granted the title of Chan Master Zhijue, and his stupa was named Fayun. In the *jiashu* year of the Yuantong era, he was further honored with the title of Guoshi Puying.

The Master then had his *Guanglu* (Extensive Record) in thirty fascicles included in the Great Canon (*Dazang*). He further commissioned a high-ranking official to inscribe the National Teacher’s spiritual conduct upon a stele.

When the fourfold assembly welcomed the likeness into the city of Zhongqing, the likeness emitted five-colored, extraordinary light. Consequently, the people turned with total faith toward the Chan school and honored the Master as the foremost [teacher] of Nanzhao.
The First Patriarch. At that time, all said: "Master Ben’s perfect eloquence was never obstructed; his therapeutic prescriptions were manifold.

Like the lingering waves of a vast ocean, amidst clouds gathering and rain falling, he awakened the scholar-officials of the Phoenix Pavilion and the noble kin of the Imperial House, while Yongming and Shuming followed in his wake.
"I instruct [you], Sōng; perhaps we may then be peers. The eulogy says:

It is so. Alas! If one were not a true ancestral teacher, they would not utter the words from their heart; if one were not a legitimate descendant, they would not shed tears from their back.

Not uttering the words from one's heart is to be ignorant of those who come after; not shedding tears from one's back is to deceive those who came before. To be ignorant of those who come after and to deceive those who came before—this is the way of the unenlightened.
As they devour one another, the appearance and disappearance of the Original Patriarchs will continue; when, then, will this Sahā world ever come to rest?

The remainder [of the story] is as follows: When Huixi arrived, the monks did not weary of his austere and simple lifestyle, and several hundred followers joined him. The halls and corridors were dilapidated and beyond repair;

During his four terms as abbot, he made spiritual exhortation his primary duty; however, his capacity was not...

Waiting for this old villain’s malice to flare up, he slowly offered a greeting and said, "Do not take offense at my intrusion.

Regarding Chan Master Xiaoyin Yun: His courtesy name was Xiaoyin. His family registry was in Jiangzhou; he was a descendant of Chen Caoshi, a Minister of State during the Tang dynasty.

his mother, while still in the prime of her youth, cultivated pure practices. When he was a child, he beheld the marks and signs of a Buddha and cherished them with the affection due to a loving parent.
At the age of nine, he was able to rely on his paternal uncle, the Venerable Yún of Shuìlù Monastery, to become a *bhikṣu*. He then read through the Mahāyāna [scriptures] in their entirety.
Regarding the texts of the Tripiṭaka, [Zhao]qian desired to clarify his own practice; he vowed to practice the *dāna* of the Dharma for as long as he lived.
At that time, Chan Master Wanshan was teaching at Kaixian Temple on Mount Lu. Zhaoqian went to rely upon him, yet [Wanshan] did not grant him an opening.

He was fully endowed with these qualities and would surely have become a great figure in the future. In the fourth year of the Dading era, he went to reside at Wuhui on Lake Dongting;

Among the "dragons and elephants" within the assembly were Yuan’an Zhiji, Jitan Zongle, Qingyuan Huaiwei, and others, who vigorously expounded the essential points of the teachings.
He once asked a monk: "The ancient said, 'A monk’s robe from Qingzhou weighs seven pounds. Having already spoken thus, what ultimately is it?"

The commentary states: It is said, "Heaven and earth possess no complete mastery; the sages possess no complete capabilities.

If one considers the character of Master Yangshan and his disciples, it may be said that they were nearly complete in this regard. From the time Master Xi was on his deathbed until his passing, he continued to instruct his disciples and rectify the family dharma.
Master Xin, on the day before his death, summoned Zongle and his peers, earnestly entrusting them with the legacy of Miaoxi’s school. Compared to these, [the others]...
The minds of these two masters traveled back and forth across Jambudvīpa hundreds of thousands of times, yet they were still not satisfied with their aspirations.
Oh, how magnificent! Master Xuedou Wuyin.
The Chan Master’s name was Dazheng; his style name was Wuyin. He was the son of the Shi family of Poyang. At the age of fourteen, he entered the Changguo Temple to take refuge under Master Zhijie.

Upon passing his examinations with distinction, he received full ordination and became a bhikṣu. Thereafter, he burned oil lamps to continue his studies by night, diligently investigating the profound scriptures.
Master Zhijie rejoiced in Zeng’s aptitude. Seeking to travel to study under various masters, Zeng first visited Chan Master Wan of Jingxi at Mount Lu.
At Mount Yuantong Temple, there was a man named Wan who had a cold and ordinary appearance; his runny nose was dripping onto his clothes. When Zheng Yizhi wished to leave, he reflected to himself:

"If I encounter people in such a disheveled state, how can I distinguish the profound from the mundane? He therefore entered Wan’s room in private to seek an explanation of the patriarchs' mind-instructions.
Wan clapped his hands against his chest and cried out loudly, "This will kill me! Zheng, filled with doubt and fear, withdrew. There was...
The veteran monk Suan Rui was advanced in years and resided at Guotong, where he lived in seclusion in a quiet room to cultivate himself and find joy beneath the trees.
Although his name was well known, no one could approach him intimately. Chengjiu wished to seek him out for instruction, but found no opportunity.
One day, as Rui returned from using the toilet, Chengjiu followed behind him into the room. Rui asked, "Who is it? Chengjiu replied, "I have come seeking the Dharma. Rui was greatly [impressed].

Furiously, he chased him out and bolted the door. Dazheng was greatly startled and filled with doubt; seeking another opportunity, he requested an audience with Zhishou. Zhishou said, "The Buddha-dharma already has its own abbot’s quarters.
What is the point of you coming here to seek a heated bowl? Dazheng replied, "When I first arrived for my initial interview, I did not receive any instruction from the Abbot, the Venerable;
I saw nothing but his beating his breast and shouting loudly. Zhishou said, "This is like placing a head upon a head."

Zheng was suddenly enlightened; he wept and bowed in gratitude, saying, "Has my teacher’s compassionate heart truly reached this point? Rui said, "Based on your intellectual acuity, you should not remain here.
Recently, at Tiantong, there is Chan Master Yunwai Xiu, who upholds the teachings of the Dongshan lineage."
Yesterday I saw the *Xinlu* (New Record). Its skillful metaphors and lateral citations are as unrestrained as they are transcendent, and its meticulous detail is worthy of admiration.
You should follow its lead. Specifically, Xiu succeeded Zhiweng Ju; Ju succeeded Donggu Guang;
Guang succeeded Huazang Zu; Zu succeeded Jingci Hui. Hui was the son of Hongzhijue. Zhengji entrusted his lamp to Master Xiu of Yunwai. This is the lineage.
The transmission of Hongzhi continued for seven generations. One day, after descending from the Dharma hall, Master Xiù called out in a stern voice, "Today Tiantong has died a great death!
How will you save him? Zhèng replied, "Please, Master, have some food. He asked again:
"Tiantong is dying a great death today. Do not try to save him. He spoke again, saying, "How? How?
He spoke yet again, saying, "Tiantong is dying a great death today. Who will go with me? Zheng replied once more.
The Abbot went on ahead, and Dazheng followed behind. Xiu Gong laughed heartily and passed away.
Dazheng then gave a detailed account of Xiu Gong’s character to Master Zhongfeng Ben. Zhongfeng was delighted and praised him, saying: "Mount Taibai serves as a screen."
With twenty-ri of pines as his seat and his body hidden beyond the shadows of the clouds, how many have missed him?
Those who do not miss him are none other than the ancient Buddha of Xizhou returned once more. One must strictly avoid explaining this before the pivot of the teaching.

Consequently, the various quarters collectively acclaimed Master Xu as the true successor of Hongzhi. Prime Minister Toghon Temür invited him to certify his realization at Nanzen Temple south of Quzhou.
Subsequently, he traveled with his staff to various regions and preached the Dharma on six occasions. However, the dwellings where he stayed were like way-stations;

he sought people out among the grasses, never wearying of hunger or thirst. He once said, "At that time, I mistakenly entered the gate of Perfect Penetration and settled within the chamber of contemplation."
Deceived by him, I traveled to Jiangzhe, where my path was full of ups and downs; even now, I have found no final resolution.

If there were anyone who could take the place of this mountain monk and breathe through his nostrils, I would entrust both my hands to them. Although we have met, O men of measureless capacity, do not make the sound of a false rooster.
Later, while residing at Xuedou, he addressed the assembly, saying: "A thousand explanations and ten thousand expositions are not equal to meeting face-to-face."
"See yesterday was the twenty-ninth; this morning is the first day of the seventh month. I report this to you, you seekers of the profound mystery: time passes as swiftly as a flying arrow.
Those two eyes born of one’s mother—each as black as lacquer. Hurry, hurry, turn your heads back and look upon the Buddha of True Nature. After a long silence, he said, "What kind of face is that?

He then descended from his seat, went on rounds through the hall for tea, and further remarked, "Is it subtle, or is it not? The monks replied, "It is subtle, Master. He said, "Subtle indeed! He then returned to his quarters.
The monk’s nostrils have no more than two apertures. Whether profound or not, atop the banner pole there is no blue sky.
A man of realization must never fold his hands; how could a fine steed wait for the whip? Completely transcending staffs and shouts, one does not fall into the trap of words.

When the hundred birds do not come and spring has passed, the mountain retreat wins the luxury of sleeping until the sun is high. This is the realization of old age, retiring to the perfect clarity of the water of samādhi.
At the time of his passing, he was sixty-five years of age. During the cremation, two things remained unburnt:
his teeth and his prayer beads. His *śarīra* were bright and translucent. His disciple Jingyun erected a *stūpa* at the original hermitage.
The eulogy states: The principles of the Dongshu school are profound and meticulous. Yet, after several generations of transmission by those of vast wisdom, why was it unable to flourish extensively?

It is likely because students were negligent and found it difficult to enter the gate of mastery. Only when Master Wuyin exerted his power, wielding the "Lu-guo" (the sun), did [the tradition] truly shine forth.

Suddenly the sun’s chariot has turned back; how magnificent he was! If one were to discern his entire life through the brilliant clarity of these final relics, then the debt owed to the venerable monk Yuantong would be beyond words.
As for Chan Master Duanya Liaoyi:
Chan Master Duanya Liaoyi was the son of the Tang family in Deqing, Huzhou. He began to speak at the age of six, and his speech always accorded with the ultimate principle.
He frequently accompanied his mother as she recited the Lotus Sūtra; once, while pulling at his mother’s robe, he asked her, “The Buddha has emitted...”
The light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows illuminated eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction, pervading them all without exception.
"Has your mother ever seen this? he asked. His mother replied, "When the Buddha emits such auspicious light, it is like the udumbara flower; it is encountered but once in an age.
He asked again, "Why do you also say, 'I saw the original auspicious light of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara was just like this'? After a long while, his mother stroked his head and said:
She sighed and said, "My son possesses the roots of wisdom. You should further seek out those of lofty brilliance; do not remain self-effacing.
At the age of seventeen, he heard the words of exhortation from Master Gaofeng Miao and rose up with resolve, saying, "This is a great *kalyāṇamitra*. I shall go to follow him.
His mother was greatly pleased, and he eventually traveled to Lion Rock (*Śiṃhaśaila*) to pay his respects to Master Miao. The Master, admiring his upright and exceptional character, caused him to...
He called out, "Where does 'one' return? and provisionally gave him the name Congyi. Master Miao would call out "Congyi" every time, and Yi would always respond with an assent.
The Master said, "When an ox passes through a window frame, its head and horns, and all four hooves have already passed through; why then does the tail not pass through?"

He was at a complete loss for what to do. From that point on, where did his own self go? His conversation with the ox passing through the lattice window became a single, unified whole, as obstructive as the Iron Ring Mountains.
Whenever he sought instruction, he received nothing but fists or staffs. He further doubted whether the fists and staffs had anything to do with his original inquiry.
One day, while passing by the Bowl Pond, he saw snow falling from the tips of pine branches and attained realization. He immediately brought this up [to his teacher].
The Master said, "Regardless of north, south, east, or west, the great earth, mountains, and rivers are all one expanse of snow.
Before he had finished speaking, he was struck with a painful blow of the staff. Retreating, he unconsciously fell from the cliff. His fellow practitioners climbed vines to rescue him;

one of them vowed to limit himself to seven days, standing like a stake during the day and climbing trees at night, standing barefoot on the edge of the precipice until dawn. He did not even reach the end of that period.

Having attained great penetration, he struck the barrier and cried out: "Today you cannot deceive me! The Master asked, "How so? He replied, "The mountains and rivers of the great earth are all one sheet of snow;
once the sun shines upon them, they leave no trace. From that time on, he harbored no further doubts regarding the Buddhas and patriarchs.
"There is no longer north, south, east, or west. Master Miaogong then ascended the hall and said: "I have spread a vast net that covers the heavens;
though I have struck at phoenixes and snared dragons, I have never encountered so much as a shrimp or a crab. Today, however, there is a *jiaoming* insect that has flown into it.
Thirty years later, atop a solitary peak, it lets out a great cry. Now tell me, what is it crying? He raised his whisk.

The Master said, "The great earth, mountains, and rivers are all one expanse of snow. At once, he snatched away the whisk and said, "If there is but one person in the entire world who awakens to the truth and returns to the source, I know them all.
The Master then descended from his seat. Thereupon, he raised up and examined [the assembly] with words that were by no means meager;
thus, his reputation as a "First-Rank Practitioner" became widely renowned. Upon taking his leave, Deqing went to Wukang to build a thatched hut.
He lived there to serve his mother. Zile visited him, and after another five years had passed, he returned to Tianri.
Master Miao said, "There are many who speak the Way, yet you remain mired in mud and water. He replied, "Two eyes facing two eyes. Master Miao then performed the tonsure for him;
he further followed Master Yi, took the name Liaoyi, and styled himself Duanya. Thereupon, carrying a single gourd and a solitary staff, he crossed the Huai River and traveled through Yangzhou.

He traveled through Qi and Lu, visited Yan and Zhao, and ascended Mount Wutai. Wherever he went, his dialectical prowess was like a whirling wind, causing the monastic centers throughout the realm to tremble with awe.
Master Zhongfeng Ben described his life as follows: "He shattered the vast net of Māra and unraveled the lion’s bell;

passion vanished and conventional ties were severed, so that rocks split and cliffs collapsed. He seized the gold and pearls of the Elder Pang, wielding his brush with grand strokes to [transmit] the Dharma of A..."
The patriarch’s gateway stands with pillars erected and beams spanning; here and there, it is entirely free of entanglement. To inquire of Chan or the Way is to be unapproachable to human sentiment.

The great earth, mountains, and rivers are a single expanse of snow. This "head-word" has circulated to the present day, yet famous monasteries vied to establish it while disregarding its true meaning.
When the two Chan masters Ben and Yong passed away in succession, Yì finally took up residence at Tianmu.

The head temple’s abbot was already seventy years old, and his reputation for the Way had grown even more austere. The assembly never numbered more than fifty people, yet half of them had received the transmission of the Dharma from various quarters;
they came to him to rectify their practice and seek further instruction, never daring to give rise to arrogance. Once, he addressed the assembly, saying:

"If you wish to transcend the mundane and enter the sacred, to be forever liberated from worldly toil, you must strip away your skin and change your bones. You must die once and be revived again—like cold ashes sending forth a flame."
That withered wood has flourished again—how could this be taken lightly? During my many years at the old master’s place, I was struck with the great staff time and again;
it penetrated to my very marrow, yet never once did I harbor a thought of turning away.

Even until today, as soon as I am touched upon that painful spot, tears flow involuntarily. How could this be for you to rejoice and leap about? It is like biting into something that has a hint of bitterness.
He immediately turned his head away and paid no heed, failing to realize that the bitter taste can eliminate a hundred ailments.
Generally speaking, when one’s practice reaches the point where effort is effortless—like a boat sailing with the current—the helmsman must hold the rudder firmly;
should even a hair’s breadth of a divergent thought arise, take it for granted that one will lose one's life. If one reaches the state of pure unity, not a single thought should be stirred.
With a mind of diligence, you must not give rise to a single thought of indolence; you must not give rise to a single thought of seeking enlightenment;

you must not give rise to a single thought of gain or loss. As soon as a thought arises, all manner of demons will enter your heart and viscera, causing you to become deranged and to speak nonsense and delusions, so that you shall forever become a member of the demonic family, and even the Buddha would find it difficult to save you.
"Be careful, be careful! On the eve of the New Year in the first year of the Yuantong era, he addressed the assembly, saying: 'There is one matter, as vast as heaven; do you understand it thoroughly?
After a long silence, he said: 'Tomorrow. This was six days after the end of the Yuan dynasty.
Pointing to an empty space west of Fayun Pagoda, he said: 'It would be even better to erect a seamless pagoda here. He then returned and conversed with the practitioners with his usual ease, saying:"
"The old monk is going to Tiantai tomorrow," he said. A servant asked, "May I accompany you? He replied, "Riding a horse, one cannot catch up.
The following day, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. His secular age was seventy-two, and he had spent forty-nine summer retreats in seclusion.

In accordance with his final instructions, he was enshrined in a stupa at the very spot he had pointed out. He was posthumously granted the title Dashi Fohui Yuanming Zhengjue Pudu (Great Master Buddha-Wisdom Perfectly Enlightened Universal Deliverance).
When Yi first attended the funeral at Mount Zhongfeng, he smiled and said to the assembly, "Twelve years hence, there shall be another gathering for this old monk.
When the time came for his own passing, it precisely fulfilled that prophecy.

The eulogy says: To seek the point where the staff falls—how is this different from reaching for the moon in water? To leap beyond the limits under a shout—yet it is like trying to split glue stuck between one's knees.
When the Master first struck upon the critical barrier, he encountered Gaofeng’s solitary hardness; it was as difficult as pushing a carriage uphill.
From that time on, he attained realization while standing on the ground. In his daily life, he possessed the ease of one rowing a boat downstream;
he was clearly a man of heroic stature. Thus, the traces of his seeking the Way and leaving the household life are quite similar to those of Layman Lu.
He expounded the Dharma by transcribing the depths of his own mind, instructing others with truthfulness. To this day, his words are transmitted as essential exhortations for the Zen gate.
It is indeed fitting.
*Song-Yuan-Ming Sengbao Zhuan*, Scroll Nine;
*Song-Yuan-Ming Chanlin Sengbao Zhuan*, Scroll Ten.

Chan Master Yuansou Duan, whose name was Xingduan and whose style name was Yuansou, was born in Linhai, Tai, into the He clan. For generations, the He clan had been distinguished for their Confucian learning.
His mother, Lady Wang, was a profound scholar of the Five Classics; the disciples of Zhang’an all revered her as they did Cao Shun of the Han dynasty.

Everyone, [it was] the year of Yimao in Baoyou of the Southern Song that Zhuan was born. From birth, Zhuan abstained from meat. Upon seeing a śramaṇa while still in his swaddling clothes, he immediately felt joy.
At the age of six, his mother, Lady Wang, taught him the *Analects* and the *Mencius*; Zhuan recited them with effort until they were mastered.

Even the chapters and sentences of the Classics and the Masters' works could not be difficult for him to master. Whenever he encountered a profusion of worldly splendors and distractions, Zhuan would sit solemnly as if [in meditation].
While he was in meditative concentration, his mother marveled at him, saying, "This is a 'thousand-li colt' of our family. Yet, I fear he will not be of use to the world.

At that time, his paternal uncle, the Venerable Maoshang, had become a monk in his youth and resided at Huacheng Monastery in Yuhang. Just as he had returned to visit his hometown, Wenda followed him to receive the tonsure and ordination.
He traveled extensively through the monastic communities and visited Zangsou of Mount Jing, where he attained realization of the essential meaning upon the spur of the moment.
Zangsaō was pleased with him. One day, Zangsaō asked Duan, "Are you a native of Taizhou? Duan replied, "Taizhou. The Master gave a shout. Duan bowed.
The Master shouted again. Duan stood with his hands folded in *añjali*. The Master said, "I let you off thirty blows. Duan gave a nod of acknowledgment.
Zangsaō said again, "Do you know that there are no monks in my place, Southern Quanzhou? Duan asked, "What about the Master? The Master then—
Wumen struck him with his staff. Wuding held it firmly and said, "Do not say there is no monk here. The old man laughed heartily and rose.

After Wuding finished his period of study, he wandered leisurely among the mountains and waters of West Lake, calling himself a native of Hanshi Village. Yuyang Xuyong composed a verse to invite him back, saying: [Verse omitted as per instructions]
Frost-flakes fall at midnight; the sun stands high at noon. Between the vast and silent heavens and earth, there is only Hanshanzi.
Duan did not answer. He was the administrative secretary (shuji) of Jingci Monastery. At that time, Chan Master Shilin Gong resided there.
The scholar Lin Chushi of Mount Wu had long remained in seclusion, with no contact with the world. Upon suddenly seeing Duan’s writings, he responded to him solely in verse.
At the beginning of the letter, there was the phrase: "Can one who can chant the verses of the Tianbao era fail to practice the Chan of Lingnan?
Yuan-duan then traveled far to visit Xueyan Qin at Yangshan. Qin asked, "Where did you set out from? Yuan-duan replied, "From the Two Zhe.

Qin asked, "Why is your accent different? Yuan-duan said, "Shut your mouth! Qin said, "The Tadajing Bridge is high and the Jiyun Peak is steep; I do not yet know you, O *dàlǐ* (Sanskrit for 'venerable')."
Zhaoduān clapped his hands and said, "The duck has swallowed the snail; its eyes have popped out. He looked back at his attendant and said, "Bring some fine tea.
Zhaoduān replied, "It is not necessary. Thereupon, he treated him with the highest courtesy. This was during the early years of the Dàdé era of Emperor Wenzong of the Yuan dynasty.
He lived in seclusion at Huyan. At Jingshan, he shared his seat with others. In the year of Gengzi, he went forth to reside at Xiangfeng in Huzhou, where he said:

"The Way of the Patriarch Dahui was such that he would rather take this very body to undergo the sufferings of hell on behalf of all sentient beings in the great earth than ever treat the Buddha-Dharma as a matter of personal favor.
My late teacher at Jingshan, the Venerable Cangshou, throughout his entire life refused to yield the four quarters of the world [to worldly concerns]."
People! Even if Śākyamuni himself or the Patriarch Bodhidharma were to arrive, they would have no choice but to step back.
For two years, while I was in the attendants' quarters, I exhausted every stratagem and employed every skill, yet there was truly nowhere for me to settle.

Thus, I knew him to be the true grandson of Dahui. Now, as I offer this incense to him, I wish that he too— (Note: The original text ends abruptly with "也要" (also wants/also requires), suggesting an incomplete sentence. The translation reflects this.)
Everyone attested to this. In the year Jiachen (1304), an imperial edict appointed him as the head of Central India and bestowed upon him the title of Master Huiri Zhengbian.

In the year Renzi of the Huangqing era (1312), he moved to Lingyin Monastery. When Emperor Renzong convened a Great Unrestricted Assembly at Mount Jinshan, he commanded [the Master] to preside over it.

Furthermore, he was additionally titled "Buddha-Sun" (Furi). He subsequently retired to the Western Hermitage at Liangyu. During the Renxu year of the Zhi-zhi era under Emperor Yingzong, he was invited to reside at Mount Jing.
His assembly of talented disciples at Mount Jing was no less flourishing than that of Miaoxi; figures such as Chushi Qi were frequently hailed as "monastic heroes.
When the Duke Wenjing Yu served as Grand Secretary during the Yongle era, he frequented various Chan masters while simultaneously excelling in literary scholarship.
A resident of Su-zhou, who called himself the Layman Wei-xiao, frequently praised the character of Yang Dainian and extensively critiqued the recorded sayings of various masters.
However, upon reading the *Duan-chanshi yulu*, he said to his disciples: "Master Yuansou’s lifelong realization of the ultimate truth was expansive;
whether his explanations were extensive or concise, they were all grand and magnificent. Yet, the essential points remained hidden and undeveloped, as if awaiting [a later revelation]."
That person—among those of the lineage and lingering influence of Mahāmati—still possesses such qualities;
I did not expect to encounter such a one again in my old age. His proclamation was: "Those who practice their cultivation within stillness take that stillness as the ultimate goal.
Yet, that which you seek as the ultimate within stillness is not it. Those who exercise mastery amidst clamor... [He continued] with the clamor... [as the ultimate].
To find delight in bustle is not the delight you should find within it;
that which is grasped through the scriptures and teachings takes those scriptures and teachings as its foundation, yet it is not something you can grasp within the scriptures and teachings.
To study and polish oneself among teachers and friends takes those teachers and friends as one's source, yet it is not something you [possess] within your teachers and friends.
This is the substance attained through middle-level study and refinement.
This formless Vajrapāṇi has existed from the kalpa of motes of dust until the present day, like a fish submerged in a spring that leaps upward by stirring the waves.
If you seek him to the east, he stands firm to the west; if you seek him to the south, he stands firm to the north. To make him...
All people can obtain names and designations for themselves; all people cannot bestow names and designations upon others.
At all places and at all times, the myriad phenomena are your masters and the myriad dharmas are your teachers—this is precisely it.
Unless one possesses superior faculties and sharp wisdom, and the skillful means of one who does not blink when killing people, [one cannot] take the eighth consciousness...

If one merely cuts with a single stroke, how could there be a time of accomplishment? It is further said: "Within the very root of one's own house, there have accumulated many evil habits over countless lifetimes and kalpas.
If these are not illuminated and shattered, and if they are not stripped away and discarded, how can one avoid becoming obstructed wherever one encounters things during daily life?
Within all phenomena, if there is even a single point of doubt, it will immediately hinder and destroy you. Regarding all phenomena...
Within these, there may be the water of attachment that drowns and kills you; within all phenomena, there may be the fire of aversion that burns and kills you;
within all phenomena, there may be the wind of delight that blows away and kills you.
These four are the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and the twenty-five states of existence—light and darkness, form and emptiness, and the dense forest of phenomena.
It encompasses the myriad phenomena, sticking them all together everywhere like sticky glue. It drives you into the womb of a donkey and makes you enter the belly of a horse;
it is entirely up to it. Even if a thousand Buddhas were to appear in the world, they could do nothing about it.

During the forty-second year of the reign of Emperor Duan, he received the golden brocade robe three times. He kept it secret and did not wear it over his robes. As for the gold and silk bestowed upon him...

He provided relief to all who were poor and destitute. Furthermore, he was prone to anger, which grew even more severe as he aged. Whenever he took his seat, he would spend the entire day passing around meals while scolding and reviling others.

When he entered his private chamber, some would secretly ask him the reason for this, whereupon he would look around left and right; though he wished to speak, he had already forgotten what he intended to say.

Thus, among both the clergy and the laity, there were many who attained the essential meaning amidst his angry outbursts and insults. In the autumn of the *Renwu* year of the *Zhizheng* era of Emperor Shun, he manifested a slight illness and asked:
The attendant monk said, “He has already ceased exhaling, but he has not yet relinquished inhaling; he remains as one with the source of all suffering.
As for ‘the coming one who does not come,’ what is this ‘coming one who does not come’? The monk was silent. Duan sat for a long while and then said, “Look after five days.
When the time arrived, he changed his robes, sat in the lotus position, and said, “Fundamentally there is no arising or ceasing; how could there be going or coming? Then, ice flowed from his body.
Flames erupted; as the flowers of the iron trees bloomed, he passed away with one foot hanging down. He was eighty-eight years of age and seventy-six years since his ordination (*saṃghavarṣa*).
His clipped nails and hair were filled with *śarīra* relics. His entire body was enshrined on the north side of Pengtuan Peak, and he was posthumously titled "Puzhao" (Universal Illumination).

The pagoda was named Jizhao (Tranquil Illumination). During one of Zhiyuan’s days of secluded retirement at Liangyu, a foreign monk suddenly arrived leaning on his staff to inquire about the essential pivot of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Zhiyuan demonstrated for him the "Lion King’s Vigorous Stride" samādhi; the monk prostrated himself, stepped through the air, and departed.
His attendants were all struck with amazement, but Zhiyuan said, "To cover one's nose while stealing the fragrance—what is there to admire in that?"
The eulogy says: From Mahāmati to Chan Master Duan, four generations have passed—two hundred years. It was as if the tip of a powerful bow could no longer pierce even thin silk.
Yet this Master emerged from the school of Master Zhen; his Way covered three reigns, and his virtue spread across the nine continents.
With such profound roots and a long-flowing stream, was it not fitting? Some say that after the Master, those who preached the Dharma were for the most part...
The Imperial Court—could it be that they transformed their household by regarding the Golden Horse Gate as a place for recluses? No.
Who else could it be but the one who, without leaving beneath the Bodhi tree, occupies the Auspicious Seat?
As for Chan Master Shiwu Gong:
his name was Qinggong, and he was a native of Yushan. He was born into the Wen family in the *Ren-shen* year of the Xianchun era of the Song dynasty (1272).
On the night of his birth, a light pierced the northern wall of his room, and an extraordinary fragrance lingered for ten days without fading. From childhood, Gong abstained from alcohol.
Zu was of a pure and slender physique, yet possessed a profound and tranquil spirit. He glanced through the Six Classics and various histories once and never looked back again;
as for the Buddhist scriptures, they were like old possessions he had rediscovered. Consequently, he cast aside everything he owned and became a great monk (*bhikṣu*).

With a graceful and soaring manner, he sought out worthy masters to visit, first attending upon Chan Master Gaofeng Miao. Master Miao asked, "Novice monk, what do you seek by coming here? Guo replied: [He then prostrated himself].
He said, "The matter of birth and death is great; I beg you to bestow upon me the Great Dharma. Master Gong replied, "I fundamentally have no Dharma; what 'small' or 'great' could I possibly speak?
Xingong then served him diligently for three years, yet he did not attain realization. Master Miao said, "There is a blind donkey in Wenzhou and Ji'an in Huai;
you should go see them. Xingong went straight to see Ji'an. On the road, he heard that Ji'an was often arrogant and contemptuous, and had abolished the formalities of the *can* (meditation) ritual.

He made the transmission of Chan his primary concern. Those who were highly renowned were frequently subjected to deletion and pruning. Yungxiong was suspicious of this; nevertheless, in his heart he believed in Master Miaoxin’s instructions.
He thought, "If it does not accord with the truth, it will not be too late to go to Wenzhou. He eventually arrived at Xifeng in Jianyang and sought an audience with Wu'an.
Wu’an sat upright with his robe bared, receiving Yungxiong’s prostrations. He then asked Yungxiong: "You have been chasing after trivialities..."
One day, [Wumen] asked, "What do you apply your mind to? Xuyun replied, "I take 'the myriad dharmas returning to the One' as my primary koan.
Wumen scolded him, saying, "What kind of pestilence-afflicted fool are you? I am teaching you to investigate a dead word! Xuyun was struck with awe and at a loss for words. Wumen then said:
"One must not dwell where there is a Buddha; one must run swiftly past where there is no Buddha. How do you understand this?
As Guo was about to respond, Dan’an suddenly rose and said in a stern voice, "This too is a dead word," and then entered his quarters. Guo was at a loss.
He then remained firmly seated beneath the master. After a long time, when Yangqi Jian’an returned, he resumed their previous conversation and questioned Xuyun.
Xuyun replied, "One sees the road once one has mounted the horse. Jian’an rebuked him again, saying, "Having been here for so many years, you still hold such a view!
Xuyun was indignant, feeling that Jian’an had betrayed him, and thus departed. As he was leaving, Jian’an laughed and said, "Xuyun will turn back on his own. While on the road, Xuyun...
While walking through the middle [of the garden], he suddenly saw a pavilion by the wind. He hurried back immediately and reported this to Jiqian, saying:
"To not dwell where there is a Buddha is also a dead word; to rush past where there is no Buddha is also a dead word. Today, Qinggong has realized the living word.
Jiqian asked, "How do you understand it? Qinggong replied: "The season of clear spring, the rain has just cleared."

The oriole sings clearly upon the branch; Jianduan (Ji’ān) approved of this. Thereupon, he traveled through the regions of Wu and Yue, invigorating the monastic communities and widely cultivating the conditions for *prajñā*.
By chance, while ascending Mount Xiawu, he was filled with joy and subsequently constructed a thatched hermitage, naming it Tianhu.

Those who flocked to him in response to his reputation grew daily more numerous. Wuxue Zonggong frequently composed mountain-dwelling verses and eulogies to instruct them; those who cherished these works considered them—
The phrasing and sentences are refined and elegant, like the sound of mountain springs echoing at night or a jade chime ringing at dawn.
It is said that when the newly established Fuyuan Chan monastery in Danghu, Jiahe, prepared to offer formal hospitality to Wuxue Guanzhi, Guanzhi would not rise to receive them.

Master Pingshan Lin then composed the "Diagram of Pushing Open the Door" (Chiqiong paiu tu) and sent it as a letter to Guanzhi. Guanzhi sighed regretfully, saying, "Brother Lin will not allow me to remain in my high reclining. Thereupon, he himself took up his bamboo staff...
Wearing a bamboo hat, he arrived with a carefree air. Fuyuan then courageously took charge of the assembly, and before long, the fundamental principles of the school were greatly revitalized.

Many who possessed the Way gathered around his seat; for six or seven years, the monks forgot their own bodies for the sake of the Dharma, and the monastic community flourished like the Nālandā Monastery in India.
Once, when a nobleman entered the monastery to provide a meal for the monks, he saw that Guo was clad in simple hempen robes.
Xiao suspected this was a mere pretense and secretly inspected the abbot’s quarters. Aside from a palm-leaf whisk and some ritual implements, the four walls were utterly empty.
The nobleman was greatly astonished and privately asked the temple administrator, "The Master is a teacher and guide for humans and devas;
why is he so austere and frugal? This is surely beyond what people like us can endure. The administrator replied, "Indeed, our Master has always been simple in his own life..."
Although offerings were numerous, he would immediately distribute them. He constantly admonished his followers, saying, "Do not covet sweet comforts, lest you be forced to repay past debts.

A person of noble rank was moved by these words; he returned home, dispersed his family wealth, and went into seclusion. When an imperial edict summoned Yuanxiong (Yong), Yong firmly declined on the grounds of illness.
Thereupon, he was granted a golden-embroidered Dharma robe as a gift, which people considered a great honor. Wenyong Gong sighed and said, "In my youth and vigor, I was already not equal to others;
how much less so now that my physical form has failed me? How can I bear to weary myself with my name in this world of men?"
He then ascended the hall and said: "Cast off the iron shackles upon your heads; fling down the wooden ladles in your hands.
Close your eyes and leap across the Yellow River; spring forth and burst through the azure void. A lion kicks over the jade balustrade;
an elephant king snaps asunder the golden ropes. Amidst white clouds, we meet at every turn; amidst green mountains, we tread with every step. He let out a shout.

"Looking up beyond the heavens—who is such a person? Thereupon, he abandoned Fuyuan and returned to Tianhu. Official documents from Jiahe arrived one after another, and Xutang Gong composed a verse in response, which included the lines:
"An old fool who turns his back on the times; too lazy to respond to requests, I cannot obey your command to emerge from the mists and clouds.
At eighty-one years of age, Xutang did not lean on a staff when walking, nor did he use a mat when sitting. [At night] he used only a lamp.
The characters he wrote were as small as grains of millet. Once, while conversing with a guest at night, it was nearly dawn; the guest apologized for having to take his leave.

Xiong smiled and said, "If the spirits of young people are such as this, how can they hope to deliberate upon the Way? Shortly thereafter, he passed away. His disciples requested instructions regarding his funeral arrangements.
Xiong raised his voice and said: "The green mountains do not accommodate stinking corpses; once dead, what need is there to dig a pit and bury them? I, too, have no samādhi-fire;
I am but a pile of firewood that outshines the past and surpasses the future. Thereupon, he passed away in a state of auspiciousness.

After the cremation, the śarīra relics were beyond counting, appearing in five colors. He was interred at Tianhu Lake during the first month of autumn in the *wuchen* year of the Zhizheng era. His posthumous title was: [Title follows]

Chan Master Fohui Zhaozhao was revered by the King of Goryeo for his profound virtue and transformative influence. Furthermore, moved by a miraculous dream, the King requested imperial authorization to dispatch an official document to Jiangzhe, requesting that the śarīra relics be divided so they might be brought back to the kingdom for veneration.
The encomium says: "Lean and angular, yet it is like a single jade crag surging up from the heart of the blue sea;
hard and stripped bare, it is as if a thousand-fathom stone house has protruded from amidst a mass of white clouds. This is Master Gong’s own description of his humble self.
As for his Way inclining the vermilion chamber and his virtue moving foreign lands, these matters need not be discussed here.

However, throughout the more than three hundred years since then, people have recited his verses and gāthās and read his recorded sayings; they lament that they cannot honor him by ascending to the heavens of Yāma or Tuṣita.
This clearly demonstrates that the Master did not deceive the world with empty words. It is evident.

As for Chan Master Xuzhou Du of Mount Jing, whose secular surname was Shi and who was a native of Jiangkan: the people of Jiangkan were habituated to worldly vanity, yet Du took no pleasure in domestic life.
He invited friends of right faith to frequent monasteries and cultivate supramundane affinities. After long cultivation, his faculties matured, and he ultimately severed [worldly ties].

He shaved his hair and styled himself "The Empty Boat" (Xūzhōu). Upon entering the lecture halls, he mastered the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* and the Vijñaptimātratā (Consciousness-Only) teachings with penetrating precision. One day, exhausted by the day’s labors, he leaned against a desk and dozed off;
in a dream, he traveled into the secular world, where the mundane environment appeared vividly real. There was a master of divination there who, upon examining his face, remarked:

"You are a guest within the Jade Hall and the Golden Horse Gate [the imperial court]; why have you fallen among the ranks of monks? He spat at him and said: "Since I have already entered the lineage of Śākya, I shall not [be swayed by such things]."

"I have accepted your yellow arsenic [criticism]. Upon realizing this, he broke into a sweat and was filled with shame and trepidation. Thereupon, he set aside his scrolls and sat in meditation like a withered tree, remaining silent for several days.
His fellow students invited him to join their banquet, but Sengdu said, "This is not the ultimate goal; what is the use of listening to such things?
Furthermore, how can the purport of the Buddhas' nirvana be reached through the medium of words? His fellow students regarded him as mad, and Sengdu immediately took up his alms bowl and departed.
He took his bag and departed, traveling extensively throughout Jiangnan. He never allowed himself to become indolent or negligent regarding those communities renowned for their practice of the Way.
Thereupon, he visited Chan Master Wudetong at Huazang Temple in Changzhou. On that day, more than thirty people accompanied him on the visit.
Tonggong alone granted Duzhen permission to enter the hall. Having gained entry into Tonggong’s chamber, Duzhen frequently sought the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma.
Each time, Tonggong would speak in a low voice, saying, "The Buddha-dharma has plenty to wait for; I shall explain it to you when there is no one else around. Duzhen’s doubts grew even deeper.
When the night was quiet, he secretly approached Master Tong’s bedside and pleaded with him incessantly.

Tong again spoke in a low voice, "I thought there was no one here," and then he pointed at Du and tapped his own chest several times; thereafter, he closed his eyes and remained silent. Startled, Du hurried out.
Thereupon, his investigation became even more earnest; whether sitting or standing, he was like a wooden puppet. Master Huitong addressed the assembly, saying:
"To break open a single mote of dust and bring forth the Great Sutra—where the hawks fly and the fish leap, one must further discern this. Do not look with the eyes, but look with the mind;
having already seen it, strike again at the ice within the fire. Duetuo suddenly attained awakening while seated beneath him. Tong then called Duetuo by name and said: "No..."
"Who is it that takes all dharmas as companions? Duan replied, "An iron Kunlun beneath a golden incense burner. The Master said, "I thought this short fellow had some special talent;
it turns out his understanding is merely like this. Duan bowed and said, "Thank you, Preceptor, for your testimony. Tong was greatly pleased.
Thereupon, Duan attended Huazang for a long time, and their minds were in perfect accord. Like...

"Water and milk. Master Tong always exhorted Pu to transcend the mundane world. Pu addressed him, saying, "The days for practicing the Way are infinite, but the period of serving one's master is limited.
Even if your lifespan were to exceed that of Zhaozhou, I fear that my own merit is meager;
should I one day fall into the ditches and ravines, how could I ever hope to receive your teachings again? Master Tong lowered his head and was moved with deep compassion. Master Gong—
After his passing, Huidu left Huazang and traveled to Shitou City. He stayed overnight at Jiashaya Temple.

At that time, the monks of the eastern and western wings were disputing over temple property and had been engaged in litigation for several years without resolution. Huidu settled the matter with a few words;

the two monks wept in sorrow and repented their transgressions, both entrusting their households to him. Huidu laughed and departed. Thereafter, he preached the Dharma wherever he went, sometimes for long periods.
For more than thirty years, he remained as constant as a single day. He once addressed the assembly, saying: "When a heterodox person speaks the True Dharma, the True Dharma is entirely heterodox.
When an orthodox person speaks heterodox dharma, the heterodox dharma is entirely true. He struck the meditation staff and said, "True? Heterodox?
Then striking it again, he said, "Speaking of the heterodox, or not speaking of the heterodox? "If you can discern and distinguish within this, even a house made of gold [will be yours]."
This is not yet considered noble. What glory is there in fine food and brocade robes? It is further said: "The myriad dharmas are the radiance of the mind;

all conditions are but the awakening of one's nature. Fundamentally, there is no person who is deluded or awakened; it simply requires resolution today. Since there is neither delusion nor awakening, what is there to resolve?

"Ten thousand words and a thousand phrases—no one understands them; they follow the warbling orioles over the low wall. When Mount Jing was destroyed by fire, the imperial decree appointed Fadu to reside there.
At the age of eighty, Fadu strove with all his might to restore it; from the major tasks down to the smallest details, he personally supervised every labor.
He was so humble and modest that he never found leisure for himself; he treated his juniors as if they were his seniors and never referred to himself as "old.

Within two years, Jing Mountain (Jingshan) was completed. It was the Gengchen year of the Yuan Shizu era. Whenever it was the anniversary of Master Tong’s death, Fudu would unfailingly display the portrait, burn incense, offer food, and shed tears.
His disciples were moved by this and followed him with devotion, even those who had already reached old age. Thus, their poetic exchanges were exquisite.
Ye was peerless in his time. When Tan returned from India to visit his father, Dao visited him; Dao wrote a verse in large characters and entrusted it to him.
Shortly thereafter, he passed away on his meditation couch. The verse read: "Eighty-two years, riding a bottomless boat; treading the waves, I return home."
When Mingyue was alone under the heavens, Tan resided at Tiantong. Among those who entered the gate of Tiantong were Huixin and others;

As for Chan Master Fuzhong, whose given name was Huixin: he was the son of the Jiang family of Fenghua in Mingzhou. At the age of ten, he requested his parents to find him a teacher;
they sent him to a local village school with a copy of the classics. In less than two years, he had mastered all the texts with complete clarity. Ultimately...

He ceased his reading and instead resolved to study and recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Consequently, he became firm in his intention to leave the household life and take up the responsibility of the Great Dharma.

After another three years, he served as a disciple under the śramaṇa Yansi at the Fahua Monastery, where he received ordination by passing the scriptural examinations. Later, when the Chan Master Zhuxi Tan resided at Tiantong, Xìn went to visit him.
Master Tan had a gaunt face like iron; he was known for his habitual use of the "hot stick" (corporal punishment) with such frequency that it fell like raindrops.

As for those who seek instruction, even in the depths of winter they tremble with cold, yet here [Daokai] was sweating profusely. Although Xinxing was young, he entered with composure to inquire about the Great Dharma.
Daotan, seeing his vessel was level and steady, held him in high regard. Having long been refined in the furnace, Xinxing’s Way finally became thorough. He took up his staff and asked:
"When Xinghua struck Kebin, did Kebin still have a share in receiving the blow? Xinxing stepped forward and replied: "A fine lion cub! Daotan—
He deeply approved of this. Not long after, Master Tan passed away. The assembly at Xinxing Temple requested Yunwai Xiù to succeed him as the abbot of Tiantong.

Xinxing and Xiù exchanged verses with rhythmic cadence, every stroke of their composition being in accordance with the Dharma. Xiù often praised him, saying, "Master Xinxing is a crimson banner of the Caodong school and a white-browed elder of the Linji lineage.
In the Bingyin year of the Dading era, he went forth to reside at Guanyin Temple. In the Jisi year of the Tianli era...
He moved his residence to Putuo. At the beginning of the Zhizheng era, the seat at Tiantong remained vacant. Those in authority insisted that he must accept the appointment.
Xinxin said, "Since the time of the successive sages, the regulations and structures of Tiantong after their passing have no longer been as they were in former times.
Now, if you gentlemen do not reject this humble mountain-dweller, I shall simply act according to your command. If you deem it appropriate, then I, the mountain-dweller, will [accept]."
"Carrying on the legacy and following the teachings is my sole ambition. How could I dare stubbornly decline and trouble the traveling parties of the honorable gentlemen?

If it does not suit you, please discuss it further. The assembly all bowed their heads to the ground and said, "So be it. Thereupon, Xìn took charge at Tiantóng. Long-standing abuses were suddenly eliminated, and the Dharma seat was revitalized without prior expectation.
From all quarters, he was honored with a reputation for virtue. At that time, the north and south were ravaged by war and famine.

Monasteries often face hardships. At Tiantong, however, the dining hall was filled with a thousand monks; even during the summer retreat, there was no lack of provisions, and surplus grain remained to relieve the hungry and poor.
Master Chushi Qi once composed a verse for Xin, saying: "Upon the peak of Changgeng, amidst the white clouds..."
Holding the official decree, he smiles as he unfolds it from the West. Layered cliffs and peaks surround the master’s chamber;
Ten thousand pine trees encircle the Zen gate. Who took away its golden brilliance in years past? Today, Tianlong Temple ought to see it returned. I, an old man, am like one who peers at a leopard;
Through the bamboo tube, I occasionally catch glimpses of its spots. Written by the Grand Dragon of Jiangbiao, Xiangsi, Imperial Censor, who received the imperial decree.
He welcomed the messenger. The messenger came of his own accord with joy. This was in the fourteenth year of the Zhizheng era, the Jia-wu year.
Two years later, the army of Emperor Taizu of Ming descended upon Jinling. The monks of the temple dispersed like the wind, yet Faxin alone remained, sitting in *paryaṅka* without departing.

Shortly thereafter, helmets gathered around him like ants; Faxin remained solemnly in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), as if unaware of anything. When Emperor Taizu entered the temple, Faxin joined his palms in greeting.
[He] welcomed [him]. Taizu asked, "Why did the assembly of monks not see him? Xìn replied, "Even those with clear eyes find it difficult to deceive.

Taizu was greatly pleased and ordered that the monk be summoned back to the temple. Taizu once listened to Xìn’s Dharma discourse and, upon returning, remarked to his attendants, "The monk Longxiang Xìn is pure and sincere in both word and deed;
he is truly a śramaṇa of the Way in a time of Great Peace. He then changed the name of Longxiang to [Tianping].

He was granted the title of "Champion of Life" by the Heavenly Court. Although his years of religious merit were advanced, he never once used worldly sounds or sights to influence those who studied under him;
rather, his disciples transformed themselves through his example. Xìn daily recited the *Lotus Sūtra* in seven fascicles, never ceasing regardless of cold or heat. A monk asked him:
The Master was reciting a sutra. "Do you also understand its meaning? Mazu asked. Baolin said, "In the early morning I ate white congee; now I feel hungry again.
The monk said, "These words do not accord with the text of the sutra. Baolin replied, "A clear-eyed teacher is still clearly present here.
The monk laughed heartily and said, "What kind of mental state is this, Master? Baolin said, "I am glad that you have received, believed, and practiced it."

On the first day of the new year in the Dingyou year, there was a solar eclipse. Taizu summoned Xìn to inquire about it. Xìn replied, "After the eclipse, it will clear of its own accord. Taizu was again deeply pleased.
They further discussed the principles of ancient and modern *fu* and *chan* (prophecies and omens). Xìn said, "Sages and philosophers take supreme impartiality as their core intention."

Without seeking for auspicious signs or prophecies, such signs and prophecies accorded themselves. Those who are ignorant and harbor private desires will regard even a phoenix or a qilin appearing by day as merely strange creatures.
Thus it is said: "It lies here, not there. The Grand Ancestor praised this as excellent, and they concluded with mutual joy.
On the morning of the twenty-fourth day of the eighth month, he rose, bathed, and changed his robes. Summoning the assembly, he declared: "I am departing. You..."

He said, "I shall henceforth dedicate myself solely to upholding the Dharma," and passed away with eyes closed. His attendant shook him and called out, "Does the Master not leave behind even a single word to show to others?
Xinxin then opened his eyes again, took up a brush, and wrote: "Throughout my life, I have been stubborn and contrary;
For seventy-eight years, I have let it all leak out. This morning, I cast off my hands and depart; Ten thousand miles of clear sky, a single flake of snow. Thus he spoke.
With eyes closed, he passed away forever. At that time, Emperor Taizu was supervising the military at Jiangyin. One day prior, he had dreamed of Xìn coming to bid him farewell.
Upon returning to Jinling and hearing the news of the passing, it matched his dream exactly. Taizu was deeply grieved and lamented.

His attendants all remarked, "The Great Man in golden armor informed us the other day that an ancient Buddha from the celestial realm had entered nirvana. Taizu was even more struck with wonder and granted him a treasury of funds as a posthumous honor.
Gold was used to provide for his funeral expenses. On the day the reliquary was lifted, Emperor Taizu attended the offering ceremony.

He was cremated according to the Dharma on the slopes of Mount Jubaoshan, where five-colored śarīras were obtained. The Emperor ordered He Qishu to select a site on Mount Niushou for the construction of a stupa and commanded a Confucian scholar to compose an inscription for it.
As for the items enshrined at Tiantong, they were his fingernails, hair, robes, and sandals. Initially, Xincheng received the imperial decree and departed from Longxiang.
Tiantong’s attendants remonstrated with him, saying, "In these current times of turmoil and the clash of arms, those with ambition have no leisure to seek entry into the mountain forests.
Yet you alone have received the high praise of the sovereign; we do not think this is appropriate. Furthermore, it remains uncertain what will become of the world.
Xìn replied, "I and you are all equally the descendants of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; it is our duty to provide support and sustain the Dharma."
In the family of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, responding to conditions and manifesting according to the needs of beings is the natural function of their office.

If everyone were to let their minds be gripped by concerns for fortune and misfortune, burying themselves and concealing their traces, how could this be the way of great compassion and universal salvation?
Furthermore, is the field of spears, halberds, swords, and lances not itself a land of peace and bliss? Thereupon, there were many who rose with the aspiration to follow him.

The eulogy states: Although the pedagogical methods employed by the three generations at Mount Jing were each different, when one examines their essential points, they were all master craftsmen who thoroughly mastered expedient means and mastery of change.
Master Du strove for restoration until his old age; Master Xin likewise continued until his death.
It is as if one were showing the way to a wise sovereign; such is the burden of upholding the ancestral Way, truly difficult to cast off from one's shoulders.

It is like a man of Wu traveling in Chu who, while ill, hears the sounds of Chu yet continues to sing in the Wu style. If the former scholars' bitter toil was such as this, how could one possibly neglect it?
The Three Chan Masters Chushi, Yuan’an, and Mengtang.
Master Chushi, whose name was Fanqi, was a preeminent disciple of Master Yuansou Duan of Mount Jing.
He propagated the Way at Fuzhen in Haiyan, followed by Tianning, and eventually at Baoguo in Hangzhou and Benjue in Jiaxing. His virtue...

The influence of his reputation spread throughout the nine provinces. During the reigns of Emperors Yuanwen and Shunzhi, there was no venerable master of the Way from the north and south of Mount Chu or the east and west of the River Zhe who did not receive a bestowed honorary title; yet Qian alone withdrew far away and did not participate.
During the Zhizheng era, the Imperial Preceptor (Dishi) insistently conferred upon him the title "Buddhist Sun Universally Illuminating and Wise Discernment" (Furi Puzhao Hui Bian).
Qi also did not accept the signature [of this title]. In his later years, he had his disciple Jingxian succeed him as the presiding master of the Tianning Monastery.

He then separately constructed the Fangzhai (Square Chamber) to the west of the Tianning Cloister as a plan for his retirement, styling himself the "Elder of the Western Chamber. During the Zhizheng era, affairs were many and turbulent throughout the four quarters.
Among the scholar-officials who have fled to the shores of the sea to seek the Dharma, those who frequented Xizhai—such as Song Gong Jingliao and his peers—are most renowned for their vast learning.
Yet, upon entering the gate of Xizhai, they found that his profound discussions were largely focused on the North.

When some questioned him regarding the fortunes or misfortunes of the current political situation, Qian Qi would merely sing the "Hxiu-hxiu" (Rest and Ease) song, the rhythm and meaning of which remained unfathomable. In the year Gui-mao, the Imperial Preceptor of the Yuan dynasty sent a letter by hand...
Weiqi declined to attend, citing his severe illness. On the wu-shen day, Emperor Ming of the Liang dynasty ascended the throne.

Considering that this was the beginning of the era of "folding arms and breaking the drum" (a time of peace), yet those who had perished in the service of the state remained unrewarded, he dispatched four "rush-cart" missions to summon eminent śramaṇas of high conduct from throughout the realm.
He issued an edict to the Ministry of Rites to request that Weiqi ascend the seat at Jiangshan Mountain, so that both the living and the deceased might equally partake in the merit.
Regarding the benefits of the Dharma: When Emperor Gao saw Ti’s proclamations, he was greatly pleased. In the spring of the following year, he summoned him to a banquet at Wenlou.

Because Qi was advanced in years, the Emperor granted him a staff to assist his movement. Qi was then retained at the Tianjie Monastery. The following year, the Emperor again issued an edict summoning all Chan masters of the Way from throughout the realm;
they all proceeded to Tianjie. Among the more than thirty venerable elders who responded to the imperial summons, there were those who had emerged from the lineage of Yuansou.
Among them, three—Tan’uo of Guoqing, Zhiji of Shuangjing, and Qianqi—frequently entered the Yanyunlou to discuss the Way.

When Emperor Gao asked about the profound and unfathomable principles of ghosts and spirits, Qianqi cited the sutras and śāstras to analyze and explain the Emperor’s inner thoughts. However, his daily conduct remained lax and unrestrained, no different from when he was at Xizhai.

Chushi Zhen was a recluse among the bamboo groves. On the sixteenth day of the seventh month of that year, Yuqi called his attendant monk to bring ink and a brush, and wrote a verse in large characters:
"The true nature is perfectly luminous, Fundamentally without birth or extinction. The wooden horse neighs at night; The sun rises in the west.
He then said to E’o Tang, "Elder brother, I am going. E’o asked, "Where are you going? Yuqi—
With a single thunderous shout, he passed away at the age of seventy-five. His final verse was reported to the Emperor Gaozong, who ordered that he be cremated according to the Dharma.

The sun rises in the West, a phenomenon as rare as it has ever been. His emanations exceed those dwelling in the celestial realms; let him not forget to propagate the Dharma in the imperial capital.
Our brothers with white hair grow old in vain; the stupa pole has fallen and awaits someone to support it.
Master Yuan’an, whose name was Zhiji, was a native of Wu. At the age of seventeen, he became a monk and likewise received the Dharma from Yuansou Zhenkan.
During his tenure, he successively moved to four renowned monasteries. The Yuan Emperor bestowed upon him the title Chan Master Mingbian Zhengzong Guanghui.
Master Ji was tall and stood as upright as a mountain; he appeared like a solitary pine rising from a ravine. His administration of the precepts was strict and solemn. His...

Yet he was able to adapt himself to the exigencies of the times, much like the spring breeze or the timely rain reaching all things, such that people remained unaware of his influence. Because his exhortations reached the imperial court, he upheld the reputation of the Great Elder (Yuansou).
Furthermore, he delighted in receiving counsel; even when encountering a child of three feet, if the child’s reasoning was sound, he would follow it. Though he was skilled...

As for his remaining arts, he regarded himself as falling short; yet, when it came to diagnosing and eliminating accumulated abuses, he required no words or facial expressions, for he severed their source by force.
Thus, the Academician Song Lian praised him, saying: "It was not in vain that the Imperial Preceptor of the Yuan dynasty bestowed honorary titles upon both Yuanfo and Master Guyan.

Upon cremation, a fragrance like agarwood wafted over the people. His rosary, which had been used throughout his life, remained intact without breaking.
His remains were a deep azure luster, resembling blue lapis lazuli, and the *śarīra* relics accumulated there radiated light. Furthermore, there was a dream.
Chan Master Tang’uo was equal in fame to [Zhao] Ji.

His grandfather served a prominent family; they were both noble and wealthy, with silks and brocades intermingling in abundance.

Yet, while born amidst such luxury, he as a child delighted in wearing coarse cloth and furs, enjoyed a vegetarian diet, and preferred sitting in quiet chambers with his eyes fixed without blinking, like a monk in meditative absorption.
Nevertheless, when interacting with the world, his speech was as dynamic as wind and clouds, shifting and transforming beyond description. Regarding the various histories and records...

He did not read it more than once. While traveling to the Yanqing Lecture Hall in the prefectural city, he saw the *Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch* and secretly resolved to take it home to read.
