Chan Master Qianyan of Fulong:
Chan Master Qianyan, whose name was Yuanchang, was the son of the Dong family of Xiaoshan in Yue. He emerged from the lineage of National Teacher Zhongfeng Ben of Tianmu.
He established the Shengshou Monastery on Mount Fulong in Wushang to transform and guide others. His manner of engaging with sentient beings and benefiting people was as follows:

He was a peer unto the sages of antiquity. During the final years of the Yuan dynasty, there were those who donned the robes of the fields [as a pretext for office], none of whom failed to rely upon the state;
the imperial court honored them and held their reputations in high esteem. Yet when the Duke resided at Fulong, he did nothing more than labor in the fields to procure food.

Though the sovereign thrice conferred honorary titles upon him, the Duke never signed them throughout his life. Thus, those with discernment regarded him as a pillar supporting the world against a surging tide.
He was styled Gōng. By nature, Gōng was brilliant and quick-witted. When he first left his home to renounce worldly life, he sought the precepts from the Vinaya Master of Lingzhi.

At that time, the Venerable Zhongfeng Ben was staying at the Yunju Hermitage in Hangzhou. Gōng happened to attend a vegetarian feast at the Chancellor’s residence and was able to pay his respects to him there.
Ben asked, "What is your dharma-name, Upāsaka? He replied, "Yuánzhǎng. Ben then asked, "What do you do all day long?"
Master Xin then bowed twice and requested further instruction. Yuanwu had previously shown him the case of "The Dog Has No Buddha-nature.

Taking the Dharma as his object of focus, he did not produce any realization for ten years. He then sighed privately to himself, "How can a starving tiger, eyeing the meat upon a table, ever find it truly satisfying?

Thereupon, he confined himself at the mountain peak. Upon hearing the cry of a sparrow, he attained a sudden awakening. He hurried down to consult his master, but when he presented his realization, he was again rebuked.
In indignation, he returned and sat in meditation at the pass, scrutinizing the point of his awakening; yet in the end, he could find nothing there. As he paced back and forth in this state,
At night, whether walking or standing, he suddenly heard the sound of a cat’s bowl being overturned by a mouse as it fell to the ground.

He then clearly perceived Master Ben’s manner of being, whereupon he abandoned his hut and returned to Ben. Ben asked, "Why did Zhaozhou say 'there is none'? He replied, "The mouse ate the cat's rice.
Ben said, "Not yet. He replied, "The rice bowl was broken. Ben asked, "What after it was broken? He replied, "Only after it was smashed to pieces [is there truly nothing]."

A record of his writings was transmitted as far as Central India. Chan Master Xiaoyin remarked, "If Zhongfeng has such a son, what need is there to worry about the Linji school's legacy?
He immediately informed the Chancellor of the Provincial Administration, who established a famous monastery for him;
however, by then, the Master had already departed for Dong’an. His inscription on "Pine and Clouds" reads: "To see it, to speak it, and to practice it—these are still merely 'arrivals'."
This is not yet "arriving at the non-arrival. Although it is "arriving at the non-arrival," it is still not "the non-arrival of the non-arrival.
Why? For forty-nine years, the World-Honored One consumed the ready-made, idle food of the world;

with those two flaps of skin, he spoke of right and wrong, spoke of long and short, and uttered so many idle words and prolixities that they filled the world, leaving it in utter disorder. At the very end—
He realized his error. At a place where he felt ashamed and humiliated for being without attachment [to his own position], he said:

Emperor Wu three times attempted to extinguish it, yet it grew ever more fierce and flourishing. Yunmen killed it; Deshan reviled it; Linji shouted at it.

He employed the power of the Great Spirit’s hand that split Mount Taihua and the mechanism of the mustard seed that contains Mount Sumeru to construct a pavilion, inscribed with the name "Pine Cloud" (Songyun).

This is merely seeing the truth and manifesting the great dharma-gate of perfect interpenetration. Some may say that discerning demons and distinguishing the heterodox constitutes the "eye of the school," weighing and measuring with precision, and applying the upward-pointing tongs and hammer;

Thus, he esteemed the world most highly. Among those who peddle their wares for profit, there are often those who echo empty sounds and catch hollow reverberations;

As the assembly rushed to circumambulate him, Ming was already seated peacefully with his body extended, having passed away. He left behind a verse which said: "Life and death are pure truth; the great void is perfectly full.

Chan Master Lijin of Tianjie Monastery, styled Baian (some versions record his name as Wanjin), was the son of the Yao family of Wumen.

Chan Master Niguan, whose name was Zhishun and whose courtesy name was Chenggou, was the son of the Chen family of Rui’an in Dong’ou.
His mother possessed noble virtue and was diligent in her service to the Buddha. She dreamed of a monk with a halo around his head who was crossing against a vast current;

the monk called out to her, saying, "I trouble you to act as my mother; do not decline this labor. Upon waking, she immediately became pregnant. When Shun was seven years old, he possessed divine insight.
Extraordinary was the case of Chan Master Jikū of Jijikyō-in in Ōei. When [Hō]moku was a *śrāmaṇera*, Jikū instructed him in the Great Dharma;

Moku received it with faith and reverence, never showing even a moment of indolence. Many elders held him in high esteem. Once Moku had become a full monk (*bhikṣu*), he took leave of Jikū to travel as a pilgrim.
He visited various masters of great attainment and eventually reached Tenpō in Min, where he attended upon Zen Master Tettsū Gesshū. As for Gesshū:
He inscribed this as the seventh-generation transmission of this hermitage. Whenever he encountered a Chan practitioner, he would habitually ask, "Does the old monk’s tongue still exist?

Consequently, many practitioners were so intimidated that they dared not meet his sharp edge. After [the practitioner] had been permitted to participate in the hall for over a month, he attained realization while looking at a bitter gourd in the garden during a visit to the latrine.
He entered the room to present his realization, and Master Shu said, "You have only just entered the gate; why..."
"How significant this is! he said. "What further Dharma is there within the inner sanctum? I beg the Master to reveal it. The Master laughed heartily and let the matter rest.
Thereupon, Shun embraced and polished [the teaching] to its ultimate conclusion; he forgot even to wash or rinse his mouth.

Deep into the night, he would regularly enter Master Shu’s quarters to inquire about the karmic conditions (*nidāna*) of the ancient worthies, sometimes remaining until the morning bell rang before departing. Master Shu admired him from the bottom of his heart. One evening, as he was slowly...

A question was asked: "I have heard that Master Heshang had extensive encounters with the great elders of the lakes and rivers, but I do not yet know under what conditions he attained thorough penetration to the source.
Master Shu replied: "At that time, I went to Huazang and received my formal training from Master Zhuxi."
I then knew that such a thing existed; yet, there was something like an obstruction in my breast that I could not set aside.
After receiving full ordination, I studied under various elders such as Zhongfeng and Wumen. These elders never failed to point me toward the fundamental essence, but I simply could not grasp it.
Thereupon, I went to Shimen to see my late teacher, Yuanwu. My teacher likewise had no lengthy discourse, but said only: "No."
"This mind is not the Buddha, nor is it a thing. How do you understand this? At that moment, his past and future limits were severed.
One day after the midday meal, as he stepped down from his seat, he suddenly trod upon solid ground and hurried to the Abbot’s quarters. Seeing him from afar, the former master smiled and said:
"How so? I replied, "Nanquan has been caught by me. My late teacher asked, "Where is Nanquan right now? I gave a shout.
My late teacher said, "Apart from that one shout, where is Nanquan? I shook my sleeves and left.
Thereafter, I attended to him, serving as his attendant for fifteen years. Setting aside my own affairs for a moment, tell me: where do you go?
While at [the monastery], he encountered Nanquan; his verbal responses and physical demeanor were both lost, leaving him ashamed and with no place to hide.

One night, hearing the signal bell for the evening assembly, he rose from his mat and attained a sudden, great awakening. He hurried to inform Master Shu, saying, "The flaws in Nanquan have now been seen.
Shu asked, "Mind, Buddha, and phenomena are all not it—what is it? He replied, "Bricks laid on the ground; tiles on the roof."
Fū said, "Where is Nanquan right now? Shùn replied, "A hawk flies over Silla. Fū said, "Wrong. Shùn also said, "Wrong.
The next day, Fū ordered the drum to be beaten for an examination. Shùn wrung his hands up and down, looked around, and asked, "Where are the Master’s eyes?
Fū praised him, saying, "I want everyone to know. The sixth year of the Zhizheng era, the Gengchen year.
In the autumn, Master Shu passed away, and Master Shun succeeded him at the seat of Tianbao. Thereupon, the lineage of Ciyun was greatly revitalized.
Counting from Shun back to Ciyun Yuan, there were eight generations. Yuan obtained the Dharma from Jiaoshan Ti; Ti transmitted it three times to Tianzhu You.
There is a tradition concerning the transmission from Yuanweng of Tianchi. He had two successors: Daci Cheng and Tieguan Shu.
Having received the authentic seal of authority from Shun, Tieguan Shu commanded both humans and devas, and the world’s perspective was transformed.
He moved from Tianbao to Baoen, and later resided at Guiyuan; yet his skillful means of bestowing and withholding were even more cautious than when he was at Tianbao.

At that time, monastics from the south and north gathered in great numbers. The imperial court, recognizing [Fayan] Shun’s virtue, bestowed upon him robes and conferred the honorary title "Chan Master Foxing Yuanbian.
Shun then retired to Luoshan in Dong’ou, where he dug a hole in the ground for a hearth and broke off bamboo to serve as chopsticks.
He did not provide a bed nor store grain for the next day's meal. Some criticized him for such eccentricity intended to reform the world, but Shun paid them no heed. He lived in such simplicity.
Zhang Yanzhi not-hua governed Min. He firmly invited Fashun to reside at Dongchan Monastery in Min, and later moved him to Xuefeng.

Fashun’s administration of the Dharma was skillful and perfectly harmonious; his assembly was solemn without the need for formal regulations. As they listened to Fashun preach the Dharma, each attained their own realization.
For several hundred years, Xuefeng had been called "the Restoration" (Zhongxing) because of Fashun. At the beginning of the Hongwu era of the Ming dynasty, an imperial edict summoned Fashun.

When the Emperor ascended the throne at Zhongshan, he personally attended the Dharma assembly. He felt as though he had known Zhenxun from of old. Whenever Zhenxun addressed the Emperor, he referred to himself as a "monk" rather than a "subject.

At times, if he forgot and used the word "I," the Emperor praised him for his sincerity and candor. Subsequently, Zhenxun returned to the South. The Southern Kingdom (the Southern Song) sought to retain him at Jingci Monastery.
Not long after, the local authorities, acting on imperial decree, forcibly compelled Zhenxun to travel to the capital. He remained there for four months.
He wrote a verse and passed away; it was the summer of the thirteenth year of the Hongwu era. Upon cremation, the śarīra relics obtained scattered like bright pearls.
His records (*yulu*) from six famous monasteries are widely circulated in the world.

However, as he possessed many extraordinary manifestations, people regarded him as divine and even venerated him as a "flesh Buddha. I dare not add further commentary, fearing it would be disrespectful.
The encomium says: Master Zun’s reputation flourished during two reigns; his breast could swallow Mount Sumeru, and his tongue could overturn the vast ocean.

In others, such celestial blossoms would have nearly filled their meditation seats; yet this Master remained simple and austere in his conduct, truly not failing as a successor to the ancestral Bhikṣus.

He was indeed one who lived with such equanimity that he shared his being with the world, while those who followed him were but petty and narrow-minded. Thus, I praise these minute traces of his extraordinary life.
Both [views] are so; yet how could they truly be so?
At that time, there was Chan Master Wanfeng Wei.
"Wanfeng" was his style name; his secular surname was Jin, and he was a native of Dong’ou. His spiritual faculties were such that he had already submitted to Fulong Qian.
Yanchang and Fahong of Dengwei both passed away at the age of seventy-nine. The Master was originally born in their village, where various auspicious signs occurred;

these were all taken as omens concerning the Jin family. Fearing this, the Jin family prayed to the Buddha, vowing that he would become a monk. At the age of thirteen, he left the household life and attained correct knowledge and vision.
He ascended the altar to receive the full precepts and subsequently recited the *Lotus Sūtra* until he reached the passage: "All dharmas, from their very source..."

He realized that all things are inherently characterized by constant quiescence and extinction. Having attained this insight, he went to visit Zhuyan. Zhuyan presented him with the "Three Not-Sos" dialogue.

The Master then established a hermitage separately on Mount Dapeng; with a paper quilt for bedding and a straw mat for a couch, he lived in such profound seclusion as if he had forgotten his very life.
Suddenly, hearing a monk from Foji Temple cite the koan of Muzhou kicking over the water pitcher, he attained great enlightenment. He then said: "Utterly topsy-turvy!"
Nanquan said, "It has caused me to toil for half a year. If you could personally realize it right now, how could I not strike you with a fist to the chest?

Immediately, he abandoned his hermitage and entered Tiantai, ascending to Huading Peak. His spiritual resonance was such that no one could see it, yet those around him were struck with awe and trembled.
Wu Jian met him well and encouraged the Master, saying: "You should reside in the mountains to preserve the Dharma; in days to come, you shall be the one who supports the ancestral temple.
Who else but you could do so? He then went to Fulong. At Fulong, there were several thousand disciples surrounding him, all of whom were men of talent of that time.
The Master, with his local accent and long hair, advanced to pay his respects. Qianyan was struck by this and asked: "What do you bring with you?"
The Old Monk met him. The Master raised his fist. Qianyan said, "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing.
What is it? The Master drew a circle and stood with his hands folded. Qianyan said, "Do you wish to seek further instruction?
The Master covered his ears and departed. Qianyan was deeply pleased by this. One day, Qianyan took his seat and ordered the drum to be beaten; just as the assembly had gathered, the Master—
He let out a thunderous shout and, shaking his sleeves, departed. Yunyan then said, "Sombre yellow chrysanthemums fill the eyes; autumn is everywhere. Baiyun sits upright atop the green peak.
Lightly bringing forth the phrase 'no guest and no host,' one shout makes the waters of a thousand rivers flow backward. Thereupon he became renowned throughout the monastic communities.
He emerged into the world at Mount Songshan, where he addressed the assembly, saying: "The beginning of the month is the first day; its radiance..."
Gradually it emerges; at the end of the month, it is the thirtieth day. Where can its radiance be sought? Even the aged Śākyamuni would say it cannot be brought forth.
If it could be brought forth, all matters would be concluded. If there is anyone who can say it, come forward and speak! If there is none, [then so be it].
Mount Songshan addressed the assembly, revealing a message. He extended both hands and said, "I see that the lamp-lighting Buddha’s original radiance and auspicious signs are like this.
He then opened his palms and said, "The gate of skillful means is wide open; enter through here. He then clenched his fist and said:
"Shutting the sturdy gate to speak words of the home. Now tell me: how is it when neither opening nor closing?
He adjusted his robes and descended from the seat. Subsequently, he moved to Dengwu in Pingjiang and founded Dashingen Monastery.
At that time, the sovereign was titled "Buddha-Mind Son of Heaven," and many capable Chan practitioners followed him; various eminent virtuous monks entered and left the imperial court. Wenyi...
According to historical records, among the tonsured disciples gathered under the Master’s compassionate grace, there were barely fifteen hundred.
The two *ācāryas*, Puchi and Shengxue, served as their leaders. The Master received them solely through the authentic essence of the Way.

Once the Chan style within the realm was rectified, when scholars sent letters to inquire after the Master’s health, they generally ceased to write unless it was specifically to seek instruction in the Dharma; some even followed him for a long time [without further correspondence].
Travelers seeking even a single word from him could not find it; whenever they requested it, he would decline on the grounds that he was advanced in years.

When the Attendant-at-Large, Lord Lu, sent a messenger with a query regarding an ancient master’s karmic encounter, the Master said to the messenger, "When your master first selected for office, was it possible for him to go to the capital?
The messenger was startled and replied, "How could one receive an official post without paying court to the Son of Heaven?"
The Master smiled and said, "What of it? Let them choose the Buddha. Although the Master did not employ elaborate rhetoric or outward displays, his vast and unfathomable capacity was often like this.
At the beginning of the Hongwu era, an imperial decree was issued to select men of renowned virtue from the various mountains;

when the Master’s name was mentioned in the discussions, Master Song Jinglan firmly interceded, saying, "It must not be so. This old man is a native of our Zhejiang province, and I have long known him."
As for this man, he is nearly at the age of decrepitude and by nature prefers tranquility and withdrawal; he certainly cannot obey the command.

Furthermore, it would be no small beauty to leave this old man here as a model for those living beneath the forest trees. If he were pressured, he would surely follow in the footsteps of Lord Zhao of Fenyang.
Those in charge of the deliberation sent a private scout to investigate, but the Master had already been feigning illness and closing his door long ago. From his youth until—
In his old age, his daily devotions were never slackened even for a moment. During the day he attended to monastic affairs; at night he sat in the full lotus posture, remaining solemn until dawn.
When an attendant monk requested that he rest, the Master said, "You are the one who is truly busy; I, the old monk, have long been at rest.
On the twenty-ninth day of the first month of the *Xinyou* year of the Hongwu era, he gathered the assembly to recite a verse and then suddenly passed away. The verse says: "Seventy-nine years..."
A single flavor, the weeds cleared; hands clapped off from the precipice; the bright sun shines in the sky.
The one who succeeded at the Dharma seat of Dengwu was Master Baozang Chi. Following Chi, there further emerged Huixian.
As for Chan Master Xubai Huiyan:

he was a native of Chu and belonged to the Wang clan; his courtesy name was Xubai. At the age of seven, he knew how to recite the names of the Buddhas, doing so without ceasing whether awake or asleep.
Another seven years passed, and at fourteen, he paid homage to Chan Master Zhanran of Miaojue Temple and received the tonsure. Upon receiving the tonsure—

Recently, suddenly auspicious light radiated in all directions, appearing in five colors. Deeply moved and filled with joy, [the Master] said, "This śrāmaṇera will certainly be the one who points south in the future.
He thus named him Huiyan. As for the Master’s character, he was extraordinary and upright; he honored those close to him and respected his elders as if he were starving or parched.
However, his nature was rigid and he did not know how to speak softly; what he heard would come out of his mouth like the presentation of a contract. People...
They collectively named him Chuzhi. Whenever there was a difficult task to be undertaken, he would invariably urge Master Fa to act; both of them hit the mark with perfect precision.
Zhanran would frequently summon Master [Fa] and say, "The vast expanse of time—do not let it slip away by a moment. He replied, "I shall not let it slip away."
Whenever Zhàn looked at him, the Master would stop his work and leave. One day Zhàn asked, "What are you doing today? The Master replied, "I am slicing radishes.
Zhàn said, "You only know how to slice radishes. The Master said, "I also know how to kill people. Zhàn suddenly extended his neck. The Master said, [and cut it off].
"Generals who surrender are not executed. Zhan stuck out his tongue and rose. Zhan later moved to Shushan. The Master went separately to visit Songyin at Yunjian;
upon seeing a solitary pine, he felt a clear sense of self-assurance. He traveled extensively through various monasteries, refusing to be constrained by any, until he reached Pingjiang.
Jian Guolin [was meditating]. Guolin threw down a meditation cushion and said, "Try to explain this. He replied, "This very news is fundamentally beyond words;
upon the breaking of the meditation cushion, the earth bursts asunder and heaven cracks open. Guolin admired his spiritual brilliance and pointed him toward Dengwu Mountain.
He led the staff to see him off at the gate, patted the Master’s back, and said: “Only by ascending the peaks of Mount Tai and Mount Hua does one first realize the vastness of the universe;
only by casting the bait of the five-strand line can one speak of the depth of the azure ocean. You must go; do not delay. The Master respectfully assented. At that time:
Chan Master Baozangchi succeeded to the seat at Dengwu. Although those who came forward were as numerous as surging clouds, those who departed were like a flowing river;
this was because he was so cautious. The Master went to visit him. Master Baozangchi asked, "The mind is not the Buddha, and wisdom is not the Way.

How do you understand this? The Master stepped forward, joined his palms, and stood there. Master Baozangchi rebuked him severely. The Master, filled with indignation and doubt, retired to the meditation hall to practice.
He sat upright and did not sleep. By the second watch of the night, he had attained a thorough and penetrating realization of Linji’s fundamental tenets;
thus, the way of master and disciple was harmonized. After Master Chigong passed away, the Master secluded himself in Anxi for thirty years, remaining as steadfast as on a single day.

During the Yongle era, his reputation for the Way spread widely, and from famous capitals and market towns, offerings of heavy tribute arrived one after another. The Master declined them all; his integrity and character were stern and cold. One—
Yao Sida, who was renowned for his illustrious reputation in the world, wished to compose a preface for the Master; however, the Master declined.
Sida sighed and said: "Alas! In the midst of mountains collapsing and ponds overturning, one who stands firm facing the sun, whom no beckoning can summon—such a person is you.
As for the crawling of a lame tortoise or the talk of a soaring dragon, how could these ever be relied upon?"
Ah! Those who possess discernment all highly praise Master Yao’s ability to know men.

Haizhou Yongci, since leaving the Gorges, had carried his own views and treated others with haughty arrogance, refusing to register as a guest at various monasteries. The Abbot of Linggu forcibly appointed Ci to lead the assembly.
There was a practitioner of meditation named Ci (Cí). He highly praised the Master’s extraordinary and transcendent skillful means, yet he could not find satisfaction in his heart.
When the time for the Master’s passing drew near, Ci went to pay his respects. The Master cast off his [Ci's] precious attachments and severed his entanglements. Ci then took refuge in him.
Subsequently, on the fifth year of the Dàzhèng era, the Master manifested his transformation while free from illness. Prior to this, he had left behind a farewell verse which said: "The character..."
He entrusted [the items] to Chihai Chu. "Seek me," he said, "and I shall have no reward. On the day after next, the western wind smiled and nodded its head.
Furthermore, he sent the robe and alms bowl via the Elder Baian Ming to deliver them to Dongshan. At that time, Chihai Chu had been teaching at Dongshan for three years.
The Chan Master Dongshan Haizhou Cishi, whose secular name was Yongci (erroneously written as Puci), had the Dharma name Haizhou.

He was born in the twenty-seventh year of the Hongwu era of the Ming dynasty, the Jiashu year (1394), in the Yu family (erroneously recorded as the Qian family of Chushan) in Chengdu, Sichuan. At a young age, he heard it said that the matter of birth and death is of great importance.

He pressed his hands to his chest and did not go to bed for ten days. Resolving to travel to Daisui Mountain (erroneously written as "Pōshān") at Jingde Temple in Pengxian, he went to pay homage to Chan Master Duzhao Yue and earnestly sought the essentials of the Dharma. Yue was pleased with his upright character, sincerity, and gravity.
He could serve as a pillar and beam for the Dharma-gate, and so [the Master] ordained him. In the *guisi* year of the Yongle era, [his disciple] passed away.
The Master eventually entered the Western Mountains, remaining in seclusion in a hermitage for eight years. There, he and his shadow were companions; suddenly, they attained resonance.

He then abandoned the hermitage to go and pay his respects to Master Dachu. At that time, he was twenty-eight years old. Upon first receiving half of the Master’s robe, the Master suddenly asked: "Before your parents..."
Before his passing, [Shishuang] said, "Quickly, bring it forth. The Master stepped from east to west. Chushi said, "Not yet; speak further. The Master said, "Our two eyes face each other.
Chushi looked at the Master with a stern expression. The Master hurried away. Later, he went to Dongpu to visit Wuji, and upon reaching Linggu, he met Xuefeng.
Because Xuefeng recognized that the Master’s realization was precise and correct, he invited him to be the first patriarch of Linggu.

The Master had already personally authorized [him] to take his seat. He frequently engaged in physical contests with his peers, which Feng observed with secret alarm; yet the Master paid no heed to this.

At the conclusion of the retreat, he brushed off his robes and went to Anxi, where he found his spiritual affinity under Master Xubai Tan. Master Tan regarded him as the true successor to the orthodox lineage of Linji.
He entrusted his affairs to his teachers and patrons, and the Master then took his leave. He subsequently lived in seclusion at Mount Niushou and other mountains.

In the *ding-si* year of the *Zhengtong* era, when the Master was forty-four years old, he finally assumed charge of the Eastern Mountain Yishan Chan Temple. Having long cultivated himself in obscurity, he now widely propagated the Great Transformation;

veteran practitioners from all quarters humbly submitted their hearts and admired his character and conduct. Yet, as the Master gazed with tiger-like intensity upon the opportunities presented by those who came to him, his breath remained still and silent.

Before his teachings had even fully unfolded, many had already withered away in spirit. In the sixth month of the fifth year of the Zhengtong era (19th year of the sexagenary cycle, 1440), Master Tian passed away.
Among the assembly of students from the southeast, all turned toward Dongshan; kings and nobles humbled themselves to invite him with due ceremony.

The Master never used a single word to pry open the aperture of wisdom for anyone; thus, although everyone at that time felt complete love and respect, none could distinguish between intimacy and distance.
When the monastics and laypeople were preparing the site for the Master’s burial after his passing, there was a man named Fan Zuotou who lost his axe and injured his foot.
In intense pain, he asked for wine. The Master said to him, "Fan Zuotou, an injury to the foot is still tolerable; suppose, however, it were [the head]..."
When he was about to have his head removed, there were a thousand *shí* of wine provided for him as his new head. "Can this new head drink? [Fàn asked]. At these words, Fàn realized his place;

he immediately requested ordination as a monk. The Master accepted him and appointed him as a fire-attendant (*huótóu*). He applied himself with such intensity to reach the ultimate realization that he did not notice his face being singed by the flames, which felt like being mowed down by a blade.
Upon taking a mirror to look at himself, he danced with joy and presented a verse to the Master. The Master gave his approval. When...
At that time, those who entered and left Mount Dongshan were all acclaimed as eminent talents; many placed their hopes in the Master, yet he merely watched them with his eyes.
There were even those who had already occupied the high seat and whose reputations resounded throughout the land, seeking entry into the meditation hall, but the Master paid them no heed.
Some remarked, "The net of Mount Dongshan is so wide it allows fish as large as boat-swallowers to slip through. The Master smiled at this. Among them was Guxi Cheng.

The Chan Master frequently visited Dongshan, where he engaged in long discussions with the Master. Delighted by the stability and solidity of his realization, the Master sighed, "He is truly the successor to Duankiao.
He then recommended Cheng to take charge of Gaozuo Temple. When Cheng first entered the monastic world, the disciples did not yet know him well;

however, the Master sealed Cheng’s Dharma discourses and sent them to various mountains. Only then did the various mountain monasteries begin to accord him great respect, while also admiring the Master’s discernment.

It is said that the virtue of Master Wei Fa reached the pinnacle of public righteousness. In the fifth year of the Tiānshùn era, the year of Xīnyí, after the Master had finished preaching the Dharma from his seat, he passed away with a single shout.
On the day of his passing, a white rainbow stretched across the sky and strange birds wailed in grief. Gǔxī Chéng wept for him most bitterly.
He was eulogized with poetry and mourned with prose, the essence of which stated: "His Way was exalted across the lakes and seas; his virtue spread throughout the Divine Land.
His compassionate salvation flourished among all living beings, and his fame moved kings and lords. He came to Western Shu to perfect the embankment of the True Dharma;
he sat upon Eastern Mountain to extensively expound the profound principles. He continued the lamp of Gaofeng for seven generations, illuminating the masses of darkness with solitary radiance."
Chao Xian followed in the footsteps of his ancestors for a hundred years, encompassing all lineages in his universal flow.

As he was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, he manifested signs of decline, and a white rainbow pierced the sun. Once he had returned to perfect stillness and his *dharmakāya* was enshrined, the night valley hid his boat.
Thereafter, Cheng no longer ascended the hall; instead, he sat in meditation and passed away at Xiangyan. The assembly at Xiangyan was deeply moved by grief, as Cheng slowly unfolded [his robe].
Muyu said, "There is no need for this," and then he passed away peacefully. The master’s disciple Zhixuan (the character "ming" in Mingxuan is an error) propagated the Dharma in Jinling.
Xuan transmitted it to Tianqi Benrui, whose dharma heirs flourished greatly. Xuan was none other than Fan Zu tou.
The Eulogy says: From Dengwu to Dongshan, the lineage was transmitted through four generations; solitary as towering pines and cedars, its root stood alone.

Since Baofeng ignited the flame that broke through the face-gate, he met the auspicious and wondrous Master Chengqi; now the branches flourish upon the cloud-capped peaks, and the leaves provide shade throughout the world.
Some may doubt that [the world] was pure in the past but has since become corrupted; yet they fail to realize that this world of mine is vast.
Within the Great Kalpa, there are twenty intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*), during which one thousand Buddhas shall appear. Up to the present, nine of these kalpas have already passed.
From Krakucchanda until my own teacher, Śākyamuni, only four Buddhas have appeared. After Maitreya and Siṃha, there will still be nine hundred and ninety-nine more.
More than ten honored ones appeared simultaneously during the fifteenth minor kalpa; with the sole exception of Ruci.
Is it appropriate, or not, to use the criteria of flourishing and decline, or purity and impurity, to compare them? Or is it not?
Chan Master Fulindu, whose name was Zhidu and style name Baiyun, was a native of the Wu family of Lishui, Chuzhou. He first resided at Puci Monastery.

Finally, he reached Fulin. While residing at Fulin, Du entrusted the hand-scroll of Gongdu’s staff to Guzhuo Jun, thereby continuing the lineage of Duanqiao. He was one who truly embodied his predecessor's spirit;
indeed, Gongdu inherited the Dharma from Fangshan Bao, and Bao succeeded Duanqiao Lun. Thus, Du regarded Duanqiao as his fourth-generation ancestor. Du...
He was silent and composed by nature. Initially, he received instruction from Chan Master Jia at Baiyun Kongzhong in the commandery.
Master Jia secretly observed Duan’s faculties and capacities, intending to humble him by making him perform menial tasks. Every time Jia called out Duan’s name, Duan would respond with a "Yes.
Jia said, "I thought it was you, I thought it was you," but Duan did not understand his meaning. Jia then sent Duan south on a pilgrimage, saying, "Sudhana, this is it."
Venerable Zhaozhou is the model for a bodhisattva’s practice of traveling on pilgrimage (xingjiao). Master Pangyun is the model for a lay practitioner’s practice of traveling on pilgrimage.
If those of today who travel on pilgrimage do not emulate these three elders, they will merely waste their straw sandals and exhaust themselves in vain.
Du traveled extensively to visit the Chan seats of both the north and south; subsequently, he returned home to pay his respects.
Jiagong said with joy, "You have come! My task is finished. One day he spoke a verse: "Earth, water, fire, and wind were prophesied by the Buddhas of old;
bury me deep in the earth, for this is the primary truth. First, it will spare the donor from the need for more firewood;

second, it will spare people from saying there are no *śarīra* [relics]. He then sat upright and passed away. Du covered his face and wept, crying, "Heaven! Heaven! Someone remarked: [The text provided ends here.]

"You weep too late," Du said, and he laughed heartily. He then took up residence in a hut at the pagoda and studied the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* daily, mastering them both thoroughly.
Nevertheless, in his daily activities, he was still unable to attain great mastery.
He sighed, saying, "To practice Chan without seeking great penetration is but foolish Chan. Could my teacher have spoken falsely? My only regret is that during my travels..."
He arrived at Tiantai to visit Wujiandu (Wujian). At that time, Master Du was renowned as a "tiger embroidered upon the patriarchal gate" and resided on Mount Huading;
the practitioners of Chan were intimidated by him. Fadu immediately proceeded to Mount Huading to pay his respects to Du and questioned him regarding the esoteric intent of the Western Tradition.
Du raised an eyebrow and looked at him, saying, "If Mount Salar peaks its head, I will tell you. Fadu shook his hand back and forth, whereupon Du—
Heng said, "At the summit of Mount Sālā, white waves overflow the heavens; flowers bloom after芒種 (Mángzhòng), and leaves fall before立秋 (Lìqiū).
Duyu said, "In my house, there are no leftover scraps or stale rice. Heng said, "Even now, there is no shortage.
Duyu joyfully gave his approval, saying, "I have lived on this mountain for forty years; I am merely an old practitioner of the Way. There is nothing particularly extraordinary about me."
In particular, the unfinished kōan of my late master is now entrusted to you. You must maintain this well.
After Du succeeded him, he felt that his late master’s final instructions rested upon his person; thus, he engaged with others according to the times and guided them according to their capacities.

[Zhaozhou] said, "Covering one's nose while stealing fragrance. At the beginning of the Hongwu era, Zongze was summoned by imperial carriage to attend a Dharma assembly at the royal capital.

Due to his foot ailment, Zongze submitted a memorial declining the invitation. Emperor Taizu issued a handwritten edict stating: "The wild crane, free from worldly intent, does not forget to soar through the heights of heaven. Though you are lame..."
The old monk Jiao was permitted to roam freely among the mountain clouds as he pleased; the Emperor then granted him leave to return to the mountains. Addressing the assembly, he said:

"The chrysanthemums bloom by the eastern hedge, their fragrance drifting thick; The sea and sky are vast and wide, the moonlight bright in autumn. Held forth in the light of the sun is the blade sharp as a razor;

It cuts through all纵横 (crosswise and lengthwise) so that the six directions are no longer received. He further admonished his disciple Zhì'ān (whose style name was Lǎnyún): "The mirror is not lacking in clarity; it is the blind who cannot see."

One who holds a goblet with its lid may do so; yet a lute, though not lacking in loftiness, is used by the deaf merely as a doorstop. Only when one possesses such a state of realization can one attain true freedom.
Otherwise, one will be completely invaded by the two maladies of "loftiness" and "cleverness," which penetrate the most vital parts of one's being.

Thus, one falsely assumes the role of a teacher and incurs sin for oneself. Therefore, my elder master Wujing never allowed himself to be bought by these maladies of loftiness and cleverness throughout his life.
Therefore, neither humans nor devas could do anything to him. In the second month of the Guiyou year, he expressed his intention to relinquish his seat.
When his disciples requested his final words, he smiled and said, "Is what I have been saying all along not sufficient? Thereupon, he passed away suddenly.

Previously, Hu Qiubi had wished to paint a thousand portraits of Ze’s *uṣṇīṣa* (cranial protuberance) to distribute among the world. When he had completed about half, a Japanese person arrived and saw them; they were all... [text ends]
They prostrated themselves and said, "This is the ancestral teacher of our country. Why is he here? They vied with one another to purchase him with gold and returned to the East. Zhan remarked:
"Whenever I read history and encounter a point where spirits commune, I only fear that it might come to an end; this is because the hearts of those in antiquity and the present are one.
As I read the *Biography of Tianzhen*, I reached the section on his meeting with the Elder Wuji. The Elder’s singular majesty—

His virtue still presses upon one from the pages of this paper; it is a pity that days cannot be extended into years, so that the remnants of this elder’s legacy might spread throughout the world and benefit this degenerate age—how fortunate this would be!
Yet his natural character and conduct bear a striking resemblance to those of his teacher;
is this not because the peach of immortality possesses its seed? Some may say that the King of Birds of the Cinnabar Mountain cannot tolerate falsehood.
As for Chan Master Puzhuang of Yunju Da’an Zhuang:
his courtesy name was Jingzhong, and he was the son of the Yuan family from Xianju in Taizhou. His family saw a Buddhist monk enter their home when he was born.
At three years of age, he understood the *paryaṅka* (cross-legged) posture and delighted in learning Sanskrit sounds. By nine years of age, he was proficient in all Buddhist chants.
He possessed a disciplined bearing, and his clan members loved him and called him "Buddha-Child" (Fotóng).

At the age of thirteen, he followed his younger paternal uncle, Master Yìn, to rely upon Chan Master Liáng of Zu'ān in Tiántóng as a śrāmaṇera. Zu'ān also loved him and continued to call him "Buddha-Child.
After some time, he received the full precepts; however, though he practiced Chan meditation, he did not attain awakening. It happened that Chan Master Yī of Liǎotáng arrived from Mount Zǐtuó.
Tianning had long heard of his reputation while still a youth. He privately rejoiced, saying, "This is the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) of my former mountain.
He hurried to pay him homage and attained the Way. Upon returning to visit Zu’ān, Zu’ān passed away. Liatang then came to reside at Tiantong.
He met Chan Master Shuzhong Yun, who had retired to Mount Cui in accordance with an imperial decree. Liatang appointed Zhuang as the envoy to Mount Cui.
When Zhuang conversed with Yun, Yun marveled greatly at him, saying, "Tiantong’s Dharma brother has found such a person;
he will not have failed the late Master Zitan. Zhuang had previously styled himself Damai (the "Dullard") and compiled his miscellaneous writings into the *Damai Ji*.
Cheng presented it to Chen. Chen read it and said with great joy, "My nephew shall have a great name in this age; it is only a pity that I am old.
Yet, orchids are fragrant because they grow in seclusion, and pines are long-lived because they bend. My nephew, you must strive for this. He then composed a long verse as a gift, which said:
"The Candle Dragon breathes fire that burns the void; Everywhere, rivers and streams are utterly dried up. Just now..."
The divine monk has passed away from this world; who now shall overturn the celestial pitcher to wash away the scorching heat?

The sun rises high at my thatched gate, yet the bolt remains unloosed—surely not for the sake of a single mouthful of food that I should harbor idle grief. In the southern and northern villages, the green rice withers;

in the upper and lower fields, yellow dust flows. Suddenly, outside the bamboo grove, I hear a knocking: "Nephew, why have you come to these forest ravines? A scroll of yellow oil-paper is in your hand..."
Bring it here! I see your new work, as lustrous as jade and radiant as pearls. As I unfold and read it, my mind’s eye opens; it is as if I were drinking from a cup of nectar.
My aged heart is suddenly refreshed and cleared; henceforth, I shall not fear the collapse of the lineage’s mainstay in this final age.
Listen to these words of mine: do not rashly utter them before those lacking wisdom. The stone tiger before the mountain bites the hare—*ṭha-sa*.

Zhuang served as the moderator at the Great Assembly on Mount Jinshan alongside Chan Master Xingyuan. The following year, he went to Jinling and was hosted at Tianjie Monastery.
There, he engaged in debate with the most eminent and high-ranking figures, such as Man’an; his spiritual acuity exhausted their depths.
The scholar Zhou Mengxiu was also present in the assembly at that time. He asked Chan Master San: "In Confucianism there are Confucian masters;
in Chan there are Chan masters; in the scriptures there are scriptural masters. All craftsmen and artisans likewise have their teachers.
What, then, is 'unlearned wisdom' (asaikṣa-jñāna)? Master Zhuang replied: "The seven emotions and the five desires. Xiu said: "If that is so, then it is unlearned wisdom."

Zhi said, "This is not the ultimate standard" (one edition reads: "An called it the ultimate standard"). Zhuang stretched out his right foot and said, "Since I arrived in the capital, I have become lame in one leg.

The dignified decorum of Mazu and Baizhang had for the most part fallen into neglect. When Zhuang arrived at Beichen, he vigorously restored it, like the stupa-banner of Prabhūtaratna emerging from the void.
Furthermore, pitying the long-abandoned state of Yunju, he brought a dozen or so Chan disciples to settle in thatched huts upon the old site.
Piling firewood for beds, Zhuang ascended the seat and addressed the assembly, saying: "Yesterday we cleared the wasteland; today I request..."
"O people! You have cleared away the thorns and briars; you have removed the tiles and rubble. The original foundation is now clearly visible.

There remains only the tree in the center that no one has been able to uproot. Today, this mountain monk cannot help but employ another expedient: with a sharp blade, I shall prune away the profuse branches and leaves;
with a blunt hoe, I shall deeply dig out the perverse and inverted roots. When the work upon the solid ground is completed as a single whole, you shall dwell [in peace]."
The mountain was hewn by the axe until not a trace remained. Thereupon, the halls, pavilions, and corridors of Yunju emerged as a manifestation of illusion.
Monks who heard of its fame returned there as if coming home; at that time, it was celebrated throughout the world as "Yunju of the World.

In the autumn of the fourteenth year of the Hongwu era, the Emperor Gao Di composed an inscription for Mount Lu and issued a handwritten edict ordering the *zhuangzhu* (estate manager) to oversee the project. Many kinds of auspicious omens occurred, dazzling the mountains and rivers. The weeds...
The Emperor issued another edict, and was greatly pleased with him. In his later years, Zhuang accepted the imperial decree to preside over Mount Jing.

The style of Zhuyuan was once again revitalized in the southeast. He once asked a monk, "I have recently received an official document; our primary task is to 'set things in order' (*dadian*). The monk replied, "I am not a spy.
Zhuang said, "Even so, you must still undergo interrogation. The monk said, "Venerable Master, do not use your position to oppress others. Zhuang—[the story concludes here].
He extended his hand and said, "Bring forth the official seal for inspection. As the monk hesitated, Zhuang struck him with his palm. On another occasion, he spoke in a stern voice:
"The entire world of the ten directions is the Heart-Seal of Vairocana. Tell me, in whose hands does the seal-ring now rest?
A monk was about to offer a reply when Zhuang said, "Go away; come back at another time. Zhuang possessed quick discernment and left no lingering affairs behind.
He never forgot those he encountered; even amidst a multitude of ten thousand people moving about, he perceived them all at a single glance. Furthermore, he delighted in encouraging others;

if a person possessed even a small virtue, Zhuang would praise them for the rest of the day. Consequently, the monastic community referred to him as "Dāyán (Stupefying Hermit), whose tongue-wind covers the leaves.

In the first year of the Yongle era, when Zhuang was fifty-eight years old, he ordered the drum to be beaten to announce his passing. It happened that two practitioners from Jiangyou arrived, and Zhuang—
He escorted him back to the abbot’s quarters, where they conversed with great joy. They sat in discussion until midnight; Zang’s spirit was twice as vigorous as before.
The two practitioners looked at each other and sighed, saying, "This matter is extremely difficult; it cannot be grasped through deliberation or conjecture. Zang said, "Difficult, indeed difficult!

In its myriad forms and thousandfold aspects, even without deliberation it remains obscure. It is like a thunderclap in a clear blue sky, or waves surging across level ground—there is nothing to be said."
This is the true teaching; other views are not the correct contemplation. One may sink into delusion and waste vast eons, yet the realization lies only on the tip of a hair.
Do not let yourself sit idly within the Han-yuan Palace while seeking Chang’an at every turn you meet. One said: "This matter is extremely easy;
it is simply that one cannot take it up oneself. Zhuang also said: "Easy, easy! Though there are many approaches, they lead to a single principle. Cease all taking up, and forget this."

His reputation shone through antiquity and reached into the present; his influence spanned heaven and earth. He knew both existence and non-existence, and in benefiting others, he simultaneously benefited himself.

While the true vehicle of Prajñā was ever-luminous, his own thoughts were preoccupied with the mundane affairs of worldly toil. Having uprooted the long-standing vine-like roots of affliction, Śākyamuni did not require the prediction of Dīpaṃkara.
This very morning, when the bell tolled, Master Zhuang passed away peacefully. Upon his cremation, wherever the smoke and flames reached—
All [the remains] were recovered as *śarīra*, along with an unbroken white pearl. A stupa was erected on the southern slope of Lingxiao Peak.

He was truly a dragon among monks—of this there is no doubt. Yet, that he expounds the Dharma in accordance with the times is like the water of the Upper Pond.
Chan Master Chushan Qi was a native of Tang’an.
His name was Shaoqi, and his surname was Lei. At the age of eight, he entered a local school; though he received no formal instruction from a teacher, he knew how to recite the texts by heart.
The following year, he lost his father and consequently abandoned his secular studies to learn the world-transcending Dharma under Master Xuan.
Chan Master Jitong was fond of Qi; whenever they conversed, it would often last until the end of the day.
Whenever they reached a crucial point, [Qi] would not dare to challenge his words, but instead knelt to request further instruction. Jitong sighed and said, "Your spiritual capacity is too sharp;
it is difficult for you to enter the Way. Only if there remains some doubt can it be cured. Qi was startled and asked, "Can a wooden puppet enter the Way? Jitong laughed and said:

"To enter the Way, one must be like a wooden puppet. Qi grew indignant and hurried out; Yì became increasingly suspicious of him. After a day and night had passed, he shook his robes and rose, saying, "Does my master intend to deceive me?
He entered again, and as before, he tried to pry it open. Tōng simply held it up with his palms, turning it over and showing it to him from all sides.
Qi did not understand and finally turned away. He traveled extensively to consult various masters of learning, but found no realization anywhere. Then he heard of Wú...
Master Jiwu resided at Donglin in Puzhou. At Donglin, the Zen tradition was such that anyone who arrived with their meditation pack (*yebao*) was accepted immediately.

Qianqi asked, "What have you attained? He replied, "Originally, there is nothing lost; what is there to attain? Qianqi said, "I am here to study..."
"What can that which is brought forth in the future do? He replied, "Not a single dharma exists; from where could learning come?

[The Master] asked, "Have you fallen into emptiness? He replied, "I am not even 'I'; who falls and into what emptiness? [The Master] asked, "Ultimately, how is it? Wuqi said, "The water is shallow and the stones appear;

"Regarding his supernatural powers, they were like those of the old Master Zhaozhou’s 'Mu' (No) kōan—how could one ever resolve them? Qiji was about to offer a reply when Master Wugong repeatedly rebuked him and sent him away.
Deeply ashamed, Qiji did not dare look up for several days. Suddenly, hearing the signal board strike, he attained a sudden, expansive realization that swept away all lingering attachments.
He hurriedly donned his robes and offered his prostrations of gratitude; Master Wugong approved him and subsequently entrusted him with the lineage of Duanqiao.

When Qi traveled to transform others through his teachings, the lineage of the "Broken Bridge" was already in decline. By the time Master Wu took up the mantle, only seven people had received the Dharma.
Qi entered the world of teaching last of all; he first presided over Tiantzhu, then moved to Mount Xuan, and later, after leaving Touzi, became the abbot of T'ien-ch'eng Temple in Chengdu.
His descendants flourished, greatly revitalizing the tradition, and it was through him that the Dharma was truly propagated.
Furthermore, among the sixteen attendants was one named Zu Jie, who was the youngest in age and styled Guian.
He served Qi with great diligence; the monastic community respected his strictness and admired his wisdom.

Once, when a young novice from the distant region of Xianglin came forward to offer tea, Qi drank it and then looked at the boy and said, "Do people call you 'the simpleton'? Jie replied, "He is also out of step."
At that moment, Qiji asked, "How do you see this? Jie called for a cup to be brought; as the lad approached, Qiji said, "If you can speak, I shall return it to you.
There was no reply. Qiji then looked at Jie, who said, "This very state beyond words is not separated by even a hair's breadth."
Qiji said, "For what reason did he say nothing? Jie called to the attendant, "Why do you not offer a greeting? The attendant offered a greeting. Qiji passed the cup to him;
the attendant received it and departed with the words, "Take care. Jie asked, "Can one say that he was speechless? Qiji replied, "Yes."
"Just like this boy, being so direct and decisive—is this caused by ignorance (*avidyā*), or is it because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is thus?
He replied, "If one is deluded, there is ignorance accumulated over kalpas; if one realizes it, it is the original Buddha-nature.

Qī said, "In that case, does he know it exists, or does he not know it exists? He replied, "If he knew it existed, it would not serve as a cause for delusion. If he did not know it existed, on the contrary—"

[The Master] interrupted him. Qí said, "Do you have knowledge, or not? Zǔjiè replied, "I do not know that there is [knowledge]. Qí said, "If you do not know that there is, how can you know the School (the Dharma-lineage)?
Zǔjiè said, "If a sage were to have knowledge, he would be the same as an ordinary person; if an ordinary person were to have knowledge, he would be the same as a sage.
Qí said, "When you look at this old monk, is it knowing or not? Zǔjiè said, "It is the great function at the moment of encounter; whenever it is raised..."
Quanzhen said, "What is there to say about 'knowing existence' or 'not knowing existence'? Take me, for instance:
as I now speak a word or remain silent, analyzing right from wrong and distinguishing names and forms—is my perception the same as or different from that of the boy just now?"
Jie said, "The eye that discerns phenomena and the wondrous function of non-action—though their essential nature is the same, their spheres of application are vastly different.
[The other] asked, "Since you speak of 'discerning phenomena,' how can there be 'non-action'? Jie replied, "Wisdom-illumination is not consciousness; wondrous function is not existence.

Since the function is not a function, the action is also not an action. Although there is discrimination, in reality there is no capacity for discrimination. [The other] said, "Now, facing the myriad..."
"The Dharma and its objective characteristics are distinct and diverse; how could one fail to understand each of them clearly through discernment?
Jie said, "Does the teaching not say: 'When I press my finger, the Sea-Seal manifests light; it is known with perfect clarity, not arising from mental thought'?
Qi said, "Excellent! This may truly be called the king of geese choosing the milk. Not long after, Jie was stricken by illness. Qi went down to visit him and encountered Xinxang.
Xuanze was seated at his side. Qiji asked him, “What is the mind? Xuanze replied, “When the mouth opens, there is no room for sentiment.
Qiji said, “Not yet. Xuanze looked at Xin and said, “Why do you not prostrate? Xin then said, “I take my leave. Xuanze remarked, “You have presented yourself.
Qiji asked, “Since you are thus, can you still produce a verse that reveals the essence? Xuanze replied, “The Heart-Seal of the Patriarchs—how could it be described?”
The Transmission records: "There is a statement that is clear and distinct; it does not reside in words, but must be personally realized before the pivot [of the teacher's mind].

One day, when Jie was on the verge of death and making moaning sounds, Qiji asked him, "Does the phrase upon which you relied during your daily practice still serve you at this moment? He replied, "It serves."
[The Master] said, "Since you have attained mastery, why do you cry out in pain? He replied, "When it hurts, one cries; when it itches, one laughs.
Qī asked, "As for this one who cries and laughs, who is he? He replied, "The four elements are without self; even the one who cries is not real.
Within the essence of stillness, there is truly no experiencer. Qī asked, "Where is the host right now? He replied, "The autumn wind does not [blow]."
[The Master] fanned [him]. Fragrance wafted from the cassia blossoms. Qiji said, "If that is so, then the entire world is free from concealment.

[Changqing] replied, "Throughout vast kalpas there has been no separation; how could there be any interval now? [Daokai] asked, "Are you not ill?

The Master went directly to Mount Wutai, where he dwelt at Bimora Cliff for thirteen years. During this time, Tang Gong Hezheng, the Grand Music Master, came to the mountain to inquire about the Way.

Upon meeting the Master, Shan felt as if they had been bound by a long-standing karmic affinity. He proposed that the Master return south with him, but the Master consented on the condition that the stupa for Layman Yue’an had not yet been erected.
When they reached Jingxi, Shan urged the Master to accept an invitation from Longchi. Longchi was formerly the site of Chan Master Yiyuan’s monastery;

The Great Master’s style was one of vast wisdom. He had several disciples, yet when he faced them, it was as if ten thousand fingers were pointed at him.

Thereupon, all the aspirants gathered; through his striking with the whisk and fly-whisk, many emerged with brilliant insight and departed. After serving for barely six years, he retired from his duties and traveled again to the Capital of Yan (Beijing), residing at Puzhao Temple.

He showed [the whisk] to the various officials, saying, "At that time, did Confucius still know there was this? They all replied, "We do not know.

His revelations were mostly of this kind; thus, the Way of Xiaran flourished once more in Yan and Zhao. Although the conditions of the north and south differed, [the influence spread].
Scholars who braved both cold and heat stood in an unbroken line at his feet; those surrounding him were all men of great capacity.

Yuechuan sided with Qingliang, asserting that Sengzhao’s *Wubhiquanlun* (Treatise on the Non-Transmigration of Things) was incorrect; at that time, no one in the world could withstand his arguments.

Throughout his life, he was as if hungry and thirsty, regarding the fundamental tenets of the school as his own sole concern.
Thus, throughout the lifetime of Master Ren, there was not a single day that he did not ascend the hall or enter the inner chamber. He often used the lines, "The gate before my door is deserted;

When asked about the statement, "Prajñā is without cognition, yet there is nothing it does not know," few among the students were able to grasp its essential point. The Master said, "In these times, many people can speak of it."

He was a man who greatly revitalized the lineage of the Hutuo River. In the year he entered parinirvāṇa, he was sixty-six years of age.

Yet the father and son, Xiangyan and his disciple, have caused the Dharma-thunder to shake the earth, striking at the very head of this severe and cold era.
Below, he dispels the ignorance of the myriad species; above, he rectifies the succession of a thousand years. How magnificent and auspicious!

At the age of twenty-nine, he finally left home and went to visit the Chan master Miaozhen at the foot of Mount Qinwang. There, Miaozhen raised an ancient koan to challenge him.
The Master studied this repeatedly, for seven days without knowing sleep or food. Suddenly, he collapsed against a rock;

When one is fast asleep and when one is dead and cremated, the mind and its nature do not meet—teeth cannot clench them together. One must seek the Great Function within this very state before it can be attained.

"The wild foxes of recent times all speak of 'mind-nature Chan,' yet they do not know whether their surname is Zhang or Li. Please, grant me some instruction."
The Master offered a turning phrase on their behalf, hoping that the patch-robed monks of the world would cast off their stench. The Master replied:

Second, regarding the ninety-six kinds of *yuanxiang* (perfect circles) of Muzhou Daoyi and Yangshan Huiji: they encompass six meanings; in which one meaning are they all subsumed? Third, an ancient said: [text continues].

"Then the responsibility for this omission of the records falls upon me.

Postscript to the *Biographies of the Jewel-like Monks of the Southern Song, Yuan, and Ming*:
The Patriarchs said: "Buddha" refers to the purity of the mind; "Dharma" refers to the luminosity of the mind; "Path" refers to being without [obstruction] everywhere.
The obstructing, the pure, and the light are three yet one; all are empty and lack substantial existence. How profound these words are!

Therefore, those who enter the patriarch’s chamber and ascend the patriarch’s seat penetrate to the very bottom of the abyss. They wield the great function of spiritual power, cutting down the forest of views and severing the net of heterodoxies.
Like dripping lion’s milk, like striking the master lute-string, they are such that neither sages nor ordinary beings can depict them, nor fathom their depth.

It is precisely for this reason. My teacher, Venerable Huanting Rong, with the intention of inheriting the past and initiating the future, produced a transcribed copy in one volume and presented it to Lei, saying:
"This is what I have collected over twenty years while traveling between Jiang and Hu after leaving Mount Konglu.
It is the authentic record of the great capacity and great function of the various venerable masters of the Southern Song, Yuan, and Ming dynasties. You should strive to uphold it."
Lei withdrew and treasured these words, reading them through until he had full insight.

He observed that our Master, for the sake of the Way and the Dharma, was like a skilled craftsman who exerted great effort, tracing his lineage back through twenty generations to the Patriarch Xuedou Lǒng, and further to the various schools of Dahui and Dongshan, totaling fifty-three masters.

Their sublime songs and excellent counsels were passed down from master to master as they harmonized with the Way. The temporal teachings of this era possess both the eyes and the essence in their entirety.
How magnificent is this literature! It is truly as the saying goes: when a single moon reflects upon a river, the moons in a thousand rivers all shine together;

when one Buddha appears in the world, the Buddhas of the three periods of time are simultaneously revealed. This is surely not false. Some may say: "This lineage begins from below the Three Buddhas, starting with Fodeng Zhenji."
Why did it cease with the generations of the patriarchs such as Boshan, Yunmen, and Tiantong?
Furthermore, in this present age, those who extend compassion and wield the fly-whisk abound throughout China; could it be that they have ceased because right and wrong have not yet been settled?

I replied: "No, no. During the Shunzhi and Kangxi reigns, there were indeed many venerable elders who, whether teaching in accordance with the times or transforming through adversity, achieved the correspondence of practice and realization.
For the most part, they were memorialized by our late teacher, the Elder Hongjue Muan, whose stele inscriptions and biographies detail his life most thoroughly;
these have already circulated throughout the land and are celebrated as imperishable. As for the present day..."
This is the public consensus of the world. With the discerning eye of our Master, he has sifted and evaluated the five schools without erring by even a hair’s breadth;
even Dahui and Zhongfeng could not surpass him. How could I, a mere youth, dare to add further redundant words like a snake’s foot?

Nevertheless, disregarding my own ignorance and folly, I have accepted my Master’s command to supplement and collect the great figures from within the five hundred years of the Dongshan and Linji schools.
Regarding those who propagated the Dharma-transformation, there were forty-one individuals who participated in the compilation by my teacher; together they finalized fifteen volumes.
These were entrusted to the Duke of Kuaiji, Dalong, who collated them into a collection to provide for future worthies and sages. As the Sutra says:

Among all forms of offering, the Dharma-offering is supreme. By causing this mind-dharma of the separate transmission outside the teachings to be widely propagated and disseminated, the principle of great capacity and great function throughout ten generations, past and present, will blaze forth without interruption.
Written on the day of the Buddha’s Enlightenment in the Jiachen year of the Kangxi era by the disciple Xing Lei.
